# M3.4 editorial corrections

Every Game overview changed in Milestone 3.4: **671** of 773. Each entry gives the text before and after, the error classification, the NES-specific evidence and the verification result. No text was written or checked by a model; independent auditors checked each record against the original NES manual page images and NES-specific sources, and every change was reviewed against deterministic text rules and the proper-name evidence check. Source references are for editorial review only; the product shows no sources.

**Classification:**
- **substantive:** a rule, mechanic, item effect, structure, count, player mode, control, invented detail or other-version detail was wrong.
- **name only:** only a name differed from the release's own US manual or on-screen text.
- **unsupported detail generalized:** nothing contradicted, but specific claims had no NES-specific support.
- **rewrite:** the text was substantially about another version or another game and was rebuilt from NES evidence.

## 10-Yard Fight (`8e844d77da01f86a`)

- **Classification:** rewrite; error types: other-version detail, wrong rule, unsupported specific, wrong name
- **Queue:** main (m32-audit-medium-risk)
- **Manual:** 10-Yard Fight (USA, Europe); page images inspected: yes (p02, p03, p04, p05)
- **Verification:** level D; remaining uncertainty: Exact condition for advancing from one level to the next in the NES version is not stated in the manual, so the text only says play starts at high school level and moves up.

**Before:**

> American football action unfolds on vertically scrolling fields displayed from a top-down perspective. Participating teams compete across accelerated matches without choosing specific offensive or defensive formations before snaps.
>
> On offense, the quarterback receives the ball and can execute an option run, pitch out to a running back, or pass downfield to a distant receiver. Field goal attempts and punts are also options, while returning a kickoff for a touchdown awards twenty thousand points. When defending, the player steers one chosen teammate while the computer directs remaining defenders. Victories across both halves move competitors forward through high school, college, professional, playoff, and Super Bowl tiers.

**After:**

> American football action unfolds on vertically scrolling fields displayed from a top-down perspective, with the offense always moving up the screen. A 1 Player Game sets the player against the computer, and a 2 Player Game sets two players against each other.
>
> On offense, the ball carrier can run, throw a side pass to the left or right lateral receiver, or throw a forward pass to the forward receiver. Kicks are aimed with an arrow, and a field goal can be attempted when the goal post is in view at the snap. Gaining ten yards in four downs earns a new set of downs. When defending, the player chooses which of two defenders to control and can make flying tackles. Play starts at the high school level and moves up through college, pro, and playoff levels to the Super Bowl level; the 1 Player Game also allows any of these five levels to be chosen.

**What was wrong and why it changed:** Removed arcade-derived kickoff score bonus, formation claim and option-run/running-back terms; rewrote offense, defense and level progression from the NES manual; added player modes.

**Contradicted by NES evidence:**

- Quarterback can run (option run), pitch out to a running back, or pass downfield — Manual: the ball carrier runs, throws side passes to the left or right lateral pass receiver (B + direction) or a forward pass to the forward receiver (A). No 'option run' or 'running back' terms. Reworded. (manual p04-p05)

**Other sources checked:** https://tasvideos.org/Forum/Topics/19940 (Japanese release; not used for final text)

## 1942 (`e868400409c70876`)

- **Classification:** substantive; error types: unsupported specific, wrong control, other-version detail
- **Queue:** recheck (m32-audit-low-risk)
- **Manual:** 1942 (Japan, USA); page images inspected: yes (p01, p04, p05, p06, p07)
- **Verification:** level C; remaining uncertainty: Midair collision costing a life is corroborated only by one NES review ('avoiding collisions and enemy fire'), not the manual. 'Pacific Theater' rests on Tokyo objective plus HG101's US-to-Japan route description.

**Before:**

> Piloting a Lockheed P-38 Lightning aircraft known as the Super Ace, the player shoots down opposing planes across vertically scrolling air battles. The game takes place in the Pacific Theater of World War II, tasking the pilot with reaching Tokyo to destroy an entire enemy air fleet. A single incoming projectile or midair collision destroys the craft and costs one life.
>
> Evasive maneuvers include a designated roll button, which lets the aircraft temporarily loop out of harm's way to avoid hazards. Players collect various power-ups during flight, such as an upgrade providing two smaller escort fighters in a wingman formation. Two players are supported.

**After:**

> Piloting a fighter plane known as the Super Ace, the player shoots down opposing planes across vertically scrolling air battles. The game takes place in the Pacific Theater of World War II, tasking the pilot with reaching Tokyo to destroy the remaining enemy aircraft. A single incoming projectile or midair collision destroys the craft and costs one life.
>
> Evasive maneuvers include a designated loop button, which lets the aircraft temporarily loop out of harm's way to avoid hazards. Players collect various power-ups during flight, such as an upgrade providing two smaller escort fighters in a wingman formation. Two players are supported in alternating turns.

**What was wrong and why it changed:** Generalized 'Lockheed P-38 Lightning aircraft' to 'fighter plane' (no NES source names the type); replaced 'an entire enemy air fleet' with the manual's 'the remaining enemy aircraft'; 'roll button' to 'loop button' (manual: Loop the Loop); added 'in alternating turns'.

**Contradicted by NES evidence:**

- Objective: reach Tokyo to destroy an entire enemy air fleet — Manual: 'To win you must reach Tokyo and destroy the remaining enemy aircraft.' 'Entire enemy air fleet' is the encyclopedia wording; replaced with the manual's. (manual p05)
- A designated roll button lets the plane loop out of harm's way — Button A does a 'Loop the Loop' to avoid attacking enemies; it is a loop, not a roll. Fixed the word. (manual p05, p06)

**Other sources checked:** https://videogamecritic.com/nesaa.htm?e=13064; https://www.hardcoregaming101.net/1942-2/; https://www.cubed3.com/games/reviews/nes/1942

## 1943 - The Battle of Midway (`9f54aafa367247b9`)

- **Classification:** substantive; error types: other-version detail, wrong name, unsupported specific
- **Queue:** escalation (m32-audit-corrected)
- **Manual:** 1943 - The Battle of Midway (USA); page images inspected: yes (p03, p04, p05, p06)
- **Verification:** level D; remaining uncertainty: Energy draining with time and special attacks costing energy rest on an NES Game Genie code list (almarsguides), not the manual. Earlier M3.2 fix (no piercing lasers) confirmed by manual p06.

**Before:**

> Destroying the opposing fleet across the Pacific theater of World War II forms the core objective of the mission. Piloting a P-38 Lightning aircraft, the player targets hostile air and sea forces following an assault on an American carrier. Survival depends on managing a depleting fuel meter that serves as health, which empties constantly over time unless replenished.
>
> Controlling the fighter in vertical flight, the pilot fires standard guns, executes aerial loop maneuvers, and can trigger special lightning attacks by spending fuel. Eliminating entire squadrons of red aircraft yields item drops that can be shot to cycle between health boosts and alternate weapons, including shotguns, three-way shots, burst fire, and heavy shells.

**After:**

> Destroying the enemy fleet in a 1943 battle off the Midway Islands forms the core objective of the mission. Piloting a P-38, the player targets hostile air and sea forces. With only one life, survival depends on an energy meter that serves as health, which empties slowly over time and from enemy attacks unless replenished.
>
> Controlling the fighter in vertical flight, the pilot fires standard guns, executes defensive loop maneuvers, and can trigger the special attacks Lightning, Cyclone and Tsunami by spending energy. Shooting red planes yields POW items that can be shot to receive energy or alternate weapons, including the Shot Gun, 3-Way Shot, Auto and Super Shell. Before play, points are distributed among offensive power, defensive power, energy level, special weapons and special weapons time limit, and a password lets play resume later.

**What was wrong and why it changed:** Removed the arcade carrier-assault story and 'Pacific theater' framing in favor of the NES story (fleet battle off Midway); 'P-38 Lightning' -> 'P-38'; 'fuel meter' -> energy meter with one life; named the three special attacks; 'entire squadrons of red aircraft' -> 'red planes'; weapons given their manual names; added the NES power-up point distribution and password.

**Contradicted by NES evidence:**

- Eliminating entire squadrons of red aircraft yields item drops — Manual: 'Shoot red planes to receive POW.' No squadron requirement stated. (manual p06 (p.10))

**Other sources checked:** https://almarsguides.com/retro/walkthroughs/nes/games/1943thebattleofmidway/gamegenie/energyinvincibilitycodes/; https://www.hardcoregaming101.net/1943-the-battle-of-midway/

## 3-D WorldRunner (`c457644ccfb93f89`)

- **Classification:** substantive; error types: wrong name, invented detail, unsupported specific
- **Queue:** main (nes-native-untouched)
- **Manual:** 3-D WorldRunner (USA); page images inspected: yes (p02, p03, p04, p07)
- **Verification:** level D; remaining uncertainty: 'Forward-scrolling third-person' rests on the control description rather than an explicit manual statement.

**Before:**

> Defeating the evil leader Grax and clearing planets of invading alien creatures serves as the core mission in this forward-scrolling third-person adventure. Players control Jack the WorldRunner, who must run, jump across bottomless canyons, and bypass or blast hostile beings like blob monsters. Progress spans eight separate worlds divided into distinct quadrants, each monitored by a running timer on the bottom status bar.
>
> Because forward movement is continuous, players can adjust Jack's running pace and shift horizontally across the path. Pillar-like structures along the route contain helpful upgrades, granting laser missiles and temporary invincibility, alongside score-raising bonus stars. Reaching the end of a world's final quadrant triggers a battle against a large serpentine creature, allowing full multidirectional movement to conquer the threat before proceeding.

**After:**

> Stopping the invasion of Solar System #517 by Grax and his gang of Alien Serpentbeasts serves as the core mission in this forward-scrolling third-person adventure. The hero must run, jump across bottomless canyons, and avoid or shoot attacking enemies such as the Menacing Meanies. Progress spans eight separate worlds divided into quadrants, and a timer runs while the player advances.
>
> Because forward movement is continuous, players can speed up, slow down, and move left and right across the path. Columns along the route hold items, most of them helpful, granting laser missiles and temporary invincibility, alongside score-raising Super Stars; some release poisonous Magic Mushrooms instead. A Serpentbeast guards the end of every world and takes several hits to defeat, and the most dangerous of Grax's brothers waits in the eighth world. Pressing SELECT switches the display to a 3-D mode for use with 3-D glasses.

**What was wrong and why it changed:** Removed the unconfirmed name Jack, 'blob monsters', the status-bar timer placement and the boss-fight movement claim; used manual names; added the 3-D mode.

**Contradicted by NES evidence:**

- Running timer on the bottom status bar — Bottom display lists score, world number, world quadrant, bonus stars, lives left; a timer exists (Cosmic Clock resets it) but its position is not stated. Reworded. (manual p03 (image))

## 720 Degrees (`df696ce2af90b18c`)

- **Classification:** substantive; error types: wrong rule
- **Queue:** escalation (m32-audit-low-risk)
- **Manual:** 720 Degrees (USA); page images inspected: yes (p02, p03, p05)
- **Verification:** level D; remaining uncertainty: Player count rests on the arcade-history NES listing and the absence of any multiplayer mode in the manual.

**Before:**

> Four distinct competitive events are accessed through a central hub neighborhood: the ramp, downhill, slalom, and jump. The single-player game puts the player in control of a skateboarder navigating the streets, using everyday features as ramps to perform aerial maneuvers and earn points.
>
> Points generate tickets, which grant entry into the skate parks. While roaming the streets, a timer steadily counts down, warning of a pursuing swarm of killer bees that ends the session if the skater is caught. Successfully reaching an event before the timer expires allows the skater to compete for points, cash, and medals. The accumulated money pays for gear upgrades that enhance skating performance across future challenges.

**After:**

> Four distinct competitive events are accessed through a central hub neighborhood: the ramp, downhill, slalom, and jump. The single-player game puts the player in control of a skateboarder navigating the streets, using everyday features as ramps to perform aerial maneuvers and earn points.
>
> Points generate additional tickets, which grant entry into the skate parks. While roaming the streets, a timer steadily counts down, warning of a pursuing swarm of killer bees that stops the skater if caught. Successfully reaching an event before the timer expires allows the skater to compete for points, cash, and medals. The accumulated money pays for gear upgrades that enhance skating performance across future challenges.

**What was wrong and why it changed:** 'Points generate tickets' -> 'additional tickets' (the player starts with three); bees 'end the session' -> 'stops the skater' (three lives).

**Contradicted by NES evidence:**

- Bees end the session if the skater is caught — Bees 'stop you in your tracks'; the player has three lives, so being caught does not end the whole game. Reworded. (manual p05, ocr TIME BAR)

**Other sources checked:** https://www.arcade-history.com/game/54861/ (720 Model NES-72-USA, players: 1, via search result)

## 8 Eyes (`3493f7621d964af7`)

- **Classification:** substantive; error types: wrong rule
- **Queue:** escalation (nes-native-untouched)
- **Manual:** 8 Eyes (USA); page images inspected: yes (p03, p04, p05, p07, p09, p19, p20)
- **Verification:** level D; remaining uncertainty: Castle of Ruth being Level 8 is inferred from the manual's structure rather than stated in one sentence.

**Before:**

> Set across castles located in different parts of the world, 8 Eyes tasks the player with clearing eight levels ruled by dukes to recover the 8 Eyes jewels. The first seven castles may be tackled in any sequence. Finishing a level awards Orin a new sword, and every castle boss has a vulnerability to a specific blade. Hidden clues scattered through the stages indicate the intended progression. Once those seven areas are beaten, the Castle of Ruth unlocks as the final stage, leading to the return of the recovered jewels to the Altar of Peace in a specific sequence.
>
> Controlling both Orin and Cutrus simultaneously is required in single-player mode, with limited commands available for the companion. Alternatively, two participants can join in a cooperative mode where one person directs Orin and the second operates Cutrus.

**After:**

> Set across castles located in different parts of the world, 8 Eyes tasks the player with clearing eight levels ruled by dukes to recover the 8 Eyes jewels. The player picks which of the first seven castles to enter, but they must be cleared in a certain order. Finishing a level awards Orin a new sword, and every castle boss has a vulnerability to a specific blade. Seven scrolls hidden in those stages hold hints for placing the jewels. Once those seven areas are beaten, the Castle of Ruth unlocks as the final stage, leading to the return of the recovered jewels to the Altar of Peace in a specific sequence.
>
> Controlling both Orin and Cutrus simultaneously is required in single-player mode, with limited commands available for the companion. Alternatively, two participants can join in a cooperative mode where one person directs Orin and the second operates Cutrus.

**What was wrong and why it changed:** 'May be tackled in any sequence' -> chosen freely but must be cleared in a certain order; hidden clues indicate jewel placement (seven scrolls), not level progression. Earlier 'Castle of Ruth' fix confirmed.

**Contradicted by NES evidence:**

- The first seven castles may be tackled in any sequence — 'The levels must be played in a certain order because each Boss Enemy is only vulnerable to one sword.' The player selects which of the first seven to begin with (ocr 'SELECTING A LEVEL'), but finding the correct order is the first goal. (manual p07 (image))
- Hidden clues indicate the intended progression — The seven scrolls of jewel placement contain hints for placing the eight jewels into the altar, not for the level order. (manual p07 (image))

## Abadox - The Deadly Inner War (`c4d4ff0bd283656c`)

- **Classification:** substantive; error types: wrong rule, invented detail, other-version detail
- **Queue:** main (nes-native-untouched)
- **Manual:** Abadox - The Deadly Inner War (USA); page images inspected: yes (p06, p07)
- **Verification:** level D; remaining uncertainty: Weapons-chart names were read from clear OCR rather than the chart image.

**Before:**

> Set in the year 5012, the narrative follows Second Lieutenant Nazal on a mission to fly inside Parasitis, a colossal alien organism that consumed the planet Abadox and engulfed a hospital vessel carrying Princess Maria. Controlling the surviving military craft, the player journeys through the interior of the beast to rescue the captive princess before the monster consumes more worlds.
>
> Gameplay alternates between horizontal side-scrolling stages and vertical levels that scroll downward in stages two, four, and six. The player shoots enemies resembling anatomical organs, including brains and eyes, while collecting power-ups such as speed enhancements, shields, homing missiles, and offensive upgrades like lasers, spread fire, and three-way guns. A single enemy projectile destroys the ship, stripping away collected upgrades and returning the player to the previous checkpoint. The final area requires escaping through the creature's rectal cavity before the alien implodes.

**After:**

> Set in the year 5012, the narrative follows Second Lieutenant Nazal, the lone survivor of the World Alive Force, on a mission inside Parasitis, a formless creature that engulfed the planet Abadox and swallowed a hospital ship carrying Princess Maria. Leaving his spacecraft and flying with a power pack, Nazal battles through the interior of the creature to destroy its Core and rescue the captive princess.
>
> Gameplay alternates between horizontal side-scrolling stages and vertical levels that scroll downward in stages two, four, and six. The player shoots creatures such as eyeballs, worms, and skeleton fish, and must destroy Guardian monsters to advance. Power capsules provide upgrades such as a speed boost, orbiting barrier shields, layers of armor, guided missiles, a Laser Gun, and the Tresbeam and Star Beam, which fire in three and five directions. The player starts with three lives, and continuing restarts the current stage with only basic fire power.

**What was wrong and why it changed:** Fixed the player as a soldier with a power pack, replaced unsupported one-hit/checkpoint and escape-ending claims with the manual's objective, lives and continue rules, and used manual enemy and weapon names.

**Contradicted by NES evidence:**

- The player controls the surviving military craft — Nazal is 'the lone survivor of the Force'; he jettisons from his spacecraft and ignites his power pack. Reworded. (manual OCR introduction)
- Final area requires escaping through the creature's rectal cavity before it implodes — Manual: 'Enter the black inner chamber and destroy The Core! Find Princess Maria and rescue her!' Removed. (manual p07 (image))

## Action 52 (`96861646aadc9534`)

- **Classification:** unsupported detail generalized; error types: wrong name, unsupported specific
- **Queue:** main (m32-audit-medium-risk)
- **Manual:** Action 52 (USA) (Unl); page images inspected: yes (p01, p27, p28)
- **Verification:** level D; remaining uncertainty: Game premises come from the manual's one-line descriptions; actual gameplay of individual games was not verified.

**Before:**

> Divided into fifty-two distinct games, this compilation offers a collection across multiple genres for the system. Most of the included selections function as scrolling shooters or platformers.
>
> Among the various titles featured in the collection is The Cheetahmen. Players navigate through these dozens of different individual entries provided on a single cartridge.

**After:**

> Fifty-two separate games are collected on this single cartridge. Each comes with a short premise: in Fire Breathers the player fights dragon riders in the midnight skies, Jupiter Scope uses the Star-Zap laser against a growing meteor shower, Ninja Assault sets the player against the Zin-Zan evil ninja tribes, and in Robbie and the Robots Robbie leads his good robots against his evil brother Brainy.
>
> The final entry, The Action Gamemaster, follows a boy who is dragged into the television while playing a video game, becomes one of three Cheetah Men, and must fight off the bad guys from the previous 51 games.

**What was wrong and why it changed:** Replaced the unsupported genre breakdown and the title 'The Cheetahmen' with the manual's game 52 title and premise, and added premises of several listed games.

**Contradicted by NES evidence:**

- A title called The Cheetahmen is included — Game 52 is titled 'The "Action Gamemaster"', in which a boy becomes one of three 'Cheetah Men'. Corrected name. (manual p28 (image))

## Addams Family, The (`005c48a5984e3b75`)

- **Classification:** rewrite; error types: other-version detail, wrong name, invented detail, wrong item effect
- **Queue:** main (m32-audit-medium-risk)
- **Manual:** Addams Family, The (USA); page images inspected: yes (p03, p05, p06)
- **Verification:** level D; remaining uncertainty: Room names, Thing, Lurch, swimming and gondola were read from clean OCR rather than page images.

**Before:**

> The Addams Family features side-scrolling platform action. Controlling Gomez Addams, the player works to rescue abducted relatives from Abigail Craven, Tully Alford, and the Judge. Navigating the mansion interior and exterior grounds occurs non-linearly, with the central Hall of Stairs providing access to various areas such as the kitchen, the portrait gallery, and the games room. Gomez must run, jump, and duck past environmental hazards like swinging pendulums and lakes of fire, while defeating ghosts, mutants, and other creatures by stomping on them.
>
> Progress requires solving situational puzzles and defeating bosses that guard captive family members, such as a large bird in the garden. Gomez can acquire power-ups including speed-boosting shoes, a sword, a ball-striking golf club, and a flying hat. To rescue Morticia, the player must collect one million dollars found throughout the rooms and secret caches before facing the Judge in the final boss battle.

**After:**

> The Addams Family features side-scrolling platform action. The family has been evicted, and its members have gone to the house to reason with the family attorney, Tully Alford; when Gomez Addams arrives, Morticia, Lurch, Granny, Pugsley, and Wednesday are missing. Controlling Gomez, the player searches the house and its grounds, starting in the Garden at the base of the Big Tree and moving through areas such as the Crypt, the Kitchen, the Attic, and the Rooftop.
>
> Gomez jumps, swims in the Pond, and paddles a gondola on the Secret River, and he defeats skulls, ghosts, and other enemies by jumping on them. Progress requires finding keys and objects and solving puzzles, such as finding the parts of a potion needed to shrink Pugsley. Once rescued, Thing can shield Gomez from enemies three times, and manuscripts from the library let Lurch play helpful music. To free Morticia, every family member must be rescued and one million dollars collected.

**What was wrong and why it changed:** Bounded rewrite from the NES manual: removed Abigail Craven, the Judge, Hall of Stairs, bird boss and the shoes/sword/golf club/hat power-ups; added NES story, locations, Thing, Lurch, swimming and gondola.

**Contradicted by NES evidence:**

- Gomez rescues relatives abducted by Abigail Craven, Tully Alford and the Judge — NES manual: family evicted; family attorney Tully Alford is after the fortune; Abigail Craven and the Judge not mentioned. Other-version detail. (manual OCR story)
- Hall of Stairs hub with kitchen, portrait gallery, games room — NES rooms include Garden, Crypt, House, Kitchen, Freezer, Furnace, Dining Room, Conservatory, Gallery, Library, Attic, Rooftop; no Hall of Stairs or games room. (manual OCR Game Scenes)
- Power-ups: shoes, sword, golf club, flying hat — Not in NES manual; NES helpers are Thing (shield three times) and Lurch's music. Other-version detail. (manual OCR)
- Final boss battle against the Judge — No Judge in NES manual. (manual OCR)

## Advanced Dungeons & Dragons - DragonStrike (`22e92af92aed2d8d`)

- **Classification:** rewrite; error types: other-version detail, wrong rule, wrong player mode, invented detail
- **Queue:** main (nes-native-untouched)
- **Manual:** Advanced Dungeons & Dragons - DragonStrike (USA); page images inspected: yes (p04, p06)
- **Verification:** level D; remaining uncertainty: Whether the 2 player game is cooperative or alternating is not stated in the manual; the text does not specify.

**Before:**

> Completing aerial combat missions during the War of the Lance is the main goal in this high-fantasy flight simulator. Set in the realm of Krynn, the narrative places the player in control of a riderless dragon battling evil forces. Missions involve navigating hostile skies while seeking to unlock different endings.
>
> Players engage various airborne threats, including enemy dragons with or without riders, manticores, wyverns, gas spores, and sivak draconians. Surface hazards also exist, as ground archers target the dragon if it flies too low. Combat options include a recharging magical breath attack, as well as claws and bite attacks unleashed by sweeping closely above foes. Finishing missions rewards players with extra hit points and access to more powerful dragon choices, specifically bronze, silver, or gold dragons, which adjusts subsequent assignments and the story finale.

**After:**

> Freeing the continent of Ansalon from the dragonarmies is the goal in this shooting game, in which the player guides one of the good dragons through a series of missions toward a final battle at Neraka. A 2 player game is also available. At the start, the player chooses a Bronze, Silver, or Gold dragon, each with its own speed, armor, health, and pair of breath weapons: lightning and repulsion gas, cone of cold and paralyzing gas, or cone of fire and chlorine gas. The chosen game level sets the dragon's starting health and mission.
>
> During a mission, the dragon dives and climbs to avoid obstacles such as trees, walls, and buildings, and attacks enemy forces with its breath weapons. Breath weapons weaken as the dragon loses health. Destroyed enemy dragons and army bases sometimes leave items that raise speed, armor, or health or give temporary protection. A password is shown after each completed mission.

**What was wrong and why it changed:** Bounded rewrite: the text described the computer flight-sim version; replaced with the NES shooting game's dragon choice, breath weapons, game levels, items, passwords and 1-2 player option.

**Contradicted by NES evidence:**

- High-fantasy flight simulator — 'DragonStrike is a shooting game.' Other-version detail. (manual p04 (image))
- Recharging breath attack plus claw and bite attacks — NES dragons have two breath weapons on A and B; no claw or bite attacks described. (manual OCR dragon pages)
- Finishing missions unlocks bronze, silver, or gold dragons — Bronze, Silver and Gold dragons are chosen at the start of the game. (manual OCR 'Choose a dragon')

## Advanced Dungeons & Dragons - Heroes of the Lance (`df2609c80e818bb9`)

- **Classification:** unsupported detail generalized; error types: unsupported specific
- **Queue:** escalation (m32-audit-corrected)
- **Manual:** Advanced Dungeons & Dragons - Heroes of the Lance (USA); page images inspected: yes (p03, p04, p05, p06, p07)
- **Verification:** level D; remaining uncertainty: Minor nuance: Goldmoon and Raistlin can cast combat spells from the front rank without leading (manual p06), which the text's 'only party member that ... attacks' slightly simplifies.

**Before:**

> Retrieving the sacred Disks of Mishakal from the ruined city of Xak Tsaroth forms the ultimate goal, requiring a confrontation with the ancient dragon Khisanth. A single player leads an adventuring party through this fantasy setting within a side-scrolling action format.

> Retrieving the sacred Disks of Mishakal from the ruined city of Xak Tsaroth forms the ultimate goal, requiring a confrontation with the black dragon Khisanth. A single player leads an adventuring party through this fantasy setting within a side-scrolling action format.
>
> The lead character is the only party member that moves and attacks on screen, though fallen heroes leave their bodies behind. Rather than remaining passive reserves, all four front-rank companions can sustain damage from hostile strikes, and heroes can be swapped into the lead position via menu options. Individual adventurers utilize varied abilities based on role-playing statistics, ranging from close combat weaponry and ranged bows to defensive healing spells and offensive wizard magic.

**What was wrong and why it changed:** 'ancient dragon Khisanth' -> 'black dragon Khisanth' (manual wording). M3.2 corrections about the lead character and front-rank damage confirmed by manual p05 and p07.

**Contradicted by NES evidence:**

- Confrontation with the ancient dragon Khisanth — Manual calls Khisanth 'the black dragon' / 'the powerful black dragon'; 'ancient' is not in the NES manual. Changed to 'black dragon'. (manual p03, p04 (image))

## Advanced Dungeons & Dragons - Pool of Radiance (`38e5253131d26439`)

- **Classification:** substantive; error types: wrong count, wrong rule, unsupported specific
- **Queue:** escalation (m32-audit-low-risk)

**Before:**

> Set in the Forgotten Realms port city of Phlan, the story begins as the city council recruits adventurers to reclaim the surrounding ruins from invading monsters and an evil force. A single player assembles a party of up to six characters, selecting each member's race, class, gender, alignment, and attributes, or chooses an existing group.

A single player assembles a party of up to five characters, selecting each member's race, class, gender, alignment, and attributes, or uses ready-made characters, and can hire one non-player character.
>
> Gameplay involves moving from area to area to clear out hostile creatures and earn experience points. In town, characters trade gear, hire non-player characters, visit temples for healing, and accept commissions. Battles feature round-based tactical encounters in which more agile characters tend to act first, with commands including casting spells and bandaging dying comrades, culminating in an encounter with the evil leader.

**What was wrong and why it changed:** Party size corrected (five player-made or ready-made characters plus one hired NPC, not six created); 'consult non-player characters' -> 'hire non-player characters'; removed 'commands are executed immediately' (NES uses dexterity-ordered segments with spell delays); 'fallen' -> 'dying' comrades.

**Contradicted by NES evidence:**

- Party of up to six characters, each member's race, class, gender, alignment and attributes chosen — Up to five player characters plus one hired non-player character; 'Only 5 characters may join the party'. Only the five are created by the player. (manual p04, p05 (images))
- Round-based tactical battles where commands are executed immediately — Each character acts in a specific segment of the round, earlier with higher dexterity; spells may be delayed before going off. (manual p15 (image), ocr combat menu)

**Other sources checked:** https://flyingomelette.com/games/reviews/a/addpoolofradiance.html (NES review)

## Adventures in the Magic Kingdom (`185e4adb2cbcb71e`)

- **Classification:** substantive; error types: wrong name, invented detail, other-version detail
- **Queue:** recheck (nes-native-untouched)
- **Manual:** Adventures in the Magic Kingdom (USA); page images inspected: yes (p03, p04, p05, p06, p07, p08, p09)
- **Verification:** level D; remaining uncertainty: Manual spells the Autopia rival 'Peg leg Pete' (lowercase 'leg'); kept as printed. The attraction is headed 'The Haunted House' but called 'Haunted Mansion' elsewhere in the same manual.

**Before:**

> Finding six silver keys to open the Cinderella Castle gate allows the Disney parade to begin after Goofy leaves the golden key inside. Mickey Mouse enlists a custom-named protagonist to recover these keys by navigating a Disney park overworld map to select different attractions. Completing the mission requires conquering five ride-based levels and solving a trivia quest.
>
> Two top-down stages involve racing Panhandle Pete around obstacles in Autopia and directing a train along the correct tracks on Big Thunder Mountain Railroad. Side-scrolling gameplay appears in the Haunted Mansion, where the player throws candles at ghosts, and Pirates of the Caribbean, which tasks the player with rescuing six villagers. Space Mountain switches to a first-person perspective to pilot a spaceship, dodge asteroids, and shoot enemy craft. Children scattered throughout the park present the trivia questions about Disney films and characters to award another key.

**After:**

> Finding six silver keys to reach the Enchanted Castle allows the Disney parade to begin. Mickey Mouse enlists a custom-named protagonist to recover these keys by navigating a Disney park overworld map to select different attractions. Completing the mission requires conquering five ride-based levels and solving a trivia quest.
>
> Two top-down stages involve racing Peg leg Pete around obstacles in Autopia and directing a train along the correct tracks on Big Thunder Mountain. Side-scrolling gameplay appears in the Haunted Mansion, where the player throws candles at ghosts, and Pirates of the Caribbean, which tasks the player with rescuing six villagers. Space Mountain switches to a first-person perspective to pilot a spaceship by following navigation signals and reacting to incoming meteors. Friends of Mickey Mouse scattered throughout the park present the trivia questions about Disney characters and events to award another key.

**What was wrong and why it changed:** Cinderella Castle -> Enchanted Castle (manual name) and removed the unsupported Goofy/golden-key detail; Panhandle Pete -> Peg leg Pete; Space Mountain 'dodge asteroids, and shoot enemy craft' replaced with the manual's navigation-signal and meteor description; trivia askers 'Children' -> 'Friends of Mickey Mouse' and topics to 'Disney characters and events'.

**Contradicted by NES evidence:**

- The castle is Cinderella Castle — The US NES manual calls it the Enchanted Castle. (manual p04 (page 7), p05)
- Autopia race against Panhandle Pete — Manual: 'Peg leg Pete challenges you to a rough and ready auto race.' (manual p08 (page 15))
- Space Mountain: dodge asteroids and shoot enemy craft — Manual describes following navigation signals and pressing A or B when a meteor appears; no enemy craft. Replaced with the manual's description. (manual p09 (page 16))
- Children scattered through the park ask the trivia questions about Disney films and characters — Manual: 'several friends of Mickey Mouse' ask trivia questions 'about Disney characters and events'; a silver key is awarded for the final correct answer. (manual p06 (page 11))

**Other sources checked:** https://www.honestgamers.com/743/nes/adventures-in-the-magic-kingdom/review.html

Controlling Bayou Billy, the player navigates side-scrolling beat-em-up segments using punches, kicks, and jump kicks to defeat humans and animals like crocodiles or guard dogs. > Gameplay shifts styles during specific stages. First-person rail shooting segments allow the player to eliminate gunmen and bosses using a standard controller or an NES Zapper while collecting ammunition, health kits, and temporary power-ups. Earlier M3.3 fix (dynamite) confirmed correct.

**Contradicted by NES evidence:**

- Objective is rescuing a kidnapped fiancee from Godfather Gordon — Manual calls Annabelle 'your best girl' (girlfriend); Gordon holds her on his plantation. No fiancee in the US manual; StrategyWiki also says girlfriend. Godfather Gordon name supported (p09). (manual p03 (image))
- Player controls vigilante Billy West — US manual names the hero only 'Bayou Billy'/'Billy'; 'Billy West' and 'vigilante' do not appear in the manual. (manual p03 (image))
- Health-restoring drumsticks — Manual name is 'Raw Meat' (replenishes Life Line); renamed per naming rule. (manual p06 (image))
- Defensive body armor — Manual item is the 'Bullet Proof Vest', which partially eliminates damage; renamed. (manual p06 (image))

**What was wrong and why it changed:** Replaced the unsupported television-show framing with the manual intro wording; removed unsupported specifics (four Joust opponents, shifting platforms, opponent at top of screen, rapid pursuers, multi-screen wall, side-scrolling/overhead description, sprinting on conveyors) and restated each event from the manual; added the five-events-by-four-levels structure.

**Before:**

> Winning the game requires players to guide a chosen token across multiple board levels by solving picture puzzles. Participants select pieces shaped like high-heeled shoes, a bugle, an ice cream cone, or a teddy bear. While a picture slowly forms, a die counts down from six. The first person to buzz in freezes the timer and gets 25 seconds to spell out the answer. Submitting more than one error or running out of time locks that participant out, allowing rivals to attempt a guess. Entering a correct solution awards the puzzle color and advances the piece across the board.
>
> Collecting all four colors raises the token to the next tier. Up to four competitors take part, with players doubling up on two controllers if more than two humans compete. Boards feature three or four tiers based on difficulty, which also governs available hints. Later tiers introduce Feature Squares and Drop-Out Squares that drop tokens down.

**After:**

> Winning the game requires players to guide a token across multiple board levels by solving picture puzzles. Each participant is assigned a marker shaped like shoes, a trumpet, a teddy, or an ice cream. While a picture slowly forms, a die counts down from six. The first person to buzz in gets 25 seconds to spell out the answer. Submitting more than one error lets rivals attempt a guess before the die reaches zero. Entering a correct solution awards the puzzle color and advances the piece across the board.
>
> Collecting all four colors raises the token to the next tier. Up to four competitors take part, with players doubling up on two controllers if more than two humans compete. Higher boards and harder difficulty settings show fewer hint dots in each picture. Certain boards add Feature Squares, and the highest difficulty adds Drop-Out Squares.

**What was wrong and why it changed:** Pieces are assigned, not chosen, and named per the manual (bugle -> trumpet; dropped 'high-heeled'); removed 'freezes the timer' and the time-out lockout; replaced the three-or-four-tiers count with the manual's hint-dot rule; Feature Squares on certain boards and Drop-Out Squares on the highest difficulty, without the unsupported 'drop tokens down'.

**Contradicted by NES evidence:**

- Participants select their pieces — Markers are assigned by player number: Player 1 Shoes, Player 2 Trumpet, Player 3 Teddy, Player 4 Ice Cream. (manual p05 (page 8))
- Pieces are high-heeled shoes, a bugle, an ice cream cone, a teddy bear — Manual names Shoes, Trumpet, Teddy and Ice Cream; 'bugle' is wrong and 'high-heeled' could not be confirmed from the small screenshots. (manual p05 (page 8), p06 (page 10))
- Later tiers introduce Feature Squares and Drop-Out Squares that drop tokens down — Feature Squares appear on certain Game Boards; Drop-Out Squares appear on the highest level of difficulty. Their effect ('drop tokens down') is not described. (manual p05 (page 7))

**Other sources checked:** https://www.raregamer.co.uk/?p=11959

Other pipes, manholes, and landmarks contain Bonus Rooms granting junk food, fuel, keys, or extra lives. Some enemies drop items when jumped on, while stars provide firepower until a life is lost. A concluding adventure follows once all thirty are returned.

**What was wrong and why it changed:** Fixed the clone rule (clones follow Marty's every move and must be lured off a platform), the time-machine remote wording, the street connections, 'moving' to 'movable' platforms, Bonus Room locations and rewards, item drops from some enemies, and star firepower lasting until a life is lost.

**Contradicted by NES evidence:**

- Clones mimic Marty's past actions and must be pushed off ledges — Each jump leaves a clone that follows his every move; he must lure it off a platform before it touches him. (manual p04 (image))

## Bad News Baseball (`467a2e53c7af4c60`)

- **Classification:** substantive; error types: wrong count, wrong rule, unsupported specific
- **Queue:** main (nes-native-untouched)
- **Manual:** Bad News Baseball (USA); page images inspected: yes (p03, p04, p05, p07, p08, p14, p15, p16)
- **Verification:** level D; remaining uncertainty: Girls' mode roster details (new names) not independently verified, so left general.

**Before:**

> Defeating every opposing team stands as the ultimate objective in this baseball simulation. In the primary single-player campaign, participants challenge twelve fictional squads in any desired sequence until every opponent has been conquered. While wins and losses go untracked, pitchers gradually drain a stamina meter that requires multiple matches of rest to fully regenerate. Play progresses through standard baseball actions, including choosing from four pitch styles, attempting stolen bases, and substituting pinch hitters or runners, with contests concluding in ties after twelve innings. Passwords provided after matches preserve defeated rivals and current pitching fatigue.
>
> Available options include single-player and two-player matches, a spectator mode, and customizable All-Star games across two distinct leagues. Competitors arrange batting orders, field positions, and pitching rotations among rosters featuring varying individual ratings. An alternate configuration also supplies entirely separate female rosters for each club.

**After:**

> Defeating every opposing team stands as the ultimate objective in this baseball simulation. In the primary single-player campaign, participants challenge the other eleven fictional teams in any desired sequence until every opponent has been conquered. While losses go uncounted, pitchers gradually drain a stamina meter that only partly recovers after each match. Play progresses through standard baseball actions, including choosing from four pitch styles, attempting stolen bases, and substituting pinch hitters or runners, with contests concluding in ties after twelve innings. Passwords provided after matches preserve defeated rivals and current pitching fatigue.
>
> Available options include single-player and two-player matches, a spectator mode, and customizable All-Star games across two distinct leagues. Competitors arrange batting orders, field positions, and starting pitchers among rosters featuring varying individual ratings. A hidden girls' mode also replaces the players on every club with female players.

**What was wrong and why it changed:** Twelve opponents corrected to the other eleven teams (12 teams total); 'wins and losses go untracked' narrowed to losses; stamina recovery reworded to manual's partial recovery; 'pitching rotations' changed to starting pitchers; female-roster sentence generalized to the girls' mode.

**Contradicted by NES evidence:**

- Single-player campaign challenges twelve fictional squads — There are 12 teams in total; the player picks one and plays the game's other 11 teams. (obscurevideogames.com NES review; manual p16 (teams fictional))
- Wins and losses go untracked — Losses are not counted, but the password remembers which teams have been beaten. (obscurevideogames.com NES review)
- Players arrange batting orders, field positions and pitching rotations — Manual describes batting order, fielding positions and choosing the starting pitcher; no rotation feature. Changed to 'starting pitchers'. (manual p07 (image))

**Other sources checked:** https://obscurevideogames.com/category/nes-bad-news-baseball/ (NES review); http://web.archive.org/web/2022/https://strategywiki.org/wiki/Bad_News_Baseball

## Barker Bill's Trick Shooting (`4da0d4900b297274`)

- **Classification:** substantive; error types: wrong rule, invented detail, wrong name
- **Queue:** main (nes-native-untouched)
- **Manual:** Barker Bill's Trick Shooting (USA); page images inspected: yes (p05, p06, p07)
- **Verification:** level D; remaining uncertainty: None material.

**Before:**

> Barker Bill's Trick Shooting tasks the player with targeting carnival objects using a light gun. Players begin with ten chances and aim to accumulate points by hitting targets right before they break or disappear. A chance is deducted whenever a target is missed or an unauthorized subject, such as an animal or an assistant, is struck. In most modes, shooting a diamond grants an extra chance, and running out of chances ends the session.
>
> Play spans four carnival formats. In Balloon Saloon, airborne balloons are targeted without shooting an accompanying dog. Flying Saucers involves hitting tossed plates while avoiding Barker Bill, Trixie, and a parrot. Window Pains requires timing shots through open windows at falling items. **After:**

> Barker Bill's Trick Shooting tasks the player with shooting carnival targets with a light gun. Players begin with ten credits and score points by hitting targets, with many scores depending on a target's height or how quickly it is hit. Each mistake, such as letting a target escape or shooting an animal, costs a credit. Shooting the diamonds that sometimes appear adds credits, and running out ends the session.
>
> Play spans four carnival formats. In Balloon Saloon, rising balloons are targeted without shooting a dog. Flying Saucers involves hitting saucers thrown by a man and his assistant before they reach the ground, while avoiding a bird. Window Pains requires shooting falling items through open windows. Fun Follies cycles through these challenges and adds stages: Trixie's Shot, where coins held out or thrown by a dancing woman are hit; a diamond-enhanced slot machine for extra credits; and Bill's Thrills, where items a man throws toward the woman's head are shot down.

Light rewording to stay within 160 words.

**Contradicted by NES evidence:**

- A chance is lost for a miss or for shooting an animal or an assistant — Mistakes are letting balloons escape, items falling on the woman's head, and shooting the dog or bird. Shooting an assistant is not listed. (manual p05-p07 (image))
- Flying Saucers: avoid Barker Bill, Trixie and a parrot — A man and his assistant throw saucers; only shooting a bird is a mistake. Not named Barker Bill/Trixie here; 'parrot' not stated. (manual p05 (image))

> Five levels structure this platforming adventure, sending the hero across Gotham City Streets, the Axis Chemical Plant, Gotham Sewers, a Mysterious Laboratory, and the Gotham Cathedral Belltower. Beast, Maxiezeus, Nightslayer, and Shakedown.

- Minions Deadshot, Heat Wave, KGBeast, Maxie Zeus, Nightslayer, Shakedown — All appear, but manual spellings are Heatwave, K.G. Beast and Maxiezeus. (manual p09 (image))

Shooting the Pick-up Carrier or searching hidden holes yields pick-ups such as a smart bomb, a three-way shot, a shield, a Super-Sting and the sidekick Junior, who adds firepower and guards Bee 52; all pick-ups are lost with a life. A second player can take part as Bee 53.

**What was wrong and why it changed:** Bounded rewrite from the manual: removed the unconfirmed twelve-level count and 'every flower' rule, the invented lightning bug, the projectile/stinger directions and Junior's orbit; added the manual's pick-up sources and types, hive-raiding ants, pick-up loss and Bee 53.

**Contradicted by NES evidence:**

- Randomly appearing lightning bug or hidden holes award stronger projectiles or extended stinger — Pick-ups come mostly from shooting the Pick-up Carrier and some are hidden in holes; manual names no lightning bug and lists many pick-up types (bomb, rapid reload, Megashot, 3-way, Junior, autofire, 1 UP, shield, Super-Sting). (manual p06, p07, p08)

> Controlling biblical figures, players lift and carry objects across sidescrolling stages in three separate games based on Old Testament stories. In Noah's Ark, the protagonist must gather food and animals to transport them into the vessel. Stone tablets bearing Bible quotes give Noah clues and strength.
>
> In Baby Moses, the player directs the mother of Moses to carry her infant son safely to the river while evading soldiers and hazards. In David and Goliath, players initially guide David to gather sheep while stunning predatory bears and lions with acorns, as scorpions and charging mountain goats block the way. **Before:**

> Bible Buffet combines board game navigation with real-time action stages for up to four participants. Players take turns spinning an onscreen spinner to advance tokens across twelve food-themed lands toward a finishing circle. Spinner outcomes and special board spaces can grant extra movement, inflict turn penalties, open shortcuts, or present three-question Bible quizzes selected from specific categories. > Bible Buffet combines board game navigation with real-time action stages for up to four participants. Players take turns spinning an onscreen spinner to advance tokens across twelve food-themed lands toward a finishing circle. Spinner outcomes and special board spaces can grant extra movement, inflict turn penalties, open shortcuts, or present three-question Bible quizzes selected from specific categories. Landing on an action square sends the player into an action sequence to collect food and locate the exit.
>
> Inside action screens, players maneuver through areas filled with stationary, walking, and harmful food items. Walking food can be stunned using thrown utensils such as spoons, forks, and knives, or dazed with timed preservative blast barrels before collection. Bonus weight is awarded for quickly gathering multiple stunned items. When all players finish, awards recognize the first finisher, the highest food total, and the most quiz stars.

**What was wrong and why it changed:** 'detonated with timed preservative blast barrels' -> 'dazed with timed preservative blast barrels' (the blast makes food dizzy).

- Walking food 'detonated' with timed preservative blast barrels — The barrel blasts after about 2 seconds and makes certain foods dizzy; the food is not detonated. (manual p07 image)

**Before:**

> Guiding a caveman named Bignose atop a newly invented wheel, the player rolls through prehistoric terrain to recover stolen bone savings from Leroy the Lizardman. Hostile creatures harm Bignose on contact. A club serves to strike adversaries, and collecting rock icons enables launching projectiles that can increase in quantity, speed, and piercing power. > The game spans five sections containing four levels each, culminating in an encounter with Leroy and a boss equipped with an energy meter. **After:**

> Guiding a caveman named Bignose atop a newly invented wheel, the player rolls through prehistoric terrain to recover stolen bone savings from Leroy the Lizardman. Hostile creatures harm Bignose on contact. A club serves to strike adversaries, and collecting rock icons enables launching projectiles that can increase in quantity, speed, and piercing power. Gathering twenty-five bones awards an extra life, while bouncing on mushrooms can produce bonuses, hazards, or higher jumps.
>
> The game spans five sections containing four levels each, and every section ends with an encounter with Leroy, who usually brings a monster; an energy bar appears during boss fights. Hidden levels are found by bouncing on mushrooms or falling in the right place, and completing a bonus stage earns a continue. Two alternating multiplayer modes are included: Tag Mode, which alternates control when a player loses a life, and a timed competition where participants take turns gathering bones across five stages.

- Secret levels and bonus rounds offer opportunities to earn continues — only completing a bonus stage is said to win a continue; hidden levels are found by bouncing on mushrooms or falling in the right place, with no continue reward stated (manual p01 Bonus Stages / Hidden Levels)

## Bigfoot (`32fa00d52f39b053`)

- **Classification:** rewrite; error types: wrong rule, unsupported specific

- **Manual:** Bigfoot (USA); page images inspected: yes (p02, p03, p04, p05, p06, p07, p09, p10)
- **Verification:** level D; remaining uncertainty: Truck colors and the order in which rival trucks replace bankrupt ones may be accurate but are only in the source encyclopedia article.

> Operating the blue Bigfoot monster truck, players compete in various racing events against rival trucks. The primary objective is to advance through each level while minimizing vehicle damage. ## Black Bass, The (`99806081ba58c0a1`)

- **Classification:** substantive; error types: wrong rule
- **Queue:** escalation (m32-audit-corrected)
- **Manual:** Black Bass, The (USA); page images inspected: yes (p04, p15)
- **Verification:** level D; remaining uncertainty: None material.

**Before:**

> Anglers navigate a boat across a lake to cast lines and reel in catches during tournament matches. The primary goal is to catch numerous black bass before the scheduled closing time, which begins at 6:00 A.M. and shifts depending on the date. Fishing begins by picking a spot on the water and casting out a lure with a chosen amount of meter power.
>

**After:**

> Anglers navigate a boat across a lake to cast lines and reel in catches during tournament matches. The primary goal is to catch numerous black bass during each fishing day, which runs from 6:00 A.M. until a closing time that shifts depending on the date. Fishing begins by picking a spot on the water and casting out a lure with a chosen amount of meter power.
>
> Moving the lure realistically through the water attracts nearby fish. Once a fish bites the bait, the angler works to haul it toward the landing net while using thumbing brakes to control its runs. Winding in a hooked fish too fast sets off a warning sound, and letting it reach the edge of the screen can cut the line. Between casts, players can adjust their strategy by changing lure types and colors based on conditions.

**Contradicted by NES evidence:**

- Goal is to catch many black bass before the closing time, which begins at 6:00 A.M. and shifts with the date — fishing runs FROM 6:00 A.M. TO closing time; the closing time (4:00 P.M. on June 5th) is extended until August 5th and then decreases. The closing time does not begin at 6:00 A.M. (manual p04 (image))
- Winding too rapidly risks snapping the line and losing the tackle — winding too fast triggers a ringing warning sound; the line is cut when the fish reaches the screen edge or sometimes when it jumps. Nothing says fast winding snaps the line or loses tackle (manual p15 (image))

Defeating subterranean bosses grants vehicle enhancements that allow the tank to scale walls, hover, and travel underwater.

**What was wrong and why it changed:** Replaced 'downward lightning strikes' with a direction-neutral lightning attack and 'traverse deep areas' with the manual's underwater Dive function.

**Other sources checked:** https://www.hardcoregaming101.net/blaster-master/

- **Verification:** level D; remaining uncertainty: Setting list combines the story page (shopping mall, warehouse, prison, sewers, abandoned building site) and chapter blurbs (department store in Chapter 1).

**Before:**

> Members of the Blues Brothers band must escape police officers and assorted vigilantes in an effort to reach their concert on time. Players navigate platforming stages centered around jumping challenges while seeking out required attributes, such as a guitar, located within the surroundings.
>

Two players can take part in the adventure simultaneously, with the camera remaining focused on only one participant as the view scrolls across the environment.

- Members of the Blues Brothers band must escape police officers and assorted vigilantes to reach their concert on time — Jake and Elwood must find their own way to the stage after Sheriff McGraw sabotages all routes; police enemies exist (Evil Cop, riot police), but no vigilantes and no escape-from-pursuers premise; 'vigilantes' is a detail from another version (manual p04 (image) Back in Town)
- Players seek required attributes, such as a guitar, located in the surroundings — the stated goal is to reach the EXIT of each level; pickups listed are notes (energy), hearts (extra life) and springs. No guitar or required items (manual ocr Object of the Game; p08 (image) Bonus/Accessories)

## Bomberman (`2967746c2a434c97`)

- **Classification:** substantive; error types: wrong item effect, unsupported specific
- **Queue:** main (m32-audit-medium-risk)
- **Manual:** Bomberman (USA); page images inspected: yes (p01, p03, p04, p05)
- **Verification:** level D; remaining uncertainty: Overhead view rests on StrategyWiki description and the manual's labyrinth wording rather than a manual screenshot. Starting life count not verified, so removed.

**Before:**

> Bomberman features maze action where the player guides a bomb-making robot trying to escape an underground facility and reach the surface. Viewed from an overhead perspective, each of the fifty stages requires eliminating every hostile creature and uncovering an exit door concealed beneath destructible obstacles. The character drops explosives that detonate after a brief delay, projecting flames in four directions to clear paths and destroy adversaries across eight distinct enemy behaviors. Bonus stages also appear between regular levels to provide extra points.
>
> Demolishing blocks reveals power-up panels that grant benefits, including persistent upgrades to blast range and bomb capacity as well as temporary abilities like walking through blocks or manual bomb detonation. Touching foes or bomb blasts costs one of three starting lives. If the stage timer expires or an explosion hits the exit, extra enemies appear. Passwords allow progress to be resumed.

**After:**

> Bomberman features maze action where the player guides a bomb-making robot trying to escape an underground facility and reach the surface. Viewed from an overhead perspective, each of the fifty stages requires eliminating every hostile creature and uncovering an exit door concealed beneath destructible obstacles. The character drops explosives that detonate after a brief delay, projecting flames in four directions to clear paths and destroy adversaries across eight distinct enemy behaviors. Bonus stages also appear between regular levels to provide extra points.
>
> Demolishing blocks reveals power-up panels that grant benefits, including persistent upgrades to blast range and bomb capacity as well as abilities that are lost along with a life, such as walking through bricks or detonating bombs by remote control. Touching foes or bomb blasts costs a life. If the stage timer expires or an explosion hits the exit, extra enemies appear. Passwords allow progress to be resumed.

**What was wrong and why it changed:** Replaced 'temporary abilities' (wall pass and detonator are kept until a life is lost, not time-limited) and removed the unsupported 'three starting lives'.

**Contradicted by NES evidence:**

- 'Temporary' abilities like walking through blocks or manual detonation — Wallpass and Detonator are not time-limited; they are kept until a life is lost. Wallpass passes through destructible bricks only. Reworded. (StrategyWiki Gameplay; manual p03 (remote controlling explosion panel))

**Other sources checked:** http://web.archive.org/web/2019/https://strategywiki.org/wiki/Bomberman; http://web.archive.org/web/2019/https://strategywiki.org/wiki/Bomberman/Gameplay; http://web.archive.org/web/2019/https://strategywiki.org/wiki/Bomberman/Walkthrough

- **Classification:** unsupported detail generalized; error types: wrong name, unsupported specific

> Escaping from prison serves as the primary goal after Black Bomber frames the titular hero for a bank robbery. Controlling Bomberman, the player drops explosive charges inside maze-like rooms to demolish obstructing blocks and eliminate foes. Hidden beneath certain destroyed blocks are items that alter bomb attributes, such as expanding blast radii or allowing bombs to be detonated by remote control. Each stage also conceals an exit door within one of its destructible blocks, granting passage to the following level. Upon receiving a game over, players receive a password that allows a later return to the last level reached.

**What was wrong and why it changed:** Replaced the non-manual villain name 'Black Bomber' with the US manual's 'Bomberman's evil twin' (bank heist); generalized the password to what the manual states (return to the last level reached); 'Vs Mode' to 'VS Mode'. **Contradicted by NES evidence:**

- Black Bomber frames Bomberman for a bank robbery; escaping prison is the goal — the US manual calls the culprit 'Bomberman's evil twin', who pulls a bank heist and frames him; Bomberman must blast out of the jail. The name 'Black Bomber' does not appear (manual p03 (image))

## Bubble Bobble (`31523322db8f94e7`)

- **Classification:** substantive; error types: other-version detail, wrong name

The 'two worlds of 113 levels each' wording is the manual's; StrategyWiki's NES page describes 113 levels with a second 'Super' mode, which is consistent but worded differently.

**Before:**

> Bubble Bobble features platform action where players guide the bubble dragons Bub and Bob through single-screen stages to rescue their kidnapped girlfriends. Characters run, jump across platforms, and fall through bottom gaps to reappear at the top of the screen. Floating bubbles follow unseen air currents and can be bounced on to access higher areas.

Clearing a stage requires blowing bubbles to trap adversaries and then popping them, which turns foes into collectible items. Floating bubbles follow unseen air currents and can be bounced on to access higher areas.

The earlier M3.2 correction (two worlds of 113 levels) is confirmed by the manual. All other sentences kept word for word.

**Contradicted by NES evidence:**

- Bub and Bob are bubble dragons — The US NES manual calls them 'jolly round dinosaurs' with 'magic bubble blowing powers'; changed to 'two bubble-blowing dinosaurs'. (manual p03 story (image))
- They rescue their kidnapped girlfriends — Manual: 'two of their brontosaurus buddies had been abducted by Baron von Blubba'; 'set off to find their friends'. Changed to 'two friends kidnapped by Baron von Blubba'. (Take on the NES Library repeats the girlfriend story, but the US NES manual is the naming and story authority here.) (manual p03 story (image, zoomed))

> Stairs, doorways and pipes connect the floors, and Bugs can safely pass the rascals by going through doorways and pipes. Levels contain tools to counter enemies, including boxing gloves, magic carrot juice that briefly makes Bugs invisible, and objects such as safes, wooden crates, buckets, and ten-ton weights that can be pushed into foes or dropped on them. Clearing a level grants an additional life. Passwords allow players to resume progress at specific stages.

**What was wrong and why it changed:** Names changed to the manual's 'Wiley Coyote' and 'Sylvester'; 'invincibility potions' changed to magic carrot juice that makes Bugs invisible; the unsupported enemy-movement sentence replaced with the manual's stairs/doorways/pipes and safe passage; 'Defeating enemies awards points' removed. The earlier M3.2 corrections (all carrots; safe, crate, bucket, 10-ton weight) are confirmed.

**Contradicted by NES evidence:**

- Rescue Honey Bunny, kidnapped by Wile E. Coyote, Yosemite Sam, Daffy Duck and Sylvester the Cat — Story supported, but the US manual spells the names 'Wiley Coyote' and 'Sylvester'; text changed to the manual names. (manual p03, p07 (image))
- Invincibility potions — Manual: 'By drinking the magic carrot juice, Bugs Bunny will become invisible for a short time.' Changed to 'magic carrot juice that briefly makes Bugs invisible'. (manual p06 (image))

**Other sources checked:** http://web.archive.org/web/2022/https://strategywiki.org/wiki/The_Bugs_Bunny_Crazy_Castle; https://www.honestgamers.com/3147/nes/the-bugs-bunny-crazy-castle/game.html (no mechanics)

- **Classification:** rewrite; error types: wrong name, wrong rule, invented detail
- **Queue:** main (nes-native-untouched)
- **Manual:** Castle of Deceit (USA) (Unl); page images inspected: yes (p01, p02, p03, p04, p05, p06, p07, p09)
- **Verification:** level D; remaining uncertainty: None material.

**Before:**

> Set within a castle of shifting realities, this side-scrolling platform adventure follows a young magician named Cebo. The narrative centers on Phfax, an ancient guardian who wielded Emerald Magic to protect the sacred stones of Rune. After centuries of dwelling inside the stones' energy plasma, Phfax lost his sanity, causing his hallucinations to manifest as six deadly beings that took the Runes. Cebo must venture through the fortress to recover the stolen artifacts amid pervasive sensory deceptions.
>
> The player navigates the environments as the trapped protagonist, relying on defensive magical abilities to survive. Throughout the journey, the character possesses a single spell with which to confront hazards and defend against hostile forces encountered inside the structure.

**After:**

> Set within the Castle of Deceit atop Mount Althus, a gateway to six other universes, this side-scrolling platform adventure follows a magician apprentice named Eebo. The narrative centers on Phylax, who guarded six magical stones called the Runes of Guarding. After centuries of dwelling within the stones' energies, Phylax lost his sanity, and the stones gave life to his hallucinations, creating six deadly beings that stole the Runes. Eebo must venture through the castle to recover them amid illusions, traps, and monsters.
>
> Eebo jumps and casts an attack spell that fires spheres of magical energy. Some doors require magic keys, while others are guarded by Phylax's specter. The journey spans ten levels with bosses such as O'Donna, Skult, and Combustra, ending with Phylax in the Ante Room.

**What was wrong and why it changed:** Corrected names (Eebo, not Cebo; Phylax, not Phfax; Runes of Guarding); removed the 'wielded Emerald Magic' misreading; the spell is an attack spell, not defensive; added keys, spectre doors, ten levels and bosses from the manual. Editorial adjustment: US spelling.

**Contradicted by NES evidence:**

- Young magician named Cebo — Name is Eebo. (manual p03 page 1 ('Eebo, Magician Apprentice'), p06 page 6)
- Guardian named Phfax — Name is Phylax. (manual p02, p03, p07)
- Phfax wielded Emerald Magic to protect the sacred stones of Rune — The stones are the Runes of Guarding; manual calls Phylax 'a mystic Emerald Magic' (apparently truncated; the French text says an emerald magician). Removed the 'wielded Emerald Magic' reading. (manual p03 page 1)
- Trapped protagonist relying on defensive magical abilities; a single spell — Button A casts an attack spell firing spheres of magical energy; protagonist not described as trapped. (manual p06 page 6)

## Castle of Dragon (`6887230077d8eefa`)

- **Classification:** rewrite; error types: other-version detail, wrong name, wrong item effect, unsupported specific
- **Queue:** main (m32-audit-medium-risk)
- **Manual:** Castle of Dragon (USA); page images inspected: yes (p02, p03, p04, p05, p08, p09)
- **Verification:** level D; remaining uncertainty: NES level count and names not documented in the manual; left out. GiantBomb, TV Tropes and RetroAchievements pages returned 403.

**Before:**

> Guiding Geraden, Duke of Menlary, the player battles hostile legions across platforming environments to rescue Princess Amoreena from the dragon cub Zuriv and the Dragon Master Darklaza. Crouch maneuvers allow the Duke to protect himself using his shield as he confronts threats.
>
> The quest spans three distinct stages: Wenlary Castle, Heresy Forest, and Darklaza's Castle, each divided into smaller sections where sections of the final fortress can be chosen and replayed. Defeating bosses and sub-bosses yields armor, throwing knives, maces, or magical fire waves and lightning bolts, though most acquired armaments and spells are temporary enhancements.

**After:**

> Guiding Geraden, Duke of Menlary, the player battles hostile legions across platforming environments to rescue Princess Amoreena from the Dragon Cub and the Dragon Master Darklarza. Crouch maneuvers allow the Duke to protect himself using his shield as he confronts threats.
>
> The quest leads to Darklarza Castle, where Geraden must face the Dragon Master himself. Geraden starts with only a basic sword. Defeating certain bosses yields armor and new weapons such as throwing knives, a mace, the Sonic Sword, which emits a deadly sound wave, and the Lightning Sword; the two special swords last only a limited time. Fairies, the souls of Darklarza's escaped victims, bring the gift of life, and the Dragon Slayer is the only weapon strong enough to pierce the Dragon Master's flesh.

**What was wrong and why it changed:** Removed arcade names (Zuriv, Wenlary Castle, Heresy Forest) and the unsupported three-stage/replay structure; corrected Darklaza to Darklarza; replaced 'most armaments are temporary' and 'fire waves' with the NES item list and the fact that only the special swords are temporary.

**Contradicted by NES evidence:**

- Dragon cub named Zuriv — NES manual calls him only 'Dragon Cub', offspring of Darklarza; 'Zuriv' appears only in sources about the arcade original (Dragon Unit) (manual p03 (p.2), p08 (p.11))
- Dragon Master named Darklaza — Manual spells the name DARKLARZA throughout (one typo 'Darklaza' in the tips page) (manual p03 (p.1))
- Three stages: Wenlary Castle, Heresy Forest, Darklaza's Castle — Wenlary/Heresy Forest names come from the arcade original; HG101 says the NES level structure is entirely different. No NES source for a three-stage list. (manual p03 (castle is Castle Menlary; destination is Darklarza Castle); HG101)
- Most acquired armaments and spells are temporary — HG101: throwing knives and mace are permanent; only the fire and thunder swords are temporary (manual p08 (Sonic Sword limited life span, Lightning Sword temporary); HG101)

**Other sources checked:** https://www.hardcoregaming101.net/castle-of-dragon/

## Castlevania III - Dracula's Curse (`6e8d289635ac3947`)

- **Classification:** substantive; error types: wrong count, wrong name, unsupported specific
- **Queue:** main (nes-native-untouched)
- **Manual:** Castlevania III - Dracula's Curse (USA); page images inspected: yes (p03, p04, p05, p06)
- **Verification:** level D; remaining uncertainty: In-game HUD terminology not checked. Endings source says four endings by companion.

**Before:**

> Defeating Count Dracula and his army of monsters is the primary objective of this platforming adventure. Controlling the vampire hunter Trevor Belmont, the player fights through sixteen stages, referred to as blocks, which are subdivided into smaller sections. Trevor combats threats using the Mystic Whip alongside various items. Following certain levels, the player selects between branching paths to progress toward the castle, such as an upper path across a lake or a subterranean route through caverns. Depending on the route and companion choices made, several different endings can be reached.
>
> Trevor can also team up with a single spirit companion encountered along the way. **After:**

> Defeating Count Dracula and his army of monsters is the primary objective of this platforming adventure. Controlling the vampire hunter Trevor Belmont, the player fights through Terror Levels, each with a time limit and a boss; there are seventeen in all, though the route chosen determines which are played. Trevor combats threats using the Mystic Whip alongside various items. At several points the road forks, and the player chooses which path to take toward the castle. Different endings can be reached depending on the companion who travels with Trevor.
>
> Trevor can also team up with a single spirit companion encountered along the way. Available allies include Sypha, the Mystic Warlord, who attacks with flames, frozen crystals, and lightning bolts; Grant DaNasty, a ghost pirate able to cling to walls and ceilings and jump high; and Alucard, Dracula's son, who fires a Ball of Destruction and transforms into a bat. Partnering with a new companion requires leaving the previous ally behind.

**What was wrong and why it changed:** Corrected 'sixteen stages called blocks' to the manual's seventeen Terror Levels (route-dependent) and added the time limit and boss rule; removed the unconfirmed lake/caverns route detail; replaced 'sorceress' with the US manual's 'Mystic Warlord' description; tied endings to the companion; used manual names Grant DaNasty and Ball of Destruction.

**Contradicted by NES evidence:**

- Sixteen stages referred to as blocks — US manual gives 17 levels and calls them Terror Levels; 'blocks' not used (manual p03 (17 possible levels), p04 (a total of 17 gruesome levels; called Terror Levels))
- Sypha is a sorceress who casts elemental spells — US manual calls Sypha 'the Mystic Warlord' and uses 'he'; attacks are flames, frozen crystals and lightning bolts (manual p05 (image))

**Other sources checked:** https://castlevaniadungeon.net/oldpage/cv3.htm

> Challenge of the Dragon is an action game centered on martial arts combat. Players take control of Sir Burkelot, a Dragon Style Master on a mission to rescue his companion, Lady Ninita, who has been abducted by a necromancer. Sir Burkelot traverses ten distinct worlds, starting in a village and advancing through areas such as multi-leveled grasslands, the Big Wall, a forest, and an inner castle. Along the journey, he contends with mind-controlled adversaries including ninjas, samurai, giants, wizards, and skeletons.
>
> Combat relies on a context-sensitive system where pressing the attack button triggers different martial arts techniques depending on proximity to a foe. Techniques include sword strikes, close-range knee strikes, side kicks, a shoulder butt performed during a super run, and a jumping dragon kick. The hero can also cast collected magic potions. - Starts in a village; areas such as multi-leveled zones, 'castle walls', forests and 'inner strongholds' — Ten worlds: Village, Grasslands (multi-leveled), Big Wall, Master Ninja, Rocky Haven, Forest, Wizard's Village, Outer Castle, Graveyard, Inner Castle. ## Chip 'n Dale - Rescue Rangers (`e84d90fefb92f2b6`)

- **Classification:** substantive; error types: wrong item effect, invented detail, unsupported specific

**Before:**

> Rescuing a kidnapped teammate named Gadget and defeating the villainous Fat Cat forms the central goal of this platforming adventure. Players start out searching for a missing kitten before navigating across a city map to reach the antagonist's casino and ultimate hideout. In each side-scrolling stage, the chipmunk protagonists traverse environments by walking, jumping, ducking, and collecting objects such as barrels, balls, and crates to toss at adversaries and end-level bosses. Monterey Jack occasionally smashes barricades blocking progress, while discovering Zipper bestows temporary invulnerability, and the captured Gadget offers advice.
