> Applying hues to prehistoric creatures serves as the primary task for the player, who uses provided dinosaur images and color palettes. Basic coloring options include limited variations of pink and red alongside brightly colored patterns. Players can access an additional set of patterns by pressing the Select button.
>
> Two distinct play modes dictate how the coloring process works. In free form mode, the player colors independently, whereas automatic mode requires only selecting a specific color. The game contains static pictures without animation or minigames.

**After:**

> Applying colors and patterns to prehistoric creatures serves as the primary task for the player, who chooses one of sixteen dinosaur pictures to color. Each palette offers three colors, and the remaining choices are patterns made from those colors. Pressing the Select button cycles through the different palettes, and changing the palette also changes the coloring of the dinosaur.
>
> Two coloring modes dictate how the coloring process works. In freehand mode, the player moves a cursor to any section of the dinosaur, whereas in point-to-point mode the computer selects each section automatically and the cursor jumps to the next fillable area. Switching modes requires starting the dinosaur over. The game is aimed at children ages three to six.

**What was wrong and why it changed:** Rewrote from the manual: sixteen pictures, three-color palettes with patterns, Select cycles palettes and recolors the picture, and the real difference between freehand and point-to-point modes; removed the pink/red claim and the unconfirmed no-animation/no-minigame sentence.

**Contradicted by NES evidence:**

- Limited variations of pink and red plus brightly colored patterns — Sources say red and blue, not pink and red (HG101 (each palette has 3 colors; rest are patterns of those colors); retrovolve (mostly variations on red and blue))
- Select button gives an additional set of patterns — Select cycles whole palettes, recoloring the picture (manual p04 (Select displays the different palettes); ocr p.5 (Select changes the palette and coloring of your dinosaur); HG101 (cycles through 8 palettes))
- Two modes: free form colors independently; automatic requires only selecting a color — Freehand: move cursor to any section; point-to-point: computer selects each section and the cursor jumps to the next fillable area; color is still chosen and applied by the player (manual p05)

**Other sources checked:** https://www.hardcoregaming101.net/color-a-dinosaur/; https://retrovolve.com/the-curious-case-of-color-a-dinosaur/

## Commando (`0512b4aa2220f74e`)

- **Classification:** rewrite; error types: other-version detail, wrong name, unsupported specific
- **Queue:** main (m32-audit-medium-risk)
- **Manual:** Commando (USA); page images inspected: yes (p03, p04, p05)
- **Verification:** level C; remaining uncertainty: Alternating two-player play is inferred from the manual's statement that Controller 1 moves Super Joe in both 1- and 2-player games. Whether the NES version keeps the arcade's end-of-stage gate and upward-only grenades was not verified, so those details were removed.

**Before:**

> Commando delivers run and gun shooter gameplay. Controlling a soldier named Super Joe, the player is dropped into a jungle setting to fight past waves of enemy forces. Joe carries an assault rifle with unlimited ammunition that fires in eight directions, alongside a finite supply of grenades thrown vertically toward the top of the screen. Grenades eliminate multiple soldiers at once and clear obstacles. Throughout the stages, the player can rescue prisoners of war and uncover hidden underground shelters by using explosives.
>
> At the conclusion of each level, scrolling halts while the player confronts soldiers pouring out of a fortress or gate. Eliminating their retreating officer awards bonus points. Across sixteen total levels formed by repeating four stage layouts with adjustments, players can acquire items such as enhanced machine guns, glasses that reveal concealed bunkers, and unlimited grenades, which are lost when a life ends.

**After:**

> Commando is a vertically scrolling run and gun shooter. Controlling a soldier named Super Joe, the player is landed by helicopter to fight past waves of enemy forces, rescue hostages, and keep an enemy army from controlling the world. Joe moves in eight directions, firing a rifle with the B Button and throwing a limited supply of grenades with the A Button. Throughout the stages, the player can use grenades to uncover hidden underground shelters, where hostages are held and poisonous snakes lurk.
>
> The game spans sixteen stages, formed by four campaigns of four stages each; later campaigns repeat the layouts with hidden shelters and items moved. Items include a Wireless Remote Radio that destroys every enemy on screen, a Medal of Honor that grants an extra life, Binoculars that reveal hidden shelters, and a Bullet Proof Jacket that absorbs ten enemy bullets. Other power-ups strengthen the rifle or grenades. In the two-player game, players take turns.

**What was wrong and why it changed:** Bounded rewrite: the original was built mostly from the arcade gameplay description (upward-only grenades, gate and fleeing officer, jungle, unlimited ammo) and called the Binoculars 'glasses'. Rebuilt from the NES manual (controls, hostages, shelters, snakes, items) plus HG101 and Critical Play for the sixteen-stage structure, grenade-revealed bunkers and weapon power-ups. Dropped the unverified 'unlimited grenades' and 'lost when a life ends' claims.

**Contradicted by NES evidence:**

- glasses that reveal concealed bunkers — Manual names this item Binoculars: 'will show Super Joe where the hidden shelters are'. (manual p05)

**Other sources checked:** http://www.hardcoregaming101.net/commando/; https://criticalplay.org/quick-thoughts/2020/6/26/talking-nes-and-history-capcom-commando-1986; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commando_(video_game) (to trace origin of claims only)

## Conflict (`18ca062abee6bf3b`)

- **Classification:** unsupported detail generalized; error types: unsupported specific
- **Queue:** main (nes-native-untouched)
- **Manual:** Conflict (USA); page images inspected: yes (p03, p04, p05, p06, p09, p10)
- **Verification:** level D; remaining uncertainty: The starting number of factories per side and fame-point penalties for retreat or losses could not be confirmed outside Wikipedia, so they were removed.

**Before:**

> Conflict presents hex-based military strategy across 16 scenarios. The first participant commands blue Western Bloc forces, while either a computer opponent or a second participant controls red Eastern Bloc troops. Both sides begin with two factories capable of producing air and ground units each turn. Maneuverability and defensive evasion vary depending on hex terrain types, which include plains, woods, mountains, seas, bridges, and towns. The primary objective in every mission requires players to eliminate the opposing flag tank.
>
> Commanders earn fame points by conquering cities, securing airports, and destroying adversary troops, though retreating or suffering casualties subtracts from this total. Accumulating higher fame points permits factories to construct stronger hardware such as tanks rather than infantry. Friendly forces also use captured cities and airports to repair, rearm, and refuel their ground or aerial combatants.

**After:**

> Conflict presents hex-based military strategy across 16 scenarios. The first participant commands blue forces, while either a computer opponent or a second participant controls red forces. Factories can produce one new air or ground unit per turn. Maneuverability, defense, and evasive action vary depending on hex terrain types, which include plains, woods, mountains, seas, bridges, and towns. The primary objective in every mission requires players to eliminate the opposing flag tank.
>
> Commanders earn fame points by occupying towns and airports and by winning battles. Accumulating higher fame points permits factories to construct a wider range of unit types. Friendly forces also use towns and airports to repair, rearm, and refuel their ground or aerial combatants, while supply vehicles and cargo aircraft can refuel and rearm units in the field. The sixteenth map is reserved for one player and opens only after passwords are earned on the first fifteen.

**What was wrong and why it changed:** Replaced the unsupported 'Western Bloc/Eastern Bloc' labels with blue/red forces; replaced 'two factories ... each turn' with the manual's one-unit-per-turn rule; replaced 'cities' with towns; dropped the unsupported fame-point loss rule and the tanks-vs-infantry example; added the manual's supply-unit and map 16 password rules.

## Conquest of the Crystal Palace (`a5b8e24589539b0b`)

- **Classification:** substantive; error types: wrong item effect, invented detail, wrong name
- **Queue:** main (nes-native-untouched)
- **Manual:** Conquest of the Crystal Palace (USA); page images inspected: yes (p03, p04, p05, p06)
- **Verification:** level D; remaining uncertainty: The three crystal effects and the Moon Mirror's effect rest on Hardcore Gaming 101 (with a TASVideos mention of the jump crystal), not the manual. How the Moon Mirror is obtained was not verified, so it is not stated.

**Before:**

> Conquest of the Crystal Palace features two-dimensional action platforming gameplay. Players guide the teenage prince Farron on a quest to reclaim his kingdom's stolen realm from the villain Zaras. Before setting out across the five realms, the player chooses one of three magical crystals to boost jump height, expand health capacity, or provide an infinite fireball attack. Farron fights hostiles primarily using a sword, while his canine companion Zap can be summoned directly into battle to cause damage.
>
> Along the path, defeated adversaries yield temporary power-ups that duplicate the special crystal benefits. Players can also acquire scrolls that grant long-range offensive skills, either discovered along the journey or purchased from Kim's shop. In addition to selling items, Kim serves as a reporter who provides clues. Farron can also rescue the captured Crystal Princess, who presents the Moon Mirror to assist his efforts.

**After:**

> Conquest of the Crystal Palace features two-dimensional action platforming gameplay. Players guide the teenage prince Farron on a quest to retake the Crystal Palace from the evil warspirit Zaras. Before setting out across five stages, the player chooses one of three power crystals to boost jump height, expand health capacity, or provide a fireball attack. Farron fights hostiles primarily using a sword, while his guardian dog Zap, who has his own life meter, can be called into play to protect him.
>
> Defeated enemies leave coins that must be collected within five seconds. Money buys herbs, potions, food for Zap, a Dog Whistle, and special weapons such as the Fire Scroll and Boomerang Annihilator from Kim, the shop proprietor, though not every item is sold in each shop. Kim also alerts the player to QNN news bulletins. The Moon Mirror destroys every enemy on screen once per stage.

**What was wrong and why it changed:** Removed the unsupported claim that enemy drops duplicate crystal benefits (enemies leave coins), the 'Kim is a reporter who provides clues' claim, and the unconfirmed Crystal Princess; replaced 'infinite fireball' with a fireball attack, 'realms' with stages; kept the sword, Zap and Kim's-shop material, now tied to the manual's item list and HG101's Moon Mirror description.

**Contradicted by NES evidence:**

- defeated adversaries yield temporary power-ups duplicating the crystal benefits — No source says enemy drops duplicate the crystal effects. (manual p04 (enemies leave coins); hardcoregaming101 (drops are health, a sword wavebeam upgrade, mostly money))
- Kim serves as a reporter who provides clues — Kim is the shop proprietor who alerts the player that a QNN news bulletin is on; she is not described as a reporter giving clues. (manual p05)

**Other sources checked:** https://www.hardcoregaming101.net/conquest-of-the-crystal-palace/; https://tasvideos.org/Forum/Posts/85181

## Contra Force (`0c190a8a7bfb57d7`)

- **Classification:** substantive; error types: wrong name, unsupported specific, wrong item effect
- **Queue:** main (nes-native-untouched)
- **Manual:** Contra Force (USA); page images inspected: yes (p03, p04, p06, p07, p08)
- **Verification:** level D; remaining uncertainty: The side-scrolling versus overhead split rests on the manual's five mission screenshots.

**Before:**

> Directing one of four task force operatives, players run, jump, and shoot through hostile territory to protect Neocity from a terrorist syndicate. Characters include the squad leader Burns, heavy weapons specialist Iron, marksman Smith, and demolitions expert Beans, each possessing distinct movement speeds, jumping attributes, and armaments. Across five stages, the objective requires navigating through enemy forces to confront a final boss. Odd-numbered stages use a side-scrolling perspective that allows jumping and ducking, while even-numbered stages switch to an overhead view offering eight-directional movement.
>
> Destroying environmental objects reveals briefcase items that advance an upgrade gauge. Players can confirm selections on this meter to gain character-specific weapons, turbo fire, or an invulnerable mid-air rolling attack. Pausing brings up a sub-menu to swap characters, summon a temporary computer-controlled ally, or assign a second player to join. Each operative holds three lives, and continuing remains unlimited.

**After:**

> Directing one of four C-Force commandos, players run, jump, and shoot through hostile territory to free Neo City from the terrorist group D.N.M.E. Characters include the leader Burn, heavy weapons specialist Iron, marksman Smith, and demolitions expert Beans, each possessing distinct movement speeds, jumping attributes, and armaments. Across five missions, the objective requires navigating through enemy forces to confront a boss. The first, third, and fifth missions are side-scrolling, while the second and fourth use an overhead view.
>
> Destroying enemies and objects reveals items that advance a power gauge. Players can select upgrades from this gauge, including character-specific weapons, Turbo Power that fires three times in a row, or a Rolling Attack that protects while jumping. Pausing brings up a sub-menu to swap characters, call in a computer-controlled partner for a few seconds through a Battle Plan, or add a second player. Each commando starts with three lives, and continuing is possible.

**What was wrong and why it changed:** Burns -> Burn; Neocity -> Neo City with the manual's D.N.M.E. premise; 'final boss' -> a boss per mission; odd/even rule restated from the manual's mission screenshots without the unverified eight-directional movement; removed 'briefcase', 'invulnerable' and 'unlimited' continues; tied Turbo Power and Rolling Attack to the manual's descriptions.

**Contradicted by NES evidence:**

- protect Neocity from a terrorist syndicate — Manual spells it Neo City; it has already fallen into the hands of D.N.M.E., which kidnapped the chief commissioner. (manual p03)
- squad leader Burns — Manual name is Burn ('Commando Burn and his men'). (manual p03, p08)

## Crystalis (`5ad644d368f70b61`)

- **Classification:** substantive; error types: other-version detail, wrong name, invented detail
- **Queue:** escalation (m32-audit-corrected)
- **Manual:** Crystalis (USA); page images inspected: yes (p03, p04, p05, p11, p12)
- **Verification:** level D; remaining uncertainty: The manual spells the empire 'Dragonia' while StrategyWiki uses 'Draygonian'; the final text avoids the empire name. On-screen text was not checked.

**Before:**

> Preventing the tyrannical Draygonian Empire from conquering a post-apocalyptic world and seizing an armed floating tower serves as the central mission. Awakening from cryogenic sleep with no memory, the protagonist journeys across an overhead world to stop Emperor Draygon. Controlled in eight directions, the character slashes with equipped blades, wears protective armor and shields, and triggers assigned magic spells or inventory items. Defeated creatures yield experience points that increase character levels, boosting maximum health, magic capacity, defense, and offensive strength.
>
> Progress relies heavily on four distinct elemental swords imbued with wind, fire, water, and thunder powers, which ultimately unite into a fifth blade. Alongside normal slashes, each weapon can launch charged projectiles to overcome elemental immunities and bypass environmental obstacles, including freezing waterways. Foes and bosses require sufficient character levels before attacks can inflict harm.

**After:**

> Stopping the magician Draygon, who rules a growing empire from a floating, fortified tower, serves as the central mission in a world rebuilt after a great war. Awakening after being frozen in a cave, with no memory, the protagonist journeys across an overhead world to defeat Draygon. Controlled in eight directions, the character slashes with equipped blades, wears protective armor and shields, and triggers assigned magic spells or inventory items. Defeated creatures yield experience points that increase character levels, boosting maximum health, magic capacity, defense, and offensive strength.
>
> Progress relies heavily on four distinct elemental swords imbued with wind, fire, water, and thunder powers, which ultimately unite into a fifth blade. Alongside normal slashes, each weapon can launch charged projectiles to overcome elemental immunities and bypass environmental obstacles, including freezing waterways. Foes and bosses require sufficient character levels before attacks can inflict harm.

**What was wrong and why it changed:** Rewrote the first two sentences: Draygon already rules from his floating, fortified tower (he is not trying to seize it), the non-manual 'Draygonian Empire' name was removed, 'cryogenic sleep' became the manual's frozen-in-a-cave awakening, and 'Emperor Draygon' became Draygon. The prior M3.2 correction (no jumping claim) holds; the rest is kept word for word.

**Contradicted by NES evidence:**

- Preventing the tyrannical Draygonian Empire from conquering the world and seizing an armed floating tower — Draygon already built a computer, placed it in a floating, fortified tower and rules his growing empire from it; he is not trying to seize the tower. 'Draygonian Empire' is not a manual name (the manual uses 'Dragonia'). (manual p03-p04 (image))

**Other sources checked:** https://strategywiki.org/wiki/Crystalis/Enemies (via web.archive.org 20250719 snapshot); https://strategywiki.org/wiki/Crystalis/Controls (via web.archive.org 2025 snapshot); https://strategywiki.org/wiki/Crystalis/Gameplay (via web.archive.org 2024 snapshot)

>
> Contests follow traditional baseball play with combat elements. When force plays occur, the opposing runners and fielders engage in direct battle to secure the base. Incremental damage sustained during these clashes can lead to destruction, and losing three robots results in a team forfeit. Outside of individual matches, players can participate in a pennant race of up to ten games, which allows upgrades to robotic attributes between fixtures. Pennant race progress can be saved, and both play modes support either one or two participants.

**What was wrong and why it changed:** 'Ten-game pennant race' -> up to ten games; saving limited to pennant races (not both modes); the unsupported 'each designed to excel at specific field positions' generalized to differing attributes. Other sentences kept.

**Contradicted by NES evidence:**

- ten-game pennant race — Pennant race of up to 10 games (number is chosen, maximum 10). (manual p10)
- progress can be saved across both play modes — Only pennant races and their data are saved; Open mode is a single game. (manual p10)

**Other sources checked:** https://www.hardcoregaming101.net/base-wars/

## Cyberball (`e239709320fca149`)

- **Classification:** substantive; error types: other-version detail, wrong rule, unsupported specific
- **Queue:** main (m32-audit-medium-risk)
- **Manual:** Cyberball (USA); page images inspected: yes (p01, p04, p05, p06, p08, p10, p11)
- **Verification:** level D; remaining uncertainty: None material.

**Before:**

> Athletic robotic avatars take the field under player direction in a futuristic seven-on-seven adaptation of American football set in 2022. Teams execute run, pass, or option plays on offense from computer-selected choices, while defenders coordinate short, medium, or long defensive alignments.
>
> A volatile, explosive ball substitutes for traditional downs, escalating in temperature from cool to warm, hot, and critical during use. Reaching the fifty-yard line, turning the ball over, or scoring resets the projectile to cool. Robots sustain physical wear from repeated tackles until they emit smoke, catch fire, and ultimately detonate upon impact. Ball carriers tackled while holding a critical ball also explode. Accumulated monetary bonuses allow participants to purchase faster, more durable mechanical replacements across matches supporting up to two players.

**After:**

> Athletic robotic avatars take the field under player direction in a futuristic adaptation of American football set in 2022. Teams execute run, pass, or option plays on offense from computer-selected choices, while in advanced games defenders first choose short, medium, or long yardage coverage.
>
> An explosive ball heats up with each down of a series, from cool to warm, hot, and critical. Reaching the defusion line at midfield or scoring a touchdown defuses it; if the offense fails to do so on the play after the ball turns critical, the ball explodes, usually destroying a robot, and possession passes to the other team. Robots wear down from repeated hits, and a quarterback who begins to smoke can be replaced. Cash earned by defusing the ball or scoring pays for these replacements. One player can face the computer, while two can play head-to-head or together on the same team.

**What was wrong and why it changed:** Removed the arcade-sourced 'seven-on-seven' and 'catch fire and detonate on impact' details; corrected the explosion rule (ball explodes after a failed critical down, not when a carrier is tackled) and 'substitutes for traditional downs'; dropped the unsupported turnover reset and 'faster, more durable' replacements; added the manual's DUEL/TEAM two-player modes.

**Contradicted by NES evidence:**

- explosive ball substitutes for traditional downs — Downs still exist; the ball heats with each down (five downs usually) and getting a first down is called defusing. (manual p05)
- ball carriers tackled holding a critical ball explode — Manual: if the offense fails to reach the defusion line or score on the play after the ball turns critical, the ball explodes and probably blows up one of the offense's players; possession goes to the other team. (manual p05)

## Dash Galaxy in the Alien Asylum (`227e789fef94eabc`)

- **Classification:** substantive; error types: wrong name, wrong rule, unsupported specific
- **Queue:** escalation (nes-native-untouched)
- **Manual:** Dash Galaxy in the Alien Asylum (USA); page images inspected: yes (p02, p03, p04, p05)
- **Verification:** level D; remaining uncertainty: The manual says every room on a floor must be entered before moving up, but the NES TAS author says the elevator can be taken without completing rooms; the final text avoids the floor-progression rule.

**Before:**

> Controlling space scout Dash Galaxy, the player traverses a hostile extraterrestrial facility to reach an escape ship. Dash begins the mission with four lives and a restricted oxygen supply. The structure alternates perspectives between overhead floors and side-scrolling puzzle rooms, alongside hidden and bonus chambers. On the overhead floors, the scout must solve block-moving puzzles to proceed without becoming fatally trapped.
>
> Progression to higher levels requires entering every room on each floor and turning off all of its switches, while keys allow passage through force fields. While exploring side-scrolling areas, Dash encounters wandering hostiles and must utilize trampolines that sometimes require running to execute jumps. For defense and obstacle clearance, the character carries a finite supply of bombs and remote detonators. Collecting ten stars within a stage grants temporary invincibility.

> Controlling space explorer Dash Galaxy, the player traverses a hostile extraterrestrial facility to return to his ship. Dash begins the mission with four lives and a restricted oxygen supply. The structure alternates perspectives between overhead floors and side-scrolling puzzle rooms, alongside hidden and bonus chambers. On the overhead floors, the explorer must push blocks to clear paths to the doorways.
>
> Inside each room, every switch must be turned off before the door reopens, while keys allow passage through force fields. While exploring side-scrolling areas, Dash encounters wandering hostiles and must use ladders, trampolines, and running long jumps. For defense and obstacle clearance, the character carries a finite supply of bombs and remote detonators. Collecting ten orange stars grants temporary invincibility.

**What was wrong and why it changed:** 'Space scout' became the manual's 'space explorer' and 'escape ship' became his ship; dropped 'fatally trapped'; replaced the M3.3 floor-progression rule (contradicted by an NES TAS) with the room switch rule; trampolines and running long jumps are now separate; dropped 'within a stage' and added 'orange' to the star rule.

**Contradicted by NES evidence:**

- Progression to higher levels requires entering every room on each floor and turning off all of its switches — manual says every room must be entered before moving up; the NES TAS author states it is not necessary to complete any level and the elevator square can be used directly. Reworded to the uncontested rule: switches must be turned off before a room's door reopens. (manual p03 (image) vs https://tasvideos.org/3745S)

**Other sources checked:** https://tasvideos.org/3745S (NES TAS submission text); https://tasvideos.org/1392G

**Contradicted by NES evidence:**

**What was wrong and why it changed:** Changed 'homicide detective' to Inspector; added the level route from the manual; replaced the unverified Model 29 details, misattributed remote-control cars (an enemy hazard), 'hot dogs' (chili dogs) and unverified costume/reset trivia with manual-supported controls, items, lives and passwords.

**Contradicted by NES evidence:**

- Explosive remote-controlled cars used by Harry to battle foes — Remote-control cars are enemy hazards deployed by the Toymaker in the sewers. (manual ocr p10-p11)
- Hot dogs replenish health — The item is the chili dog, restoring 50 health points. (manual p06-p07 (image))

## Donkey Kong Jr. (`950ebe68e7f74219`)

> Across several themed stages, the player controls Junior on a quest to rescue his father, Donkey Kong, from Mario's cage. Junior traverses environments by walking, jumping, and grabbing vines or chains to ascend the screen. Holding two vines allows him to climb more rapidly, while holding just one lets him slide down quickly.

> Progress requires reaching keys to unlock the cage while avoiding hazards such as Snapjaws, Nitpickers, and Sparks. Players can evade threats by leaping over them, or knock down fruit to defeat foes below. Getting bitten by a Snapjaw, pecked by a Nitpicker, colliding with a Spark, falling from a vine, or letting the bonus timer run out costs a life.

> Billy and Jimmy Lee set out to defeat the evil Black Shadow Warriors to avenge Marian, gunned down by the gang. Players guide the brothers through nine stages set across alleyways, a heliport, a helicopter in flight, an undersea base, a forest hideout, and a mansion with a trap-filled dungeon. Story cutscenes featuring text and still images precede each stage. Combat employs directional fighting mechanics, granting full access to Billy and Jimmy's techniques from the start. Alongside standard attacks, their repertoire includes the Spinning Cyclone as well as moves performed from a squatting position, such as the Hyper Uppercut and High Jump Kick.
>

Two participants can play simultaneously, with settings that determine whether attacks hurt a partner, while completing all nine stages requires playing on the hardest difficulty.

Editorial adjustment: the game's own on-screen text reads MARIAN (read-only ROM text search: 5 occurrences, tile offset +208); on-screen spelling outranks the manual's 'Marion'.

**Contradicted by NES evidence:**

- Girlfriend named Marian — US manual spells the name 'Marion' (twice); on-screen spelling not verified from the ROM (manual p02, p03 (image))
- Cyclone Spin Kick — manual name is 'Spinning Cyclone' (manual p03, p07 (image))
- Crouching moves: Hyper Uppercut and Flying Knee Kick — Hyper Uppercut and 'High Jump Kick' (a knee kick) both require beginning in a squatting position; no 'Flying Knee Kick' name (manual p07 (image))

## Dr. Mario (`d2fbe8b10f762099`)

- **Classification:** substantive; error types: wrong rule, unsupported specific
- **Queue:** main (m32-audit-medium-risk)
- **Manual:** Dr. Mario (Japan, USA); page images inspected: yes (p04, p05, p07)
- **Verification:** level D; remaining uncertainty: None material.

**Before:**

> Clearing all viruses from a medicine bottle is the primary goal in this falling-block puzzle game set in Mushroom Kingdom Hospital. Mario tosses two-colored medical capsules into the bottle, where red, yellow, and blue viruses sit in fixed starting positions. Players manipulate each falling capsule by moving it horizontally and rotating it in ninety-degree increments. Aligning four matching colors of capsule halves and viruses in a row destroys them. Any unsupported capsule pieces drop downward, potentially forming additional matches. The game ends if stacked capsules block the bottle opening.
>
> Players configure starting levels from zero to twenty and choose among three falling speeds. In the competitive two-player mode, participants race to clear their respective bottles first. Creating chain reactions or eliminating multiple viruses sends extra capsule pieces into the opponent's bottle, and winning three individual rounds secures the overall victory.

**After:**

> Clearing all viruses from a medicine bottle is the primary goal in this falling-block puzzle game set in Mushroom Kingdom Hospital. Mario tosses vitamin capsules into the bottle, where red, yellow, and blue viruses sit. Players manipulate each falling capsule by moving it horizontally and rotating it in ninety-degree increments. Aligning four matching colors of capsule halves and viruses in a row destroys them. Any unsupported capsule pieces drop downward, potentially forming additional matches. The game ends if stacked capsules block the bottle opening.
>
> Players configure starting levels from zero to twenty and choose among three falling speeds. In the competitive two-player mode, participants race to clear their respective bottles first. Clearing two or more rows or columns at once, such as through chain reactions, sends extra capsule pieces into the opponent's bottle, and winning three individual rounds secures the overall victory.

**What was wrong and why it changed:** Replaced 'two-colored medical capsules' with 'vitamin capsules' (single-color capsules exist); removed unsupported 'in fixed starting positions'; corrected the two-player garbage rule to rows or columns cleared at once.

**Contradicted by NES evidence:**

- Mario throws two-colored capsules — Six capsule types, three of them single-color (red-red, blue-blue, yellow-yellow); manual term is 'vitamin capsules' (manual p05)
- Chain reactions or eliminating multiple viruses send extra pieces — Pieces are sent for eliminating two or more rows or columns at once, not for virus counts (manual p07)

**Other sources checked:** https://www.mariowiki.com/Dr._Mario_(game)

- **Verification:** level D; remaining uncertainty: Automatic reversion when the meter empties is likely but only stated in encyclopedia-derived text; it is not asserted. TCRF appeared in search results but was not used.

**Before:**

> Players control a magical fighter who runs, jumps, ducks, and attacks using a sword to avenge the fallen land of Baljing. Holding the attack button unleashes a charged shot. Vanquishing monsters fills a metamorphosis meter, which allows the warrior to transform into a flying dragon during a jump once the meter is half full. > Players control a magical fighter who runs, jumps, ducks, and attacks using a sword to avenge the fallen land of Baljing. Holding the attack button unleashes a charged bomb. Vanquishing monsters fills a metamorphosis meter, which allows the warrior to transform into a flying dragon during a jump once the meter is half full. In dragon form, the character hovers and shoots forward across an auto-scrolling screen. This state slowly empties the gauge, and the player can also shift back manually.

Across six stages, each culminating in a guardian battle, players receive a staff that extends maximum health and fully refills it. The fighter has three lives, and up to three continues are available.

- Losing all health allows up to three continues — Losing all health costs one of three lives; three continues are available (manual p05)

> Across five distinct chapters, diverse adventurers set out on personal journeys that ultimately converge to save the world from monsters led by Psaro the Manslayer. > Across five distinct chapters, diverse adventurers set out on personal journeys that ultimately converge to save the world from monsters led by Necrosaro. **Contradicted by NES evidence:**

- Villain 'Psaro the Manslayer' — NES release calls the villain Necrosaro; manual says only 'a fierce demon' (https://questicle.net/202-dragon-warrior-iv/)
- Soldier Ragnar — US manual spells the name 'Ragner', Captain of the Royal Soldiers of Burland (manual p03 (image))
- Merchant Torneko — US name is Taloon the Arms Merchant (manual p03)
- Sisters Maya and Meena — US names are Mara and Nara (manual p03)

**Other sources checked:** https://questicle.net/202-dragon-warrior-iv/ (Necrosaro, medals traded for rare weapons, casinos); https://infinityretro.com/dragon-warrior-iv-review/ (ship and hot air balloon, wagon, Taloon)

## Duck Hunt (`7026334a7e8742b6`)

- **Classification:** substantive; error types: wrong control
- **Queue:** main (m32-audit-medium-risk)
- **Manual:** Duck Hunt (World); page images inspected: yes (p05, p06)
- **Verification:** level C; remaining uncertainty: Kill-screen sentence rests on one secondary article that does not distinguish Game A, B and C behavior after round 99. Ten-target count for Game C not stated explicitly in the manual.

**Before:**

> Shooting down appearing targets to advance through increasingly demanding rounds represents the primary goal in this light gun title. Operating the NES Zapper pointed at the television, players aim at moving marks with three shots permitted for each appearance. Every round presents ten total targets. >
> Three selectable game modes structure the action. Game A features a single duck at a time, whereas Game B deploys pairs of ducks. Game C replaces waterfowl with clay pigeons launched away into the distance. In Game A, a second participant can plug in a standard controller to maneuver the duck.

> Shooting down appearing targets to advance through increasingly demanding rounds represents the primary goal in this light gun title. Advancing requires hitting a designated minimum quota, with missed quotas ending the session. Hitting targets awards points, while downing all ten in a single round yields bonus points. Reaching past round ninety-nine leads to an erratic kill screen.
>

**Contradicted by NES evidence:**

- In Game A a second participant can plug in a standard controller to maneuver the duck — Second player uses Controller 1 (the standard controller already in socket 1; the Zapper goes in socket 2) to control the duck's flight; no extra controller is plugged in. **Other sources checked:** https://www.svg.com/305828/the-truth-behind-duck-hunts-secret-ending/

Magic beans may be in the game but could not be verified from a reachable NES source. Some items can dispose of particular enemies, so 'cannot fight enemies directly' is a simplification.

**Before:**

> Trouble begins when the villainous wizard Zaks sends a troll army to destroy the Yolkfolk village and has birds abduct Dizzy's girlfriend, Daisy. > Trouble begins when the villainous wizard Zaks sends a troll army to destroy the Yolkfolk village and has birds abduct Dizzy's girlfriend, Daisy. To save her from a cloud castle, Dizzy ventures forth to find his scattered friends and help Grand Dizzy, who is badly in need of medicine. Along the way, he meets a cast of characters including the good magician Theodore, Shamus the leprechaun, Prince Clumsy, the Shopkeeper, and Blackheart the Pirate.
>
> Controlling Dizzy, players explore diverse settings such as mines and the sea floor while solving item-delivery puzzles. The protagonist cannot fight enemies directly and must rely on items to get past them. Beyond navigating hazards, players complete action minigames such as mine cart rides and a barrel trip down a river, operate lifts, solve sliding puzzles for extra lives, and collect 100 stars distributed throughout the map to enter the castle and fulfill the quest.

The unconfirmed 'sixteen characters' and the generic list are replaced with the manual's named characters. 'Arcade minigames' became action minigames with corroborated examples, and 'elevators' became lifts (the manual's term). The unverified magic beans are removed; sliding puzzles for extra lives are added from the manual. Earlier corrections (troll army, 100 stars) are confirmed.

## Fantasy Zone (`ad14301747e0ae0f`)

- **Manual:** Fantasy Zone (USA) (Unl); page images inspected: yes (p03)

The Tengen version may share some removed mechanics, but no source covering the Tengen program (as opposed to the Sunsoft Famicom program) was found. TCRF was not used.

**Before:**

> Stages in this horizontally scrolling shooter loop continuously as players move freely to the left or right. The player directs a sentient spacecraft called Opa-Opa across the planetary zones to eliminate invading enemy bases. After every base in an area is eliminated, a boss arrives and must be beaten to advance to subsequent environments.
>

Purchased armaments carry time limits or quantity restrictions, and all equipped enhancements vanish whenever a life is lost.

On each planet, Opa-Opa must destroy every enemy base; a boss then appears and must be beaten to advance to the next planet. The game is for one player, who starts with three ships.
>
> Combat relies on a main gun alongside dropped bombs. Coins collected along the way buy speed parts, stronger guns and special bombs at the parts shop, reached by capturing a SHOP balloon, and prices rise with each purchase. Removed arcade/other-version details with no Tengen-NES evidence: looping stages, walking on feet, extra lives in the shop, weapon time or quantity limits, and losing all items on death. Added the manual's eight planets, Menons, three ships, one-player mode, rising shop prices, one-item-per-category rule and SEL balloon.

- Money buys speed upgrades, stronger weapons, extra lives and special explosives from shop balloons — No extra lives in the Tengen manual's shop list. Removed. (manual ocr pp. 2-3 (PARTS SHOP via SHOP balloon: Speedup parts, Weapon 1 beams/shots, Weapon 2 bombs))

## Faxanadu (`58f2ba801354a8e5`)

- **Classification:** substantive; error types: invented detail, wrong name, other-version detail, unsupported specific
- **Queue:** main (m32-audit-medium-risk)
- **Manual:** Faxanadu (USA); page images inspected: yes (p01, p02, p03, p04, p05, p06, p09, p10, p13, p14)
- **Verification:** level D; remaining uncertainty: None material. Whether the hero is returning home is not covered by the US manual, so it was removed rather than asserted.

**Before:**

> Faxanadu combines side-scrolling platforming with action role-playing gameplay. Controlling an adventurer named Nello, the player returns to the troubled Elven town of Eolis at the base of the World Tree. The protagonist sets out to climb the tree, discover why the water supply has stopped, and defeat The Evil One. Progression moves screen by screen through fields, towns, and dungeons across four primary overworld regions: the buttress, the trunk, the branches, and a mountain stronghold.
>
> The character walks, jumps, climbs ladders, strikes foes with bladed weapons, and casts offensive magic projectiles. Defeated adversaries leave behind experience, currency, health-restoring bread, or other items. Experience raises the hero's rank through church Gurus, who also provide password mantras to resume play. Players speak with villagers for information, spend collected gold in shops on usable gear or armor, and monitor status meters for health, magic power, items, and experience.

**After:**

> Faxanadu combines side-scrolling platforming with action role-playing gameplay. The hero sets out from the Elf town of Eolis at the base of the World Tree, where meteorites are raining down, crazed monsters run amuck, and the wells are drying up. His mission is to penetrate the giant World Tree and overthrow the Evil One, who lives in the fortress of Zenis in the Evil Place. The journey passes through towns on the tree's trunk and branches, and reaching the fortress requires solving a number of mysteries.
>
> The character walks, jumps, climbs ladders, strikes foes with bladed weapons, and casts offensive magic. Some defeated adversaries leave behind money or food that partially restores energy. Experience raises the hero's rank through Gurus, who also provide password mantras to resume play. Players speak with villagers for information, spend collected gold in shops on usable gear or armor, and monitor status meters for health, magic power, items, and experience.

**What was wrong and why it changed:** Removed the unsupported hero name 'Nello' and the 'returns' framing; replaced the water-supply objective with the stated mission; replaced the invented four-region list (buttress/trunk/branches/mountain stronghold) with the towns and fortress shown on the map; changed 'bread' to food that partially restores energy; dropped 'church' and 'projectiles'.

**Contradicted by NES evidence:**

- The hero is an adventurer named Nello — The manual never names the hero; he is only 'the Hero'. Search results describe the NES hero as unnamed. 'Nello' is unsupported. (manual p02-p14; Wikipedia search snippet)
- The protagonist must discover why the water supply has stopped — Manual: wells are drying up, meteorites are raining down on the World Tree and monsters run amuck; the mission is to penetrate the World Tree and overthrow the Evil One. No investigation of the water supply is stated as the goal. (manual p02)
- Four regions: the buttress, the trunk, the branches and a mountain stronghold — The map names Elf Town Eolis, Trunk Towns, Mist Towns, Branch Towns, the Town of the Evil Place and Fortress Zenis in the Evil Place. No 'buttress' region or count of four. (manual p03)

**Other sources checked:** https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faxanadu (search snippet only: hero unnamed in NES version)

## Final Fantasy (`fa456d852372173e`)

- **Classification:** substantive; error types: wrong name, wrong control, unsupported specific
- **Queue:** main (nes-native-untouched)
- **Manual:** Final Fantasy (USA); page images inspected: yes (p08, p11, p19, p39)
- **Verification:** level D; remaining uncertainty: Level cap and game-over behavior removed because no independent NES source was read; StrategyWiki and nesguide returned 403.

**Before:**

> Final Fantasy is a role-playing game where players control four Warriors of Light seeking to restore four darkened elemental crystals and save the world from evil forces. Play begins by assembling a four-person party from six classes: Fighter, Thief, Black Belt, Red Mage, White Mage, and Black Mage. Characters explore towns, dungeons, and an overworld map, initially traveling on foot before gaining access to a ship, canoe, and airship. Play begins by assembling a four-person party from six classes: Fighter, Thief, Black Belt, Red Mage, White Mage, and Black Mage. Characters explore towns, dungeons, and an overworld map, initially traveling on foot before gaining access to a ship, canoe, and airship. Towns offer information, items, and equipment, while dungeons feature treasure chests and boss encounters.
>
> Encountering enemies triggers turn-based, menu-driven combat where players select commands including Fight, Magic, Drink, Item, and Run. Defeating monsters yields money and experience points, allowing characters to raise their attributes and advance in level. Later in the journey, characters can undergo a class change that expands equipment and magic capabilities. Staying at an inn restores the party's hit points and magic and saves the game to the cartridge's battery.

**What was wrong and why it changed:** Renamed 'Warriors of Light' and 'elemental crystals' to the US manual's 'Light Warriors' and 'Orbs'; corrected battle commands (Fight, Magic, Drink, Item, Run); removed the unverified level-50 cap and game-over sentence, replacing the latter with the documented inn save rule; 'class upgrade' now 'class change' as in the manual.

- Four Warriors of Light restore four darkened elemental crystals — US NES manual calls the heroes 'Light Warriors' and the objects 'Orbs' ('These are the Four Orbs that you must restore'; 'the darkened orbs that you carry'). 'Elemental' is not stated. (manual p08 (image), OCR orbs passage)
- Turn-based menu combat with Attack, Magic and Item — Commands are FIGHT, MAGIC, DRINK, ITEM and RUN; there is no 'Attack' command. (manual p11 (image))

**Other sources checked:** https://guides.gamercorner.net/ff/walkthrough/game-systems (NES guide; no level-cap or game-over statement found)

Players also collect life-restoring flags, ammunition necklaces, and invincibility necklaces.

**After:**

> Controlling Ken, the player battles through eight scenes to rescue his people from the tyranny of the Emperor Heaven. Ken must defeat eight enemies, including generals of Gento and Gold Falco, whose attacks include Fireballs, White Light Bombs, and a deadly sliding kick. Ken punches, kicks, jumps, and crouches while exploring each stage left to right or up and down. At times he can enter the next room by pressing both attack buttons together and then right at an entrance. Knocking a boss down scores points, and finding and hitting its weakest point scores far more.
>
> Knocking down certain enemies produces stars that multiply Ken's strength up to seven times. Twenty knockdowns earn a shooting attack. The flag of Hokuto restores lost energy, Yulia's silver necklace restores shooting power, and her gold necklace grants Gento Karate, which lets enemies and objects pass through Ken harmlessly. A VS mode offers practice against the enemies of the first four stages.

**What was wrong and why it changed:** Rewrote from the US manual: replaced anime-derived setting and names (Raoh, Central Imperial Capital, Tentei, Hokuto Army, Kenshiro, Falco the Gold as leader) with Ken, the Emperor Heaven, generals of Gento and Gold Falco; corrected the door control (A+B then right); removed undocumented power-level abilities; kept the star, shooting and item facts as documented; added the VS practice mode.

**Contradicted by NES evidence:**

- Confronting the Four Generals of Gento and their leader Falco the Gold — Manual names Tiger and 'Blue Light Bolts' as Big Four Generals of Gento; 'Gold Falco' (stage 7) is a master of Gento Karate and one of Ken's most fearful enemies, not stated to be their leader. Stage 8 enemy is Shula. (manual p06, p07)
- Progresses across a single plane from left to right — 'explore the screen by moving from left to right or up and down'. (manual p04)
- Doors entered by pressing up while holding both attack buttons — 'Press the A button and B button at the same time and then press the right side of the Control Pad after moving to the entrance of the room.' (manual p03 (page 4))

Up to four players can participate in the World Conquest scenario.

**What was wrong and why it changed:** Replaced 'empire across historic eras' (one period only) with the Eurasian setting; replaced the unsupported 'rotating country sequences' with one turn per season; tied the three-order limit to the base country; limited four-player play to the World Conquest scenario (Mongol Conquest is one player).

**Contradicted by NES evidence:**

- oversee an empire across historic eras — Both scenarios cover one period (starting 1174 and 1205) on the Eurasian continent, not multiple eras. (manual p04 (image))

## George Foreman's KO Boxing (`cf517940496d6085`)

- **Classification:** substantive; error types: wrong rule, unsupported specific
- **Queue:** main (nes-native-untouched)
- **Manual:** George Foreman's KO Boxing (USA); page images inspected: yes (p01, p06, p07, p10, p11)
- **Verification:** level D; remaining uncertainty: None material.

**Before:**

> Taking on the role of 43-year-old boxer George Foreman, the player seeks to become the undisputed world heavyweight champion by claiming the title belts across three fictional boxing circuits. Matches unfold across three rounds, where players attempt to overcome their rivals through skilled offense and defense.
>
> During bouts, boxers can block incoming strikes, dodge attacks in two directions, and execute an assortment of punches. Contests can conclude in three distinct ways. Landing four total knockdowns against an adversary across the three rounds secures a knockout victory when the fallen opponent fails to beat the referee's count. A technical knockout occurs if a fighter goes down three times within one round. When three rounds conclude without a knockout, judges award the decision according to landed strikes, attempted punches, scored knockdowns, and accumulated damage. Progress across the career mode is tracked using passwords.

**After:**

> Taking on the role of 43-year-old boxer George Foreman, the player seeks to become the undisputed world heavyweight champion by claiming the title belts across three boxing circuits. Matches unfold across three rounds, where players attempt to overcome their rivals through skilled offense and defense.
>
> During bouts, boxers can block incoming strikes, dodge attacks in two directions, and execute an assortment of punches, and successful combinations earn Superpunches. Contests can be won in several ways. Knocking an opponent down four times in a fight wins the bout, as does a fallen boxer failing to rise before the count of ten. A technical knockout occurs if a fighter goes down three times within one round. When three rounds conclude without a knockout, judges award the decision based on punches landed, knockdowns, damage and overall command of the rounds. Passwords awarded for each title belt let players resume, and two players can fight single bouts against each other.

**What was wrong and why it changed:** Knockout rule split into the manual's four-knockdown rule and the ten count; 'three distinct ways' generalized; 'attempted punches' removed from the decision criteria; 'fictional' dropped; added Superpunches, password timing and the two-player bout mode.

**Contradicted by NES evidence:**

- Four total knockdowns secure a knockout when the fallen opponent fails to beat the count — Manual: 'Knock down your opponent 4 times in a fight and you win the bout' (no count condition). The ten count is a separate rule (p06, p11). (manual p10)
- Judges decide on landed strikes, attempted punches, knockdowns and damage — Manual: punches landed and overall command of the rounds; opponent's decision from knockouts, technical knockouts and damage. 'Attempted punches' not mentioned. (manual p10, p11)

## Ghost Lion (`1849bb687d038a43`)

- **Classification:** rewrite; error types: wrong name, invented detail, wrong rule, wrong item effect
- **Queue:** main (nes-native-untouched)
- **Manual:** Legend of the Ghost Lion (USA); page images inspected: yes (p01, p03, p05, p06, p07, p08, p09, p10, p12, p13)
- **Verification:** level D; remaining uncertainty: None material.

**Before:**

> Set within an exploratory open-world environment, this adventure guides players through a largely linear story. The narrative centers on Maria, who awakens in an unfamiliar realm after being swept down a river while searching for her missing parents. To locate them and return home, she must navigate this land and track down the mysterious White Lion. Movement is handled with the directional pad, while the face buttons govern interaction and menus. Progression relies on conversations with non-player characters, world exploration, and visiting fairy springs to recover health and record progress.
>
> Encountering foes initiates turn-based combat managed through menus. Maria can strike adversaries directly or consume items to summon allied spirits into battle. Defeating enemies provides currency, whereas increasing Maria's Hope level, Courage hit points, and Dream magic points requires finding Miracles inside treasure chests placed across the environment.

**After:**

> Ghost Lion is a role-playing adventure viewed from above. Maria's parents set out to solve the mystery of the white Ghost Lion and have not been seen for days, so after visiting the village elders she goes forth to find them and unravel the legend. Progression relies on speaking with friendly characters, examining surroundings, and visiting Springs, where winged characters record the journey and replenish Maria's COURAGE and DREAMS.
>
> Encountering foes leads to a choice to fight or run, and battles play out in turns through menus. Maria can fight with a weapon or tool she carries or call upon spirit companions such as Moja, the spirit of the spear, and Twana, who uses magic. Each call for help uses DREAMS, and the game ends when COURAGE reaches zero. Rubies come from treasure chests and defeated enemies and buy items, while fragments of hope raise Maria's HOPE and with it her capacity for COURAGE and DREAMS.

**What was wrong and why it changed:** Bounded rewrite from the manual: removed the river, 'White Lion', 'consuming items to summon' and 'Miracles'; restored the manual's story, the Ghost Lion name, Springs with winged characters, spirit companions, DREAMS cost, rubies and fragments of hope.

**Contradicted by NES evidence:**

- Maria awakens in an unfamiliar realm after being swept down a river while searching for her parents — Manual: her parents left to solve the mystery of the white Ghost Lion; after visiting the village elders Maria sets out to find them; after the story 'you will find yourself in a cave'. No river. (manual p03, p06)
- She must track down the mysterious White Lion — Manual name is the Ghost Lion (described as the white Ghost Lion); objective is to find her parents and learn the mystery of the Ghost Lion. (manual p03, p06)
- Maria can strike directly or consume items to summon allied spirits — Manual: fight with a selected tool, or call upon a spirit, which costs DREAMS points. Items are not consumed to summon. (manual p07, p09)
- Hope level, Courage hit points and Dream magic points raised by finding Miracles in treasure chests — Manual: HOPE is increased by finding fragments of hope scattered throughout the land; higher HOPE raises capacity for COURAGE and DREAMS. DREAMS are spent to call companions, not magic points. 'Miracles' not in the manual. (manual p06, p07)

## Ghostbusters II (`1ea36ebd81692d3a`)

- **Classification:** substantive; error types: wrong name, wrong count, invented detail
- **Queue:** main (nes-native-untouched)
- **Manual:** Ghostbusters II (USA); page images inspected: yes (p01, p05, p06, p07, p08, p10)
- **Verification:** level D; remaining uncertainty: '1989 film' rests on the 1989 Columbia Pictures copyright line in the manual; the film year is not stated in prose.

**Before:**

> Defeating Vigo the Carpathian in the final level serves as the ultimate objective in this side-scrolling action title based on the 1989 film. Players progress through various stages that present different tasks and control schemes throughout the campaign.
>
> Controlling a Ghostbuster in one underground sewer stage, the player must avoid ghosts and giant spiders. Gameplay additionally features a sequence where the player takes control of the Statue of Liberty before advancing toward the final confrontation.

**After:**

> Defeating Vigo, the Scourge of Carpathia, in the final level serves as the ultimate objective in this side-scrolling action title based on the 1989 film. Players progress through various stages that present different tasks and control schemes throughout the campaign.
>
> Controlling a Ghostbuster in one underground tunnel stage, the player must avoid ghosts and a pursuing spider. Other levels introduce vehicular segments where the player navigates the Ecto-1A, maneuvering around hazards and firing shots at approaching spirits. Gameplay additionally features a sequence where the player takes control of the Statue of Liberty before advancing toward the final confrontation.

**What was wrong and why it changed:** Vigo's name set to the manual's 'Vigo, the Scourge of Carpathia'; 'sewer' changed to 'tunnel'; 'giant spiders' changed to a single pursuing spider; 'Ectomobile' changed to 'Ecto-1A'. Other sentences kept word for word.

**Contradicted by NES evidence:**

- Final objective is defeating Vigo the Carpathian — Objective (defeat Vigo) is supported (p06, p07, OCR p19), but the manual names him 'Vigo, the Scourge of Carpathia', not 'Vigo the Carpathian' (film name). (manual p05 (image))
- Controlling a Ghostbuster in an underground sewer stage — Scene One is Van Horne Station, 'an abandoned underground pneumatic train tunnel', not a sewer. (manual p08 (image))
- Player must avoid ghosts and giant spiders — Manual describes a single spider 'that's dogging your steps'; plural 'giant spiders' unsupported. (manual p10 (image))
- Vehicular segments driving the Ectomobile, avoiding hazards and firing at spirits — Vehicle is named 'Ecto-1A'; driving, barricades, firing at ghosts are supported. (manual p06, p07 (image); OCR pp.11-12)

## Ghosts'n Goblins (`eea66f7bcc90d114`)

- **Classification:** substantive; error types: wrong name, other-version detail, unsupported specific
- **Queue:** escalation (m32-audit-corrected)
- **Manual:** Ghosts'n Goblins (USA); page images inspected: yes (p04, p05, p06, p07)
- **Verification:** level D; remaining uncertainty: The official description and later franchise material call the hero Arthur, but the NES manual never names him; on-screen naming in the NES ROM was not checked. The manual's 'Cross' weapon is described as a shield in one NES review.

**Before:**

> Seven guarded gates structure the journey to rescue the princess and confront the Devil. The player controls the knight Arthur on his quest against supernatural captors. Arthur must defeat various adversaries, including zombies, giants, demons, cyclopes, and dragons, while racing against a set time limit for each level.
>
> Taking two hits costs Arthur a life, sending the player back to a checkpoint or the beginning of the stage. Players can collect bonus points, extra suits of armor, and alternative weapons like the javelin, dagger, and axe. Certain weapons cannot harm specific bosses. Conquering the Devil requires navigating through the stages a second time at a higher difficulty to view the final ending.

**After:**

> Seven guarded gates structure the journey to rescue the Princess and confront the Devil. The player controls a knight on his quest against supernatural captors. The Knight must defeat various adversaries, including zombies, ravens, flying knights, unicorns, and dragons, while racing against a set time limit for each level.
>
> Taking two hits costs the Knight a life, sending the player back to a checkpoint or the beginning of the stage. Players can collect bonus points, extra suits of armor, and alternative weapons like the javelin, sword, and axe. Certain weapons cannot harm specific bosses. Conquering the Devil requires navigating through the stages a second time to view the final ending.

**What was wrong and why it changed:** Replaced 'Arthur' with the NES manual's 'the Knight'; replaced the non-manual enemy list (giants, demons, cyclopes) with manual enemy names; changed 'dagger' to the NES manual's 'sword'; removed the unsupported 'at a higher difficulty'. The earlier seven-gates correction is confirmed.

**Contradicted by NES evidence:**

- The player controls the knight Arthur — The NES manual calls the hero only 'the Knight'; the name Arthur does not appear. Changed to the manual's name. (manual p04-p05 (image))
- Weapons like the javelin, dagger, and axe — NES weapons are javelins, torches, swords, axes and crosses; there is no dagger. 'dagger' changed to 'sword'. (manual p04 (image))

**Other sources checked:** https://dailydead.com/retro-gaming-review-ghosts-n-goblins-nes/ (NES review: checkpoints, two-minute limit, game must be beaten twice); https://gameluster.com/ghosts-n-goblins-retroluster/ (NES port review: beaten twice; Satan not killed without the Shield weapon)

## Godzilla - Monster of Monsters! (`c2383e5cd8670c71`)

- **Classification:** rewrite; error types: wrong rule, wrong name, wrong count, invented detail
- **Queue:** main (nes-native-untouched)
- **Manual:** Godzilla - Monster of Monsters! (USA); page images inspected: yes (p04, p18, p19)
- **Verification:** level D; remaining uncertainty: The 'Ghidora' spelling was read from clean OCR; the characters page image was not separately opened.

**Before:**

> Players control the giant monsters Godzilla and Mothra to defend Earth against an invading legion from Planet X. Gameplay alternates between navigating a strategic grid and completing side-scrolling action sequences. On each planetary board, the player chooses a monster and shifts it across hexagonal spaces similar to a chess piece. Entering a space triggers a brief side-scrolling level set within rocky, jungle, city, or hyperspace environments populated by hostile alien forces.
>
> The overarching goal requires defeating every opposing monster on a board to proceed to the next world. Moving adjacent to an enemy initiates a forty-second, fighting-game-style duel without an on-screen timer. Opposing forces expand across subsequent planets, ranging from Earth to Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Pluto, and ultimately Planet X. On Planet X, players face all previously encountered enemy creatures before fighting King Ghidorah.

**After:**

> Players control the giant monsters Godzilla and Mothra to defend Earth against an invading legion from Planet X. Gameplay alternates between navigating a strategic grid and completing side-scrolling action sequences. On each planetary board, called a Ring Field, the player chooses a monster and shifts it across hexagonal spaces, taking turns with the enemy monsters. Moving triggers side-scrolling levels set in environments such as wilderness, volcano, jungle, ruins, sub-space, and Mecha City.
>
> The goal on each board is to advance Godzilla or Mothra to the enemy base rather than to defeat every opposing monster. Moving adjacent to an enemy allows a one-on-one, fighting-game-style duel that ends in a draw after about forty seconds. The boards run from Earth to Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Pluto, Neptune, and finally Planet X, home of Ghidora, king of the enemy monsters.

**What was wrong and why it changed:** Rewrote around the NES rules: objective is reaching the enemy base, not defeating all monsters; stage types from the manual; duel draw after about 40 seconds; Neptune added to the planet order; 'King Ghidorah' replaced by the manual's 'Ghidora'; removed the unsupported Planet X boss-rush claim.

**Contradicted by NES evidence:**

- Levels set in rocky, jungle, city or hyperspace environments — Battle stage types are Wilderness, Volcano, Jungle, Ruins, Sub-space, Mecha City and Base. (manual p19 (image))
- Goal is defeating every opposing monster on a board — 'The purpose of this game is to reach the enemy headquarters, not to beat all enemy monsters.' (manual p04 (image))
- Adjacent enemy triggers a forty-second fighting duel without on-screen timer — Fight becomes a draw after approximately 40 seconds; 'without an on-screen timer' unsupported. (manual p18 (image))
- Planet order Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Pluto, Planet X — Order includes Neptune after Pluto, before Planet X. (manual p19 (image))
- On Planet X players face all previous enemies before fighting King Ghidorah — Not described; manual names the boss 'Ghidora' and the win condition is reaching the Planet X headquarters. (manual OCR story and characters)

## Godzilla 2 - War of the Monsters (`37b5a1c9d9bc1747`)

- **Classification:** substantive; error types: wrong rule, unsupported specific
- **Queue:** escalation (m32-recovered-manual)
- **Manual:** Godzilla 2 - War of the Monsters (USA); page images inspected: yes (p03, p08, p12, p13)
- **Verification:** level D; remaining uncertainty: 'Invading' reflects the story's monster outbreak and alien invasion; acceptable but loosely worded.

**Before:**

> Eliminating all invading giant monsters across twelve independent scenarios is the primary goal of the Allied Defense Forces. Players can select any scenario, each providing distinct maps, enemy threats, and military units to command against threats such as Godzilla.
>
> Gameplay alternates between map and battle modes across turn-based rounds. >
> Gameplay alternates between map and battle modes across turn-based rounds. During the Allied turn, the player moves individual military units across the grid, launches new units from bases or the laboratory, and consults scientists for tactical guidance. Moving onto an enemy square and choosing to attack initiates battle mode, where combat plays out with animated sequences. In battle, weapons are selected while a three-reel slot machine can be stopped to adjust offensive power, defense, or hit accuracy based on matching symbols. The scenario ends in failure if the defense forces lose all military units, allow critical structures like power plants to fall, or fail to eliminate the monsters within 99 turns.

**What was wrong and why it changed:** Battle now starts only when the player chooses to attack after moving onto a monster's square (manual offers ATTACK or STAND BY); 'visits vital locations such as bases or laboratories' changed to launching units from bases or the laboratory; added the manual's 99-turn limit to the loss conditions.

**Contradicted by NES evidence:**

- Reaching an enemy square initiates battle mode — Moving onto a monster's square offers ATTACK or STAND BY; battle starts only if ATTACK is chosen. Fixed. (manual p08 (image))

> Directing a transforming protagonist called the Guardian, the player battles alien forces to trigger the self-destruction of an encroaching world known as Naju. **Before:**

> Infiltrating an underground nuclear missile complex and defeating the enemy leader guides the mission after terrorists take control of the installation. Viewed from an overhead perspective, players advance into the facility using a firearm with limitless ammunition along with a restricted stock of grenades.
>
> Keys open locked crates encountered throughout the base, revealing orbs, grenade upgrades, and improved armament. Containers also conceal fragments of the Heavy Barrel, an energy cannon assembled after gathering six individual pieces. Up to two players can participate, with the collector of the final piece receiving the assembled cannon.

**After:**

> Infiltrating an underground nuclear missile complex and defeating the enemy leader guides the mission after terrorists take control of the installation. Viewed from an overhead perspective, players advance into the facility using a firearm with limitless ammunition along with a restricted stock of grenades.
>
> Keys dropped by red terrorists open lockers encountered throughout the base, revealing weapons, ammunition, or fragments of the Heavy Barrel, a superweapon reassembled after gathering six individual pieces. Once formed, it fires super-powerful blasts for ninety-nine seconds, after which another can be assembled. Other firearms include a laser gun, a pellet gun and a flame thrower. The complex is divided into six defense perimeters sealed by blast doors, ahead of the Launch Authority Security Area. Up to two players can participate.

**What was wrong and why it changed:** Crates with orbs and grenade upgrades corrected to lockers holding weapons, ammunition or Heavy Barrel pieces, opened with keys from red terrorists; 'energy cannon' with a wide firing arc corrected to the manual's super-powerful single blasts; the unsupported final-piece rule removed; reassembly after time-out, other firearms and the perimeter structure added. Earlier M3.2 99-second correction confirmed.

**Contradicted by NES evidence:**

- Keys open locked crates revealing orbs, grenade upgrades and improved armament — Red terrorists carry keys; lockers contain Heavy Barrel pieces, weapons and ammunition; no 'orbs'. (manual p03 (image))
- Wide firing arc that eliminates most targets in a single hit — Manual: 'Super-powerful blasts, one at a time.' (manual p04 (image))

## Heavy Shreddin' (`0a23312c8e07b9af`)

**Before:**

> Guiding a snowboarder down various snowy slopes constitutes the central action of this title. The player begins the run with four lives, aiming to navigate down three different mountains to reach the end of the game. Progress requires successfully clearing consecutive events, as each stage must be completed before the subsequent one unlocks. Running out of time or suffering a fall deducts a life from the reserve.
>
> Across the campaign, the game provides five distinct events spanning eighteen total levels. Each mountain features three separate tiers of navigation: novice courses labeled with a circle, intermediate courses marked by a square, and expert courses designated with a diamond. Clearing an entire trail awards a bonus life, supporting the player in advancing through all remaining courses to finish the game.

**After:**

> Guiding a snowboarder down various snowy slopes constitutes the central action of this title. The player begins the run with four lives, aiming to complete every event and win the World Cup trophy. Progress requires successfully clearing consecutive events, as each run must be completed before the subsequent one unlocks. Falling or failing to qualify deducts a life from the reserve.
>
> Across the campaign, the game provides five distinct events spanning eighteen total levels: Downhill, Slalom, Half-pipe, Moguls and Backwoods. The first four have three levels of difficulty each, while Backwoods has six. Players turn while standing or tucked, duck under obstacles, jump, and perform four stunts, including the Hand-Plant required in the Half-pipe and the Mule-Kick used over mogul fields. Reaching the next trail awards a bonus life, supporting the player in advancing through all remaining courses to finish the game.

**What was wrong and why it changed:** Removed unsupported three-mountain structure and circle/square/diamond tier markers; replaced with manual's event names, difficulty-level counts, World Cup trophy goal and stunt moves; 'running out of time' aligned to 'failing to qualify'.

> Action takes place on a vertically scrolling main table alongside specialized bonus stages. > Scoring baskets in half-court basketball matchups forms the core goal for participants. Matches follow a two-on-two format, and players can select whether to activate or turn off winners-outs rules. **After:**

> Scoring baskets in half-court basketball matchups forms the core goal for participants. Each basket counts one point, and games run to 10, 15, 20 or 25 points in either a one-on-one or two-on-two format. Players can choose losers-out or winners-out rules and an eastern or western city court, and eight neighborhood players with different strengths are available. Pushing, charging and traveling are called as fouls, and an offensive foul gives the ball to the other side. When an athlete attempts a slam dunk within range, the view switches to a close-up, and a defender in position can still block the attempt.
>
> Aside from regular competition, the title provides an Around the World mode, in which players take turns shooting from eleven spots around the court. Two-on-two tournaments issue a password after each win, and winning 15 games brings a special ending sequence.

**What was wrong and why it changed:** Corrected two-on-two-only format to one-on-one or two-on-two; corrected 'no fouls' (manual calls pushing, charging, traveling fouls); slow motion replaced with the manual's close-up; Around the World described from manual; added point targets, court choice, eight players and tournament passwords.

- Matches follow a two-on-two format — Games can be one-on-one or two-on-two. (manual OCR mode select; p13)
- Referees call no fouls — 'Break a rule and you will be charged with a foul. When on offense a foul causes a change of possession.' (manual p15)
- Dunk attempt transitions to a slow-motion sequence and can be blocked — Manual: a close-up of the character flying toward the basket; a defender in position can block. 'Slow-motion' not stated. (manual p13)

## Hot Slots (`9e552c628e4e2ab6`)

- **Classification:** unsupported detail generalized; error types: unsupported specific

- **Manual:** none available; page images inspected: no
- **Verification:** level D; remaining uncertainty: Removed specifics (machine names Cutie Bunny/Juicy Fruits/Las Vegas, medallions, $210/$300/$450 thresholds) may well be correct but rest only on encyclopedia-derived text; a manual or gameplay capture could restore them. **Before:**

> Earning money through simulated slot machine betting serves as the primary objective, with the game revealing increasingly explicit images of hostesses as profits accumulate. >
> During each pull, the player wagers up to five medallions and presses directions on the D-pad to halt the spinning reels individually. Players may change machines between spins. Reaching a net profit of $210 displays a full-screen illustration of the machine's hostess in minimal clothing alongside dialogue. Advancing to $300 removes further attire, while achieving $450 in profit shows the hostess fully nude.

**After:**

> Earning money through simulated slot machine betting serves as the primary objective, with the game rewarding large winnings with erotic images of hostesses. Players choose among three machines, each leading to a different hostess with her own short scenes and comments.
>
> During play, the player wagers on each pull of the machine and tries to build up a profit. Winning a large amount of money in a round displays illustrations of the machine's hostess, partly clothed or nude.

**What was wrong and why it changed:** No manual and no independent NES source beyond MobyGames; machine names, medallion terms, five-coin bet limit, D-pad reel stops, machine switching and exact profit thresholds removed as unsupported specifics. Kept the three-machine structure and the erotic-reward premise that MobyGames confirms.

**Other sources checked:** http://web.archive.org/web/2023/https://www.mobygames.com/game/nes/hot-slots; http://web.archive.org/web/2022/https://strategywiki.org/wiki/Hot_Slots; https://retroachievements.org/game/4569 (blocked by 403 and an age gate; no content read)

> Ascending vertical mountain slopes to reclaim stolen vegetables from a giant condor serves as the primary goal. **Contradicted by NES evidence:**

- Fights during puck battles send the defeated skater to the penalty box — Surrounding players start fighting; a player from one of the teams is given a penalty and put in the penalty box; not described as the loser (manual p06)
