## Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade - The Action Game (`79c03fec3f459ac6`)

- **Classification:** rewrite; error types: other-version detail, wrong control
- **Queue:** escalation (m32-audit-corrected)
- **Manual:** Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade (UBI Soft) (USA); page images inspected: yes (p01, p02, p03, p04, p05, p06, p07, p08, p09, p10, p11)
- **Verification:** level D; remaining uncertainty: The manual spells the trial word 'Jehova'; the ROM's on-screen spelling was not checked. The main menu lists an 'Enter Code' option, but no NES-specific source confirmed how codes work, so passwords are not mentioned. The cup-choice detail comes from the on-screen text in the manual's level 6 screenshot ('Choose wisely, all but one of the cups is poisoned').

**Before:**

> Guiding Indiana Jones through side-scrolling environments, the player undertakes an action adventure based on the feature film. The protagonist can punch, whip, jump, and kick while navigating various stages. Challenges begin aboard a ship to reclaim the Cross of Coronado by battling hostile sailors and defeating their captain. Other destinations include solving a tile puzzle in the catacombs of Venice and exploring Castle Brunwald to locate and rescue Jones' father while fighting guards.
>
> Additional sequences require fighting soldiers atop a moving tank in the desert and escaping on a motorcycle along the road to Berlin while dodging hazards and enemy pursuers. The journey concludes inside the lost temple, where players navigate letter tiles, leap across a chasm, and identify the true Holy Grail.

**After:**

> Indiana Jones sets out to find the Holy Grail and his missing father, Professor Henry Jones, in a one-player side-scrolling action game based on the film. Indy runs, jumps and climbs ropes and ladders, fighting with his fists, a whip that grows stronger with each one collected, and a gun loaded with three bullets. Each level has a time limit; hourglasses add time and hearts restore energy.
>
> The six levels begin in caves, where torches light the way and the Cross of Coronado must be found, followed by an escape on a circus train. In the catacombs, Indy seeks four pieces forming an X and a shield, then scales the walls of Brunwald Castle for the missing pieces of Professor Jones' notebook and escapes from a Zeppelin. The final level holds three trials: jumping over blades, stepping on the letters of Jehova and making the leap of faith, followed by a choice among cups, all but one of them poisoned.

**What was wrong and why it changed:** The current text describes Taito's different 1991 NES game (ship opening, Venice tile puzzle, rescuing the father at Brunwald, tank, motorcycle, kick). Bounded rewrite from the UBI Soft US manual: one-player, movement and weapons (fists, a whip that strengthens with each pickup, a three-bullet gun), the time limit with hourglass and heart pickups, and the six levels in order (caves, circus train, catacombs, Brunwald Castle, Zeppelin, The Three Trials ending in the cup choice).

**Contradicted by NES evidence:**

- The protagonist can punch, whip, jump, and kick — Controls: B hits someone/something or uses a weapon, A jumps, SELECT selects a weapon, UP/DOWN climb ropes and ladders, DOWN crouches. Weapons are fists, whip (from level 2) and gun (from level 4). No kick is listed. (manual p04 (booklet p5), p08 (booklet p12))
- Challenges begin aboard a ship to reclaim the Cross of Coronado by battling hostile sailors and defeating their captain — Level 1 is 'Exploring the caves': find the Cross of Coronado in the caves; torches light the way; a Big Boss uses wooden beams. No ship level (this is Taito 1991 game content). (manual p08 (booklet p13))
- Solving a tile puzzle in the catacombs of Venice — Level 3 'Entering the Catacombs': find four pieces that form an X and the shield; fireballs, rats, protectors of the Holy Grail, the Fire Breather. No tile puzzle. 'Venetian catacombs' is named on booklet p3. (manual p09 (booklet p15), p03)
- Exploring Castle Brunwald to locate and rescue Jones' father while fighting guards — Level 4 'Assault on Brunwald Castle': scale the walls to find the 4 missing pieces of Professor Jones' notebook; German soldiers and a sniper. No rescue of the father is described. (manual p10 (booklet p16))
- Fighting soldiers atop a moving tank in the desert — The six levels are caves, circus train, catacombs, Brunwald Castle, airship (Zeppelin), The Three Trials. No tank level. (manual p08-p11 level list)
- Escaping on a motorcycle along the road to Berlin while dodging hazards and pursuers — No motorcycle level; level 5 is 'Escape from the Airship' (find the key to start the airplane's engine and get out of the Zeppelin). (manual p08-p11 level list)

> Staged around the events of World War II, this top-view action shooting title portrays the invasion of Normandy, beginning on June 5, 1944. The campaign centers on Paul, a combat veteran from a secret unit known as "Iron Snake."
>
> Controlling the Iron Tank, the player must establish a beachhead, break through the front lines, and infiltrate and destroy the enemy headquarters. Power-up items add rapid, armor-piercing, explosive and long-range shots, while energy items refuel the tank. One or two players can play at the same time, and a password resumes an earlier game.

**What was wrong and why it changed:** Fixed the 'codename Snake' error (Iron Snake is Paul's unit); replaced 'Nazi German stronghold' with the manual's mission; expanded the thin text with manual-supported controls, routes, radio messages, power-ups, simultaneous two-player mode and password.

**Contradicted by NES evidence:**

- Commando named Paul with the codename Snake — Paul is from Command Unit 88, a secret unit known as 'Iron Snake'; 'Snake' is not his codename (manual p03)

**What was wrong and why it changed:** Replaced the wall-toppling goal with the manual's goal; 'Horn blasts' to 'Trumpet blasts'; barrier sentence narrowed to what the manual states; 'boulders' replaced by pushable falling objects; question reward described via Bibles.

**Contradicted by NES evidence:**

- Primary goal is toppling the wall of Jericho — goal is to complete as many levels as possible, scoring points, before running out of chances; fixed (manual p02 (Object of the Game))
- Horn blasts called toots — Toots come from Joshua's trumpet; Ram's Horns are separate dropped blasts; fixed to 'Trumpet blasts' (manual p03-p04)
- Movable boulders — no boulders; pushable objects respond to gravity (wall pieces, boundaries, idols); reworded (manual p04)

> Throughout the journey, characters collect power-ups to enhance their speed, jumps, weapons, and shields across up to twenty levels. Stages also contain life-increasing pick-ups, harmful life-reducing items, and tools that reveal concealed barriers. Players must uncover hidden caves positioned within the levels to obtain essential lettered elements, avoid fireball-shooting statues, and defeat interior dragons before proceeding toward the final confrontation.

**After:**

> King's Knight provides vertically scrolling shooter gameplay. The story begins after Princess Claire is kidnapped by a Dragon in the Kingdom of Izander. Four heroes take part: the knight Ray Jack, the wizard Kaliva, the monster Barusa, and the thief Toby. Each first clears a stage alone, and in the fifth and final stage the four band together to defeat the evil Dragon and rescue the princess. During each stage, the player navigates upward while destroying or evading onscreen adversaries and hazards.
>
> Throughout the journey, characters collect power-ups to enhance their speed, jumps, weapons, and shields, raising each hero's level as high as twenty. Stages also contain life-increasing pick-ups and harmful life-reducing items, and destroying obstacles such as trees, rocks, and statues can reveal hidden items. Magic elements hidden across the first four stages, including inside a hidden cave, unlock each hero's single-use spell for the final stage. Cleared stages can be replayed to build strength.

**What was wrong and why it changed:** Removed non-manual names (Olthea, Gargatua Castle, Tolfida); corrected 'select among four heroes' to the sequential solo-stage structure; fixed 'twenty levels' (level is an item count; five stages); removed unsupported statues/dragons/barrier claims and added manual-supported spell elements and replay.

**Contradicted by NES evidence:**

- Players select among four heroes — The four strike out on their own in individual stages (Stage 1-4) and band together in Stage Five; character choice exists only in Continue Mode replays (manual p04 (image))
- Up to twenty levels — Level number on Character Select counts items collected; highest possible Level is twenty. The game has five stages (manual p07 (image))

**Other sources checked:** https://classic-games.net/nes/kings-knight/

## KlashBall (`ef63df6bcbc7e13d`)

- **Classification:** substantive; error types: other-version detail, wrong item effect, unsupported specific, wrong rule
- **Queue:** escalation (m32-audit-corrected)
- **Manual:** Klash Ball (USA); page images inspected: yes (p03, p04, p05, p06, p07, p08, p09, p10)
- **Verification:** level D; remaining uncertainty: None material; manual page images are low resolution but the cited passages are legible.

**Before:**

> KlashBall depicts a futuristic sports competition combining aspects of handball and hockey on an enclosed court. Two opposing squads try to score into each other's goals, with victory awarded to the side with the highest score at match end. An active participant controls one outfield athlete at a time, throwing the ball directly or tossing it upward for midair catches. The arena features bounce domes altering ball speed and trajectory across ten layout configurations, plus side holes that warp the ball across the field without losing momentum. Physical aggression reduces opponent stamina to slow their movement.
>
> Contenders select a team from the league standings before entering competition. Matches support a single player against the computer or two players competing against each other across knockout tournaments, league play, or single rounds. Randomly appearing power-ups electrify the ball or teleport it to allies, while collected coins purchase stat increases between rounds.

**After:**

> KlashBall depicts a futuristic sports competition combining aspects of soccer, basketball, and hockey in an enclosed arena. Two opposing squads try to score into each other's goals, with victory awarded to the side with the highest score at match end. An active participant controls one outfield athlete at a time, throwing the ball directly or tossing it upward for midair catches. The arena features bounce domes that repel the ball in formations that change each match, plus side holes that warp the ball across the field without losing momentum. Physical aggression reduces opponent stamina to slow their movement.
>
> Contenders select one of three teams, each rated for power, skill, and stamina. A single player faces the computer in knockout or league play, while two players compete against each other in knockout or single-round matches. Floor power tiles can freeze or slow opponents, restore stamina, or grant the ball, while collected coins purchase stat increases between rounds.

**What was wrong and why it changed:** Replaced 'handball and hockey' with the manual's soccer, basketball and hockey; removed the unsupported 'ten layout configurations' and speed effect of bounce domes; fixed team selection (one of three teams, not from the league standings, which the earlier correction had introduced); tied modes to player counts; replaced the Speedball-style electrify/teleport power-ups with the manual's power tile effects.

**Contradicted by NES evidence:**

- Futuristic sport combining handball and hockey on an enclosed court — handball is not mentioned; corrected to soccer, basketball and hockey (manual p03: 'Based on the primitive 1990 games of soccer, basketball and hockey'; p09 steel-walled arena)
- Bounce domes alter ball speed and trajectory across ten layout configurations — manual: domes repel the ball and 'appear in different formations for each match'; no count of ten and no speed change stated; generalized (manual p09 Bounce Domes)
- Contenders select a team from the league standings — the earlier M3.2 correction introduced this error; the League Table only shows rankings during League play (manual p06-p07: 'Select your team from the 3 teams: Verna, Lacata or Draco; each team's status (Power, Skill and Stamina levels) are displayed')
- Randomly appearing power-ups electrify the ball or teleport it to allies — tiles block shots, decrease opponent stamina, freeze or slow the opposing team, give the ball, increase stamina, protect from tackles, or reverse controls; no electrified ball or teleport (that detail is from Speedball); rewritten (manual p10 Power Tiles)

Uncaught tiles raise the drop meter, and the session ends once the limit of missed drops is reached. > Stages in this shooter shift between vertically scrolling aerial sections and horizontal side-scrolling areas. Armed with magical wings from Ares, soldiers set out to destroy a rogue alien supercomputer named Dark. Up to two players battle airborne targets with gunfire and bomb ground enemies during vertical flights to reach an end palace. After defeating a guardian and an added dragon boss, the action switches to a side-scrolling trek toward an interior boss. Optional bonus zones include escape-oriented Danger areas and hidden Lucky rooms.
>
> Collecting P icons upgrades offensive strength through multiple tiers, advancing from normal weapons to twin lasers, penetration beams, and three-way flame shots. Reaching the final enhancement transforms the warrior into a Firebird, granting wide shots and the ability to absorb damage before downgrading. **After:**

> Stages in this shooter shift between vertically scrolling aerial sections and horizontal side-scrolling areas. Armed with wings of courage and love from Ares, the God of War, two young men set out to save the world from extinction. Up to two players fly simultaneously, firing guns and, during vertical sections, missiles. The game spans five stages, and a dragon appears as a recurring boss. Flying into the whirlpool of a large face leads to a dangerous Minus stage, while destroying certain ground structures opens a whirlpool to a Bonus stage.
>
> Collecting power-up items upgrades offensive strength through multiple tiers, advancing from normal shots to twin lasers, penetration shots, and three-way flame shots. Reaching the final enhancement transforms the warrior into a Firebird, which deals four times normal damage and can withstand two direct hits before its power drops. Hearts award continues, up to a maximum of nine.

**Contradicted by NES evidence:**

- Gunfire at airborne targets and bombing ground enemies during vertical flights — Manual: Button A shoots Missiles in vertical stages only; Button B shoots Guns in vertical and horizontal stages; no bombs; reworded (manual p03 (image))
- Optional Danger areas and hidden Lucky rooms — Manual names: Minus Stage (enter whirlpool of large face; dangerous horizontal scroll) and Bonus Stage (destroy ground structures, whirlpool appears) (manual p06 (image))
- Collecting P icons upgrades weapons — Manual: destroy Item A, then collect Item B to raise power one level; no 'P icons' (manual p06 (image))
- Final enhancement is a Firebird with wide shots that absorbs damage before downgrading — Firebird: withstands 2 direct hits, damage 4 times normal shots; 'wide shots' not stated; reworded (manual p05 (image))

**Other sources checked:** https://classic-games.net/nes/legendary-wings/; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legendary_Wings (NES differences)

**Before:**

> Searching for survivors across an invaded Earth in 2112 drives the player onward while destroying hostile forces along winding highways. **After:**

> Searching for survivors across an invaded Earth in 2112 drives the player onward while destroying hostile forces along winding highways. Steering a four-speed superbike, the player accelerates, shifts gears, and fires built-in machine guns to eliminate obstacles and enemy Quadrunners. **Before:**

> Driving Max's Pursuit Special across a post-apocalyptic desert wasteland, the player battles hostile raiders, roadblocks, and bunkers by throwing a limited supply of dynamite. Each non-linear Road War stage requires collecting food, water, fuel, and money to survive. Service stations allow these collected resources to be traded for repairs, extra fuel, dynamite, and the Arena Pass needed to advance.
>
> Players also can stop at sheds to explore abandoned mines on foot from a pseudo-3D perspective, using a shotgun against hostile survivalists while scavenging for supplies, ammunition, and a crossbow. **After:**

> Driving across a post-apocalyptic desert wasteland, the player battles enemy gang cars, road barricades, and gang fortresses using a limited supply of dynamite. Each road stage requires gathering fuel, ammunition, food, and water to survive. Service stations allow food and water to be traded for repairs, extra fuel, ammunition, dynamite, and the arena pass needed to advance.
>
> Players also can explore abandoned mine shafts on foot, using a shotgun against post-nuclear mutants while scavenging for supplies, first aid kits, and keys. Once an arena pass is secured, the player enters a cave-like opening to the Arena, where enemy cars try to push the player off the edge or through trap doors into a bottomless pit, and the exit opens only after enough enemy cars are destroyed. **Contradicted by NES evidence:**

- Collect food, water, fuel and money — No money: food and water are bartered; supplies are fuel, ammunition, dynamite, food and water. (manual Playing the Game, Supplies; HG101)
- Sheds lead to abandoned mines explored on foot from a pseudo-3D perspective — HG101: mine shafts are viewed from overhead. 'Sheds' not established. (https://www.hardcoregaming101.net/mad-max/)

**Other sources checked:** https://www.hardcoregaming101.net/mad-max/ (NES 1990 section)

Roaming enemy dolls attempt to collide with the player, costing a life on contact. Flipping adjacent or occupied tiles pushes dolls away and exposes hidden items beneath. Hostile figures are eliminated by driving them into the walls, or by launching off attack panels into them. Clearing a stage requires destroying every doll, though some levels conclude if all tiles become unflippable in a stalemate.
>
> Each world contains ten levels and ends with a boss encounter. Two players can join simultaneously in cooperative play, tracking lives separately until both players run out.

**What was wrong and why it changed:** Changed 'girlfriend' to 'best friend'; replaced the cap-and-vest description with Bon-Bon; 'hidden patterns' became 'hidden items'; dropped unconfirmed 'blocks'; renamed spinner tiles to the manual's attack panels. Other sentences kept word for word.

**Contradicted by NES evidence:**

- Bon-Bon rescues his girlfriend Candy from her own dream — Candy is trapped in her own dream; Bon-Bon is 'her best friend', not her boyfriend; corrected (manual page 4 (p03 image))

**Other sources checked:** https://takeontheneslibrary.com/tag/candy; https://www.honestgamers.com/11991/nes/mendel-palace/review.html; https://questicle.net/?p=402

- **Classification:** substantive; error types: wrong rule, wrong name, other-version detail
- **Queue:** escalation (m32-audit-corrected)

**Before:**

> Defeating the Space Pirate leader Mother Brain and retrieving stolen Metroid creatures are the ultimate goals of bounty hunter Samus Aran. Players direct Samus through the cavernous subterranean landscape of planet Zebes, navigating two-dimensional interconnected environments connected by doors and elevators. > Destroying the Mother Brain and stopping the space pirates' plan to multiply the stolen Metroid are the ultimate goals of bounty hunter Samus Aran. Players direct Samus through the cavernous subterranean landscape of planet Zebes, navigating two-dimensional interconnected environments connected by doors and elevators. She starts the mission equipped with only a standard jump and a weak, short-range beam. Exploring the world reveals hidden upgrades, while vanquished foes sometimes drop energy or ammunition.
>
> Progress relies on acquiring equipment that grants new mobility and combat capabilities to access sealed regions. Samus can collect the Maru Mari to roll through narrow passageways, lay bombs to uncover concealed paths, and perform a somersaulting Screw Attack to destroy adversaries. Earlier Maru Mari correction confirmed (manual p14).

**Contradicted by NES evidence:**

- Goals: defeat the Space Pirate leader Mother Brain and retrieve stolen Metroid creatures — the mission is to destroy the Mother Brain and the Metroid, which the pirates plan to multiply; nothing says retrieve, and the manual calls Mother Brain a 'Giant Mechanical Organism', not the pirates' leader (manual ocr story; p21 right ('Conquer the unknown organism, the Metroid and destroy the almighty Mother Brain'))
- Hidden upgrades; foes frequently drop energy or ammunition — manual says 'sometimes', not frequently (manual ocr p.14 ('an energy ball is sometimes given off'); p14 right ('Collect missiles from defeated enemies'))
- Ice Beam, Varia Suit, missiles, capacity-expanding tanks — item is named 'Varia', not 'Varia Suit'; Ice Beam, Missile Rocket and Energy Tank confirmed (manual p12-p14 (images))
- Defeat two major bosses, Kraid and Ridley, before the route to the final confrontation opens — manual calls Kraid and Ridley Mini-Bosses; defeating both builds the bridge to Tourian (manual p11, p17 right, p21 left, p10)

## Michael Andretti's World GP (`77c9100f4d3f291d`)

- **Classification:** substantive; error types: wrong count, wrong rule, other-version detail, unsupported specific

- **Verification:** level C; remaining uncertainty: That the rival drivers are pseudonyms of real drivers is inferred from the altered spellings in the manual, not stated outright.

**Before:**

> Michael Andretti's World GP puts players behind the wheel in a simulation-style Formula One competition. Across a circuit of sixteen international tracks, drivers aim to negotiate courses filled with sharp and wide turns. Successful navigation requires regulating speed for corners and manually shifting gears on three of the four selectable vehicles. Tires degrade over distance, making at least one stop at a pylon-marked pit area necessary during each event to swap them out.
>
> Vehicles lack physical collision mechanics, meaning opposing cars can pass directly through one another without causing spins or blocking movement. Competitors are based on actual drivers who appear under pseudonyms, except for Andretti himself. Across Grand Prix mode's two competition levels of up to sixteen rounds each, available automobiles differ in top speed and engine pitch, with a Chevrolet model standing as the fastest option.

**After:**

> Michael Andretti's World GP puts players behind the wheel in a simulation-style Formula One competition. Across a circuit of sixteen international tracks, drivers aim to negotiate courses filled with sharp and wide turns. Successful navigation requires regulating speed for corners and manually shifting gears on three of the four selectable vehicles. Tires degrade over distance, so drivers can pull into a pylon-marked pit area during an event to swap them out.
>
> Competitors are based on actual drivers who appear under pseudonyms, except for Andretti himself. Across Grand Prix mode's nine competition levels of up to sixteen rounds each, available automobiles differ in horsepower and torque, with the Chevy Lola offering the most horsepower.

**What was wrong and why it changed:** Restored nine Grand Prix levels (manual p05, p07; the earlier M3.2 change to 'two' was wrong); pit stop made optional rather than required; removed the no-collision sentence (Famicom-article detail, no NES source); car differences changed from top speed and engine pitch to horsepower and torque, and 'Chevrolet model ... fastest' to 'the Chevy Lola offering the most horsepower'.

**Contradicted by NES evidence:**

- Tires degrade, making at least one pit stop necessary each event — tires lose grip with long racing, screeching or running off track; 'you can pull in to the pit stop'; nothing says a stop is mandatory (manual p04 right, p05 left)
- Grand Prix mode has two levels of competition of up to sixteen rounds — the M3.2 correction from nine to two was itself wrong (manual p07 left (image): 'separated into 9 levels of competition, each level having up to 16 rounds'; p05 right: 'in 9 levels of competition')
- Cars differ in top speed and engine pitch; a Chevrolet is fastest — manual distinguishes the cars by horsepower, torque and transmission; Chevy Lola 630HP is the most powerful (Honda 622, Ferrari 617, Mugen 605); top speed and engine pitch not stated (manual p09 left (image))

**Other sources checked:** https://games.multimedia.cx/?p=394; https://www.honestgamers.com/3776/nes/michael-andrettis-world-grand-prix/game.html (no review content)

## Mickey's Adventure in Numberland (`d3b0627673e6dea5`)

- **Classification:** rewrite; error types: wrong name, wrong rule, wrong item effect, invented detail
- **Queue:** main (nes-native-untouched)
- **Manual:** Mickey's Adventure in Numberland (USA); page images inspected: yes (p03, p04, p05, p06, p07, p08, p09, p10, ocr.txt (all))
- **Verification:** level D; remaining uncertainty: The word 'Disney's' rests on the Mickey Mouse character itself; the manual pages viewed do not print a Disney credit line (the cover image was not inspected).

**Before:**

> Stopping Pete from robbing Numberland requires gathering each number from one through ten. The player directs Disney's Mickey Mouse across five distinct environments: Number City, Number Factory, Space Center, Number Museum, and Pete's Hideout. Advancing between these consecutive stages depends on correctly solving elementary math problems.
>
> Throughout the journey, Mickey defends against opposing creatures by throwing balls of bubblegum as weapons. Three separate difficulty settings are available for the player to select. Mickey cannot lose all his lives or die during the experience unless the game is set to the hardest difficulty level.

**After:**

> Big Bad Pete has made off with the Number Molds that Numberland needs to make its numbers, and the player guides Disney's Mickey Mouse to recover them. A map leads to five locations: The City, the Number Factory, the Space Research Center, Number City Museum, and Big Bad Pete's Hideout, which opens only after the other four are completed. Each location has two stages, and each stage hides a magic number to collect before Mickey reaches the Phone Booth at its end. The booth leads to a Number Machine, where solving a simple number problem, such as addition, subtraction or number ordering, releases a stolen mold.
>
> Three difficulty settings are available: Normal, Advanced and Super Advanced. In the two harder settings, Mickey collects Bubble Gum and blows bubbles to stop enemies. Only in Super Advanced can Mickey lose a try, and even then he can always continue.

**What was wrong and why it changed:** Bounded rewrite from the US manual: objective is recovering the stolen Number Molds (not gathering numbers 1-10); location names corrected; map selection and Number Machine puzzles replace 'consecutive stages'; gum is blown as bubbles (harder modes only), not thrown; life-loss rule corrected (Super Advanced only, always continue).

**Contradicted by NES evidence:**

- Stopping Pete from robbing Numberland requires gathering each number from one through ten — Pete has made off with the Number Molds that Numberland needs to make all the numbers; Mickey recovers the molds from Number Machines and returns them to the Mayor. Numbers 1 to 10 are mentioned only as the range Normal mode deals with and the magic number boxes cycle through. (manual p03, p09 (images))
- Five environments: Number City, Number Factory, Space Center, Number Museum, Pete's Hideout — Names are The City, the Number Factory, the Space Research Center, Number City Museum and Big Bad Pete's Hideout. Count of five supported. (manual p05 (image))
- Advancing between consecutive stages depends on solving elementary math problems — Locations are chosen from a map (not consecutive); at the end of each level a Number Machine poses a simple number problem (grouping, addition, subtraction, ordering) to release a mold. Pete's Hideout opens only after the other four are completed. (manual p05, p09 (images))
- Mickey throws balls of bubblegum as weapons — Mickey collects Bubble Gum and blows bubbles (B button) that eliminate obstacles or enemies, in Advanced and Super Advanced modes only. (manual p03, p04, p06 (images))
- Mickey cannot lose all his lives or die unless on the hardest difficulty — Only in Super Advanced can Mickey lose a turn, and he is always given the opportunity to continue, so progress is never lost; no game-ending loss is described. (manual p04-p05 (images))

**Before:**

> Milon's Secret Castle features platform gameplay where the player guides a boy named Milon through Hudson's Secret Castle. The evil warlord has seized the realm's musical instruments and imprisoned Queen Eliza. Milon navigates through the fortress by running, jumping, and shooting magic bubbles. These bubbles damage monsters and shatter soft blocks, revealing hidden paths, shops, and items. Locating music boxes transports Milon into bonus stages to gather musical notes for cash.
>

**After:**

> Milon's Secret Castle features platform gameplay where the player guides a boy named Milon through Hudson's Secret Castle. The evil warlord has seized the realm's musical instruments and imprisoned Queen Eliza. Milon navigates through the fortress by running, jumping, and shooting magic bubbles. These bubbles damage monsters and shatter soft blocks, revealing hidden paths, shops, and items. Locating music boxes transports Milon into bonus stages to gather musical notes for cash.
>
> The fortress contains multiple floors, side towers, and a well, requiring the defeat of seven bosses and the Evil Warlord to finish the game. Slain bosses drop crystal balls that augment bubble abilities and unlock access to higher levels. Honeycombs located in rooms replenish health and extend the life meter. A single life is provided, though players can continue by holding left and pressing Start after securing the initial crystal ball.

Earlier M3.2 correction (Castle Garland -> Hudson's Secret Castle) verified correct against manual p03.

**Contradicted by NES evidence:**

- Seven bosses must be defeated to finish the game — Objective is to destroy the seven demon-monsters AND the Evil Warlord, and find two secret items to save Queen Eliza; StrategyWiki: the quest ends only when Milon defeats the real Maharito, a final boss beyond the seven crystal bosses. 'Seven bosses' alone understates. (manual p03 (image); StrategyWiki Gameplay)

## Mission - Impossible (`6b04b87ab30e8859`)

- **Verification:** level D; remaining uncertainty: None material.

**Before:**

> A terrorist organization called the Sinister 7 has abducted both a prominent scientist and IMF operative Shannon Reed. Tasked with solving this kidnapping case, the IMF team tracks their targets from the canals of Venice to the Swiss Alps, aiming to infiltrate several multi-floor enemy installations to rescue the captives.
>

Because each operative possesses different skills required to finish the mission, the player can swap between them at any moment during play. Discretion remains critical throughout the mission. **After:**

> A terrorist organization called the Sinister Seven has abducted both a prominent scientist and IMF operative Shannon Reed. Tasked with solving this kidnapping case, the IMF team tracks their targets from the canals of Venice to the Swiss Alps, working through six areas to rescue the captives.
>
> From a top-down view, the player directs three IMF operatives named Max, Grant, and Nicholas. Because each operative possesses different skills required to finish the mission, the player can pause and swap between them in the normal scrolling areas. Discretion remains critical throughout the mission. Harming civilians on the street gets the agent detained by a police helicopter, while being spotted by surveillance cameras inside enemy hideouts gets the agent locked up.

**What was wrong and why it changed:** Sinister 7 -> Sinister Seven; multi-floor installations generalized to six areas; swapping limited to pausing in normal scrolling areas; police arrest reworded to the manual's helicopter detention; surveillance consequence corrected (agent locked up, not guards alerted).

**Contradicted by NES evidence:**

- Terrorist organization called the Sinister 7 — Manual name is 'the Sinister Seven'. (manual p03 (image))
- Player can swap between them at any moment — Agents are changed while paused, in the normal scroll areas only (areas 1, 3, 4, 6); in auto-scroll areas all three are in play at once. (manual ocr p9-10 ('How to change your identity', 'To scroll or not to scroll'))
- Triggering surveillance systems alerts security guards — Eye Spy: if spotted, a buzzer sounds and the agent is promptly locked up in that room and faces the Iron Claw; no guards alerted. (manual p08 (image))

**Before:**

> The Mutant Virus: Crisis in a Computer World puts the player in an action scenario centered on a fight inside a global artificial intelligence system. The story follows Ron, who must eradicate an infectious threat managing the world's technology before humanity reverts to the Stone Age.
>
> Controlling a miniature spaceship, the player navigates rooms to contain the infection. The craft fires anti-virus projectiles alongside alternate weapon variations. > The Mutant Virus: Crisis in a Computer World puts the player in an action scenario centered on a fight inside CPI, the computer system that runs the world's databases, power grids, and traffic signals. The story follows Ron Trainer of the Computer Master Debuggers, who must eradicate a virus that has infected five critical sections of CPI before its Core is destroyed and humanity is plunged back almost to the Stone Age.
>
> Miniaturized inside an armored JetSuit, the player flies through the sectors of each section to contain the infection. The suit's Vaccine Blaster fires three types of charges that turn infected cells blue, and pickups called Counter Measures spread vaccine automatically. The virus spreads across the grid following the rules of Conway's Game of Life, and flying over active virus drains the suit's PowerPack.

**What was wrong and why it changed:** Replaced 'global artificial intelligence' with CPI, 'miniature spaceship' with the armored JetSuit, removed the green/light-blue colors and the majority rule; added Ron Trainer's full name, five sections, Vaccine Blaster charges, Counter Measures and PowerPack drain from the manual. Editorial adjustment: wording: 'according to' reads as a source attribution.

**Contradicted by NES evidence:**

- Fight inside a global artificial intelligence system — the system is CPI, which 'controls everything: from global databases and power grids ... to the timing of the traffic signals'; not described as an AI (manual p02 (image))
- Player controls a miniature spaceship — miniaturization cannot shrink 'a whole ship or even a small vehicle'; the player wears an armored JetSuit (manual p03 (image))
- Green virus cells and light-blue clean cells — infected-cell color varies by section (magenta in COMM, bright green in SEC, light purple in PWR, dark green in MEM, pink in CPU); vaccine turns cells blue (manual p04 (image))

**Other sources checked:** https://tasvideos.org/6642S; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Mutant_Virus:_Crisis_in_a_Computer_World (search snippet; encyclopedia source)

## Nightshade (`02caaf66cc43a4c5`)

- **Classification:** substantive; error types: wrong name, other-version detail
- **Queue:** main (nes-native-untouched)
- **Manual:** Nightshade (USA); page images inspected: yes (p04)
- **Verification:** level D; remaining uncertainty: Lord Muck and Ninja Mistress come from Hardcore Gaming 101 only (not named in the manual). Whether Vortex died is not settled by the manual (he was dragged off and not heard from); the text says only that Sutekh overpowered him.

**Before:**

> Ridding Metro City of crime serves as the main goal after a villain named Sutekh unites the local gangs following the death of the superhero Vortex. Taking on the role of Mark, a vigilante known as Nightshade, the player confronts Sutekh alongside several other crime bosses, including Rat King, Lord Muck, Goliath, and Ninja Mistress.

> Progressing through the game involves a mix of action sequences, point-and-click elements, and fighting segments that demand swift button inputs. Earning higher popularity increases recognition from the local citizens and grants the player entry into additional areas across the city.

**After:**

> Ridding Metro City of crime serves as the main goal after a villain named Sutekh unites the local gangs and overpowers the superhero Vortex. Taking on the role of Mark Gray, a vigilante known as Nightshade, the player confronts Sutekh alongside several other crime bosses, including King Rat, Lord Muck, Goliath, and Ninja Mistress.
>
> Progressing through the game involves a mix of action sequences, point-and-click elements, and fighting segments that demand swift button inputs. A dedicated popularity meter tracks the character's reputation, rising or dropping based on how effectively Nightshade carries out good deeds. Earning higher popularity increases recognition from the local citizens and grants the player entry into additional areas across the city.

**What was wrong and why it changed:** 'Rat King' corrected to King Rat; Vortex sequence reworded to match the NES manual; 'Mark' given his manual surname Gray. Rest kept word for word.

**Contradicted by NES evidence:**

- This happens following the death of the superhero Vortex — in the manual Sutekh had already united the bosses before Vortex fought him; Vortex was overpowered and dragged off (HG101 says he was killed). Reworded to 'overpowers the superhero Vortex' (manual story)
- Crime bosses Rat King, Lord Muck, Goliath, Ninja Mistress — 'Rat King' corrected to King Rat (manual names 'King Rat' and 'Goliath'; https://www.hardcoregaming101.net/nightshade/ lists 'King Rat, Goliath, Lord Muck, and the Ninja Mistress')

**Other sources checked:** https://www.hardcoregaming101.net/nightshade/; https://www.retrogamingroundup.com/blog/2011/2011-10-20.php; https://alexbevi.com/blog/2022/12/31/nightshade/

## Ninja Crusaders (`b1c2ae757c5ec76f`)

- **Classification:** substantive; error types: wrong name, other-version detail, invented detail
- **Queue:** main (nes-native-untouched)
- **Manual:** Ninja Crusaders (USA); page images inspected: yes (p01, p02, p03, p04, p05)
- **Verification:** level D; remaining uncertainty: The one-hit-kill property of the dragon rests on a reader comment at questicle.net; HG101 describes it as flying, invincible and shooting projectiles. Scorpion swimming ability rests on HG101.

**Before:**

> Thwarting an alien invasion that drove ninja warriors from Japan serves as the central mission in this side-scrolling action title. Up to two players can participate simultaneously, controlling the ninjas Talon and Blade as they confront extraterrestrial forces across Earth.
>
> Players collect four distinct weapons that grant special forms. Picking up a shuriken enables metamorphosis into a tiger with superior speed and jump height alongside limited attack range. The kusarigama transforms the ninja into an aquatic sea scorpion that moves sluggishly ashore. Equipping a bō allows flight as a falcon unable to attack, while the scarce sword temporarily turns the character into an invincible dragon that flies and defeats foes with single strikes.

**After:**

> Thwarting an alien invasion of Earth serves as the central mission in this side-scrolling action title. Up to two players can participate simultaneously, controlling a red ninja and a blue ninja of the Kawari clan as they confront the alien Inimicus forces.
>
> Players collect four distinct weapons that grant special forms. Picking up a throwing star enables metamorphosis into a tiger with superior speed and jump height alongside limited attack range. The chain and sickle transforms the ninja into an armored scorpion that swims well but moves sluggishly ashore. Equipping a bo allows flight as a hawk unable to attack, while the scarce katana temporarily turns the character into an invincible dragon that flies and defeats foes with single strikes.

**What was wrong and why it changed:** Removed the unsupported 'drove ninja warriors from Japan' story detail; replaced the names Talon and Blade (not in the US manual) with the manual's red and blue ninjas of the Kawari clan; used the manual's weapon names (throwing star, chain and sickle, katana); falcon -> hawk and sea scorpion -> armored scorpion per the manual.

**Contradicted by NES evidence:**

- Kusarigama -> aquatic sea scorpion, slow on land — Manual: Chain and Sickle -> 'powerful Armored Scorpion'. HG101: slow on land, swift underwater. Name changed. (manual p05 (image); HG101)
- Bo -> falcon that flies but cannot attack — Manual: the Bo transforms the ninja into an 'elusive Hawk'. HG101: bird cannot attack but can fly. Name changed to hawk. (manual p05 (image); HG101)

**Other sources checked:** https://www.hardcoregaming101.net/ninja-crusaders/; https://questicle.net/?p=359

Ryu loses a life if his physical health depletes or the timer expires. Each act concludes with a boss battle.

## Ninja Kid (`622c62d48aa244fb`)

- **Classification:** rewrite; error types: wrong rule, unsupported specific, invented detail
- **Queue:** main (nes-native-untouched)
- **Manual:** Ninja Kid (USA); page images inspected: yes (p01, p05, p06, p07, p08, p09)
- **Verification:** level D; remaining uncertainty: The removed speed-boost and owl items may exist in the game, but no NES-specific source other than Wikipedia-derived text was reachable.

**Before:**

> Ninja Kid features action gameplay structured around an overhead map. Several arches on this map transport the player into side-scrolling missions, with the specific type indicated by the shape of the arch. Completing a mission reveals two doors, sending the character back to the map or leading inside a vertically scrolling tower capped by a mini-boss. Defeating this opponent returns the character to the overhead area.
>
> Items generate randomly during side-scrolling stages, including temporary speed boosts and an owl that reveals the doorway leading to the map. Finding a scroll allows the player to enter a central hut, unlocking a fortress to confront the map boss. Whistles acquired throughout the adventure let the protagonist summon a familiar by crouching in the far left corner during the final encounter.

**After:**

> Ninja Kid pairs action stages with an overhead map of Demon Island. Gates on the map lead into four kinds of fighting fields, each with its own goal: defeating 10 demons in Guerilla Warfare, collecting 10 demon spirits in the Poison Fields, beating 10 demons from a kite in the Dog Fight, and lighting 10 candles in the Blazing Inferno. A Mystery Field can hold any of the four. Clearing a field reveals two doors: one returns to the map, the other leads into Demon Hell, a vertically scrolling stage ruled by a giant demon.
>
> Special weapons such as the Iron Star, Boomerang, Feather and Fireflame appear as objectives are met. After finding the special scroll and receiving the chanting spell at the old witch's house, the player can enter the Demon Castle. Whistles let Ninja Kid call up to three friends, Pegasus, Big Eagle and the Old Witch, by moving to the left side of the screen and squatting.

**What was wrong and why it changed:** Bounded rewrite from the manual: replaced the 'arch shape' claim with the four named fighting fields and their goals plus the Mystery Field; replaced the unsupported speed-boost and owl items with the manual's special weapons; used manual names for Demon Hell, the old witch's house and Demon Castle; corrected the whistle rule (up to three friends, left side of screen, Demon Castle fight on each map).

**Contradicted by NES evidence:**

- Several arches on the map lead to side-scrolling missions, type indicated by arch shape — The map has four kinds of Fighting Fields with distinct icons, but the Mystery Field can be any of the four, so the type is not always indicated. Rewritten with manual names and objectives. (manual p05-p06 (image))
- Whistles summon a familiar by crouching in the far left corner during the final encounter — Whistles call up to three friends (Pegasus, Big Eagle, Old Witch), one per whistle, by moving to the left side of the screen and squatting, during the Demon Castle fight on each map, not only the final encounter. (manual p07-p08 (image))

## Nintendo World Cup (`b0e4d88db0b21db4`)

- **Classification:** substantive; error types: wrong rule, wrong name
- **Queue:** escalation (m32-audit-corrected)
- **Manual:** Nintendo World Cup (USA); page images inspected: yes (p05, p06, p07, p08, p09, p10)
- **Verification:** level D; remaining uncertainty: Six players per team is read from a small manual screenshot (six names per side); the no-offsides/no-fouls claim rests on one NES review. Whether surfaces change player movement as well as the ball is a mild extrapolation.

**Before:**

> Controlling an individual soccer athlete on a six-member squad, the player guides their athlete across the pitch while issuing passing and shooting commands to teammates. Matches diverge from standard rules by removing offsides and foul penalties entirely. Competitors can repeatedly tackle or slide into opponents until they are knocked down and incapacitated for the remainder of the half. Additionally, athletes can trigger up to five specialized Super Kicks per half by pressing both action buttons simultaneously. After exhausting these shots, walking a specific number of steps before kicking activates a High Power Kick. Field surfaces such as ice, sand, or dirt alter how the ball and participants maneuver.
>
> Two gameplay modes are available. Tournament mode tasks one or two participants with selecting from thirteen national teams to defeat computer opponents. Match mode allows play across various surfaces, accommodating up to four participants simultaneously through multi-controller accessories.

**After:**

Matches diverge from standard rules by removing offsides and foul penalties entirely. Competitors can repeatedly tackle or slide into opponents until they are knocked down, leaving them out of play until a goal is scored or the half ends. Additionally, athletes can trigger up to five specialized Super Kicks per half by pressing both action buttons simultaneously. After exhausting these shots, walking a specific number of steps before kicking activates a High Power Kick. Field surfaces such as ice, sand, or soil alter how the ball and participants maneuver.
>

**What was wrong and why it changed:** Knocked-down players stay down until a goal is scored or the half ends (not only the remainder of the half); field type 'dirt' renamed 'soil' as on the game's field-type screen. Earlier M3.2 Super Kick correction verified correct against manual p08.

**Contradicted by NES evidence:**

- **Manual:** Palamedes (USA); page images inspected: yes (p03, p04, p05, p06, p07, p08)
- **Verification:** level D; remaining uncertainty: None material.

**Before:**

> Palamedes features puzzle gameplay centered on matching dice. The player alters the number on a held die with the B button and hurls it toward the top of the display using the A button. Hitting a matching die removes that target from the board. Additional rows of dice emerge at increasingly shorter time intervals. The session concludes if any die reaches the bottom of the play area.
>
> Forming specific patterns, such as sequences from one to six or repeatedly clearing identical numbers, earns a special maneuver capable of clearing three to five rows simultaneously. Available play options include a solitaire mode for one player against the computer or another participant, alongside a tournament mode contested against computer-controlled opponents.

**After:**

> Palamedes features puzzle gameplay centered on matching dice. The player alters the number on a held die with the B button and hurls it toward the top of the display using the A button. Hitting a matching die removes that target from the board. The lines of dice descend faster as the player progresses through the stages. The session concludes if the dice reach the bottom of the play area.
>
> Eliminated dice collect in a window at the bottom of the screen, where they can form hands such as three or more of a kind, runs of consecutive numbers, three pairs or a total of 21. Pressing down with a hand wipes out one to five descending lines, depending on its rank. Play options include a 1-Player mode of 20 stages, a 2-Players match against another person in which cleared lines are sent to the opponent's screen, and a tournament against four computer opponents.

**What was wrong and why it changed:** Speed-up rule corrected (descent speeds up by stage); hand system restated per the manual (hands formed from eliminated dice, wiping out one to five lines, not three to five); modes corrected (solo 20-stage mode, two-player versus match, tournament against four computer opponents).

**Contradicted by NES evidence:**

- Patterns such as one-to-six sequences or repeated identical numbers earn a special move clearing three to five rows — Eliminated dice form hands in a window at the bottom; pressing down wipes out 1-5 lines depending on rank (3 of a kind = 1 line ... 6 of a kind = 4; runs of 3/4/5 = 1/2/3; three pairs = 3; total of 21 = 1; straight flush 1-6 = 5). (manual p04, p07-p08 (image))
- Solitaire mode for one player against the computer or another participant, plus a tournament against computer opponents — Modes are 1-Player (solo, 20 stages), 2-Players (match against another person) and Tournament (single player vs four computer opponents). (manual p04-p06 (image))

## Paperboy (`f1c9c4723190d6be`)

- **Classification:** substantive; error types: other-version detail, wrong rule, unsupported specific
- **Queue:** escalation (m32-audit-low-risk)
- **Manual:** Paperboy (USA); page images inspected: yes (p01, p02, p03, p04, p05, p06)
- **Verification:** level D; remaining uncertainty: Whether the NES game shows the name 'The Daily Sun' on screen was not verified; the name was removed rather than asserted.

**Before:**

> Riding a bicycle along a suburban street, the player throws copies of The Daily Sun newspaper to customer houses. Deliveries must reach a subscriber's mailbox or front porch while dodging hazards such as cars, rolling tires, and skateboarders. Crashing into hazards costs a life, and the player must collect extra bundles along the way to refill a limited paper supply. Damaging non-subscriber houses and targeting select obstacles yields bonus score.
>
> Subscribers cancel their subscriptions if they fail to receive an issue or if their property is damaged. Reaching the end of the neighborhood leads to a training course containing jump ramps and targets. Finishing the course without losing all lives advances the player to the next day's route, continuing through the week.

**After:**

> Riding a bicycle along a suburban street, the player throws newspapers to customer houses. Deliveries must reach a subscriber's paperbox or front porch while dodging hazards such as cars, tires, and skateboarders. Crashing into hazards costs a life, and the player must collect extra bundles along the way to refill a limited paper supply. Damaging non-subscriber houses and targeting select obstacles yields bonus score.
>
> Subscribers cancel their subscriptions if they fail to receive an issue or if their property is damaged. Reaching the end of the neighborhood leads to a timed training course containing jump ramps and targets. A daily report then shows any canceled subscriptions, and a player who performs well continues to the next day's route, aiming to complete a full week. Losing every subscriber also ends the game.

**What was wrong and why it changed:** Removed the unverified newspaper name; 'mailbox' changed to 'paperbox'; dropped 'rolling'; replaced the wrong progression rule (course completion) with the daily report and performance review, plus the NES-review rule that losing all subscribers ends the game.

**Contradicted by NES evidence:**

- Finishing the course without losing all lives advances the player to the next day, continuing through the week — Advancement follows the daily performance review, not completion of the course; the course is a timed bonus (45 seconds). Rewritten from the manual; an NES review adds that losing all subscribers ends the game. (manual p03 (page 2: boss reviews performance at the end of each day), p04 (page 4: Daily Report, entire week))

**Other sources checked:** https://takeontheneslibrary.com/tag/paper/ (NES review)

## Pin Bot (`f4ddb0f1a02f823e`)

- **Classification:** substantive; error types: wrong rule, wrong name, unsupported specific

- **Manual:** Pin Bot (USA); page images inspected: yes (p03, p05)
- **Verification:** level D; remaining uncertainty: Enemy details rest on one NES GameFAQs FAQ; the manual only confirms enemies that attack flippers or steal the ball and different ball shapes.

**Before:**

> Six playfield levels structure this pinball title, retaining the same table layout while changing color palettes and introducing hazards across stages. The view tracks the ball along the table while keeping the flippers fixed in the lower third of the screen. Participants accumulate points by striking targets and progressing across the planets of the Solar System from Pluto to the Sun. Reaching designated planetary checkpoints awards extra balls. Players can illuminate a grid to lift a visor, lock two balls, and trigger a multiball sequence offering doubled point values.
>
> Earning a solar bonus during multiball advances the table to subsequent levels that add hostile creatures. Later stages feature a blob that tries to consume the ball, planes dropping flipper-damaging missiles or capturing the ball, and lane-dwelling snakes. **After:**

> Six playfield levels structure this pinball title, retaining the same table layout while introducing hazards across stages. The view tracks the ball along the table while a split screen keeps the flippers in view at all times. Participants accumulate points by striking targets and progressing across the planets of the Solar System from Pluto to the Sun. Reaching designated planets lights extra balls. Players can illuminate a grid to lift a visor, lock two balls, and trigger a multiball sequence offering doubled point values.
>
> Shooting the solar ramp while a ball is locked collects the Solar Value and advances the table to subsequent levels that add hostile creatures. Later stages feature a monster that tries to eat the ball, flying enemies that drop flipper-damaging missiles or carry the ball off, and snakes in the lower slots. **Contradicted by NES evidence:**

- view tracks the ball while flippers stay fixed in the lower third of the screen — Split screen keeps the flippers shown at all times; tasvideos says bottom half. 'Lower third' unsupported. (manual ocr How to Play; tasvideos)
- earning a solar bonus during multiball advances the level — Shooting the solar ramp while one ball is locked advances the playfield to the next level and collects the Solar Value. (manual ocr Solar Ramp)
- planes dropping flipper-damaging missiles or capturing the ball — FAQ describes flies that drop missiles (levels 3-4) and grab the ball (level 4); 'planes' not supported (GameFAQs FAQ)

**Other sources checked:** https://gamefaqs.gamespot.com/nes/587511-pin-bot/faqs/18359 (NES FAQ by Brian Sulpher, fetched with curl); https://tasvideos.org/1152G

Later encounters demand surviving an overnight siege in a bunker by illuminating targets with flares and aiming a crosshair, followed by a timed third-person jungle escape ahead of a napalm strike that culminates in scoring five direct hits on Sergeant Barnes in his foxhole.

**What was wrong and why it changed:** Stage 1 'explosive mines' corrected to trip wires; final segment's 'barricaded commander with grenades' corrected to five direct hits on Sergeant Barnes in a foxhole, with the napalm deadline.

**Contradicted by NES evidence:**

- evading explosive mines, booby traps and enemy soldiers in the jungle — Stage 1 hazards are trip wires, booby traps in huts and enemy soldiers; mines are listed only in stage 4. (manual ocr stage 1)
- defeating a barricaded commander with grenades — Target is Sergeant Barnes in a foxhole, removed by 5 direct hits; in stage 4 the A button is not used and B shoots, so no grenades. (manual p20, p21)

**Contradicted by NES evidence:**

## Prince of Persia (`7b0899bfde9661d1`)

- **Classification:** substantive; error types: wrong name, invented detail, unsupported specific
- **Queue:** main (m32-audit-medium-risk)
- **Manual:** Prince of Persia (USA); page images inspected: yes (p06, p08)
- **Verification:** level D; remaining uncertainty: None material. Jaffar's defeat and the slow-fall potion rest on one NES-specific GameFAQs guide.

**Before:**

> Prince of Persia presents platforming gameplay set in medieval Persia. A single player guides an unnamed protagonist through palace dungeons to defeat the Grand Vizier Jaffar and reach an imprisoned princess before sixty minutes elapse. Progress requires running across pressure plates that raise gates, leaping over deep pits, and avoiding lethal spike traps and guillotines. Falling rocks or short falls cause damage, and dying returns the protagonist to the start of the current level while the timer continues running.
>
> Duels against enemy guards require a sword acquired during the escape. The protagonist advances, retreats, slashes, and parries attacks, with defeated adversaries either losing all health indicators or falling into traps. Three initial health units can be depleted by combat or hazards. Jars found throughout the areas hold potions that heal injuries, raise maximum health capacity, impart temporary hovering, or inflict poison.

**After:**

> Prince of Persia presents platforming gameplay set in Persia. A single player guides an unnamed protagonist out of the Sultan's dungeons and through the palace to defeat the Grand Vizier Jaffar and reach an imprisoned princess before sixty minutes elapse. Progress requires stepping on pressure plates that raise gates, leaping over deep pits, and avoiding lethal spike traps and slicers. Two-story falls cause damage, and dying returns the protagonist to the start of the current level while the timer continues running.
>
> Duels against enemy guards require a sword acquired during the escape. The protagonist advances, retreats, slashes, and parries attacks, and a guard is defeated by draining all of his health indicators. Three initial health units can be depleted by combat or hazards. Potions found throughout the areas heal injuries, raise maximum health capacity, slow the protagonist's falls, or inflict poison.

**What was wrong and why it changed:** Removed 'medieval', 'falling rocks', 'jars' and 'falling into traps'; guillotines renamed slicers (manual name); 'running across' plates became stepping on; hovering potion reworded to slowed falls per an NES guide.

**Contradicted by NES evidence:**

- Guillotines — Both the manual and the NES guide call the trap 'the slicer' / 'Slicers'. Name changed. (manual p08 (page 9); GameFAQs NES guide)

**Other sources checked:** http://web.archive.org/web/20220910034943/https://gamefaqs.gamespot.com/nes/587527-prince-of-persia/faqs/10022 (Adam Lamontagne NES guide); https://questicle.net/488-prince-of-persia/ (NES review)

> Pro Wrestling depicts competitive one-on-one wrestling matches between chosen participants. Players select from six distinct wrestlers, each possessing an individual move set. ## Puss 'n Boots - Pero's Great Adventure (`691ef0807cacd703`)

- **Classification:** rewrite; error types: other-version detail, wrong name, invented detail, wrong rule

- **Manual:** Puss n Boots - Pero's Great Adventure (USA); page images inspected: yes (p03, p04, p05, p06, p07)

**Before:**

> Stages across world locations structure this journey, taking the feline protagonist through London, Arabia, the Pacific Ocean, the American Old West, New York City, a mountainous flight area, and the Statue of Liberty. The player guides Pero, also called Perrault, on an expedition across the globe with an overall limit of 80 in-game days. One minute of real time equates to roughly one day on the countdown. Failing to complete the worldwide trip before the entire duration elapses causes an immediate game over, irrespective of any remaining lives.
>
> Navigating these locales requires the player to walk on foot as well as pilot various vehicles, including boats, automobiles, and balloons. > Seven stages structure this journey, taking the feline protagonist through the West, the ocean, Arabia, the skies of Space Wars, London, Liberty, and finally New York. The player guides Pero, the cat known as Puss N' Boots, whom Count Gruemon and the wolf scientist Dr. Gari-gari sent on a time-travel journey into the past after he helped a mouse escape. To get home, Pero must defeat both villains and use their Time Machine, while Killers from the Cat Kingdom pursue him.
>
> Navigating these locales requires the player to walk on foot as well as pilot various vehicles, including a ship, a submarine, a car, an airplane, and a balloon. Pero can switch between weapons such as a gun, bombs, and a boomerang, while items include Boots for temporary invincibility, Hamburgers that restore energy, and Pero Marks that award extra lives.

**What was wrong and why it changed:** Rewritten from the US manual: the Japanese 80-day timer, day-reducing items, 'Perrault' and instant-death water were removed; the stage list was corrected to the seven US stages in order; the US time-travel story, villains, vehicles, weapons and items were added from the manual.

**Contradicted by NES evidence:**

- Stages: London, Arabia, the Pacific Ocean, the American Old West, New York City, a mountainous flight area, the Statue of Liberty — US manual lists seven stages in order: The West, The Ocean, Arabia, Space Wars (airplane), London, Liberty (balloon), New York (final). 'Pacific', 'mountainous flight area' and 'Statue of Liberty' are not the US names; order differs. (manual p05, p06)

> Set in a future where survival is the only law, the journey puts the player behind the wheel of an armored car traversing fifty rally stages. > Set in a future where survival is the only law, the journey puts the player behind the wheel of an armored car traversing fifty rally stages. **What was wrong and why it changed:** 'a cannon' -> 'an artillery gun' for the standard weapon (the cannon is a separate special weapon). Earlier M3.2 corrections (toxic spills, support jet, three lives) verified against manual p03-p04.

**Contradicted by NES evidence:**

- The car features a cannon to shoot enemy vehicles and gun turrets — The standard weapon is an 'artillery gun' (A button fires guns); the U.Z. Cannon is a separate special weapon (manual p03, p04)

## Robo Warrior (`5431ed49f22ee818`)

- **Classification:** substantive; error types: wrong count, wrong name, unsupported specific
- **Queue:** escalation (m32-audit-medium-risk)
- **Manual:** Robo Warrior (USA); page images inspected: yes (p03, p04, p05, p06, p07, p08, p09, p10, p11, p12, p13, p14, p15, p16)
- **Verification:** level D; remaining uncertainty: StrategyWiki was read only through search-result text (site returned 403/429); the stage-count generalization avoids depending on the exact range.

**Before:**

> Robo Warrior centers on action gameplay featuring shooting and demolition. Controlling a cyborg named ZED, the player fights across the artificial world of Altile to defeat the invading Xantho Empire. The campaign consists of eight levels called Periods, divided into one to three stages. Reaching each stage exit requires clearing obstacles and adversaries to find a hidden key, with certain areas also requiring a chalice to prevent the stage from looping. Along the way, players can discover underground item stockpiles or bomb statues in Rooms of Idols for rewards.
>
> Combat relies on a rapid-fire laser gun alongside deployable bombs that eliminate hostiles and break blocks. Explosions can harm ZED, and limited bomb counts must be replenished from enemy drops. Because ZED's energy meter drains over time, players must gather energy batteries to survive.

**After:**

> Robo Warrior centers on action gameplay featuring shooting and demolition. Controlling a cyborg named ZED, the player fights across the artificial world of Altile to defeat the invading Xantho Empire. The campaign consists of eight levels called Periods, each divided into one or more stages. Reaching each stage exit requires clearing obstacles and adversaries to find a hidden key, with certain areas also requiring a chalice to prevent the stage from looping. Along the way, players can explore hidden underground passages holding special powers or bomb statues in Rooms of Idols for rewards.
>
> Combat relies on a laser gun alongside deployable bombs that eliminate hostiles and break blocks. Explosions can harm ZED, and limited bomb counts must be replenished from enemy drops and hidden bomb symbols. Because ZED's energy meter drains over time, players must gather Life Pods and Energy Capsules to survive.

**What was wrong and why it changed:** 'one to three stages' -> 'one or more stages' (StrategyWiki: later Periods have two to five); 'underground item stockpiles' -> underground passages holding special powers; removed unsupported 'rapid-fire'; added hidden bomb symbols as a bomb source; 'energy batteries' -> 'Life Pods and Energy Capsules' (manual names).

**Contradicted by NES evidence:**

- Each Period divided into one to three stages — First Period has one stage; later Periods have two to five stages (StrategyWiki walkthrough (search text))
- Gather energy batteries — Energy items are Life Pods and Energy Capsules; no batteries (manual p07, p08, p10)

**Other sources checked:** https://strategywiki.org/wiki/RoboWarrior/Walkthrough (search-result text: Periods; first Period one stage, later Periods two to five stages; eight Periods)

**Before:**

> Players control flippers to guide a ball across various pinball tables featuring bumpers and arches. > Players control flippers to guide a ball across various pinball tables featuring bumpers and targets. Participants choose from six fictional human characters, comprising four male and two female options, each using the flippers in a different way. A rock and roll styled regular pinball mode accommodates up to four players.
>
> Additional modes provide varied play mechanics. Nineball tasks players with betting chips and knocking balls into a Bingo pattern, while Sports Pinball adapts the playfield to resemble a soccer field or hockey rink. - Bomber: ball detonates after a time limit once two target switches transform into bombs — Manual: hitting the switch changes the special panel image; connecting two panel images gives results; Bomb panel: 'The ball will explode within a fixed time'. Switches do not turn into bombs. (manual p09 (image))
- Attack mode uses a switch on the right side to trigger special effects — Attack has three switches (ATTACK, HELP, STOP) making a side-moving block, Help, or a stopper appear; the illustration shows them on the left side. (manual p10 (image))

- **Classification:** rewrite; error types: other-version detail, wrong name, wrong count, invented detail

- **Manual:** Rocket Ranger (USA); page images inspected: yes (ocr all, p02, p03)

**Before:**

> Stopping Nazi Germany from winning World War II and enslaving the globe forms the central objective. Taking the role of a US Army scientist equipped with teleported futuristic artifacts, the player uses a rocket pack and radium pistol to halt enemy forces. Progress requires securing five rocket ship parts alongside 500 units of lunarium fuel to reach moon mines, shutting them down, and facing an alien ally of the opposing regime.
>
> Gameplay alternates across strategic planning and diverse action sequences. From a world map, five agents can be deployed to uncover hidden bases or slow enemy advances toward the United States. Following a timed button-press takeoff minigame, the protagonist travels globally. Encounters involve third-person aerial dogfights against aircraft, zeppelins, and ground guns, along with cover-based shootouts at fortified depots, hand-to-hand brawls with guards, and dialogue exchanges aboard airships.

**After:**

> Set in 1990, Rocket Ranger begins as ships from an alien moon descend on Europe and found Greater Leutonia. Led by Colonel Krag, the Leutonians set out to conquer the world and kidnap Dr. Barnstorff and his daughter, Jane. The player is a young American scientist who uses a rocket-powered flying suit and a laser pistol to stop them. Victory requires stealing five rocket parts from secret labs and enough Lunarium fuel to reach the alien moon before the Leutonians conquer the United States.
>
> Gameplay alternates between strategy and action. From a War Room world map, five agents can be assigned to infiltrate countries, start resistance movements, and report the locations of rocket labs and bases. Lunarium must be shared between the rocket pack and the rocket ship. Action sequences include shooting aerial torpedoes and gunners on a zeppelin, battling fighter squadrons, destroying gun emplacements at temple ruins, fistfights with lab guards, and a shootout at the lunar base.

**What was wrong and why it changed:** Bounded rewrite: the text described the computer original (Nazi Germany, World War II, radium pistol, 500 units of fuel, moon mines, takeoff minigame, airship dialogue). Replaced with the NES story and structure from the manual (1990, Leutonians, Colonel Krag, Barnstorffs, laser pistol, five rocket parts, Lunarium, War Room agents, challenge list).

**Contradicted by NES evidence:**

- Stopping Nazi Germany from winning World War II — NES story: the year is 1990; ships from an alien moon found Greater Leutonia; the Leutonians, led by Colonel Krag, set out to conquer the world. No Nazis or World War II. (manual p03 (image))
- US Army scientist with teleported futuristic artifacts — A young American scientist with his newly perfected rocket-powered flying suit; no teleported artifacts. (manual p03 (image))
- Rocket pack and radium pistol — Rocket pack supported; the weapon is a laser pistol. (manual OCR 'The Zeppelin' and 'Fuel Depot')
- Secure five rocket ship parts and 500 units of lunarium fuel — Five parts supported (one from each of five secret rocket labs); fuel amount is 'sufficient Lunarium', no 500 figure. (manual OCR 'The Objective')
- Reach moon mines, shut them down, and face an alien ally of the regime — Goal on the moon is to rescue Dr. Barnstorff and Jane at the lunar base, eliminating female Leutonian guards, then one final challenge. (manual OCR objective and 'The Lunar Base')
- Timed button-press takeoff minigame — Take Off is a destination map with a Lunarium cost check; no minigame described. (manual OCR 'Take Off')

> Ten areas form the structure of this single-player shooter, guiding secret agent Albatross through a rescue mission in the underground headquarters of a conspiratorial group. > Controlling Albatross across multi-level floors and stairs, the player leaps over obstacles, takes cover behind crates, and enters doorways to hide from hostile forces. **Contradicted by NES evidence:**

## Shadowgate (`fbc69cdaf7c14199`)

- **Classification:** substantive; error types: other-version detail, unsupported specific, wrong rule
- **Queue:** main (m32-audit-medium-risk)
- **Manual:** Shadowgate (USA); page images inspected: yes (p01, p03, p04)
- **Verification:** level C; remaining uncertainty: Lakmir and the Staff of Ages are not in the manual; they rest on one NES review (VGJUNK), with TotNL silent on them. Whether Lakmir is called wizard or druid in the NES text was not confirmed.

**Before:**

> Rooms throughout a perilous fantasy fortress form the interconnected setting of this point-and-click adventure. Assuming the role of a hero-king descendant chosen by the wizard Lakmir, the player ventures into Castle Shadowgate to stop the Warlock Lord before he summons the demonic Behemoth. Navigation relies on interacting with surroundings, managing equipment, and gathering three sacred artifacts to forge the Staff of Ages. A built-in hint system offers clues about points of interest within each chamber.
>
> Survival depends heavily on solving room puzzles while keeping an active light source. Because lit torches exist in limited quantities, they impose a constant time limit; darkness causes an immediate fatal fall. Players collect tools such as ancient weapons, a sling, and a sword to defeat specific foes. Incorrect actions and traps routinely trigger sudden deaths, permitting the player to resume from the current room.

**After:**

> Rooms throughout a perilous fantasy fortress form the interconnected setting of this point-and-click adventure. Assuming the role of the last of the Line of Kings, sent by the wizard Lakmir, the player ventures into Castle Shadowgate to stop the Warlock Lord before he raises the Behemoth. Navigation relies on interacting with surroundings, managing equipment, and assembling the Staff of Ages. A built-in hint system offers clues when any are available.
>
> Survival depends heavily on solving room puzzles while keeping an active light source. Because lit torches exist in limited quantities, they impose a constant time limit; when the light runs out, the hero stumbles to a fatal fall. Players collect tools such as a sling and a sword to defeat specific foes. Incorrect actions and traps routinely trigger sudden deaths, after which the player can resume from the previous room. Three save files are available.

**What was wrong and why it changed:** Used the manual's 'Line of Kings' and 'raises'; replaced the unconfirmed three-artifact detail with assembling the Staff of Ages; softened 'immediate' darkness death; dropped 'ancient weapons'; resume point corrected to the previous room; added three save files.

**Contradicted by NES evidence:**

- Sudden deaths; player resumes from the current room — resume is from the previous room (VGJUNK ('sent back to the previous room'); TotNL ('Dying puts you back one screen'); manual ocr p.5 ('resuming your quest where you left off'))

**Other sources checked:** http://retrovania-vgjunk.blogspot.com/2015/02/shadowgate-nes.html; https://takeontheneslibrary.com/finished/137-shadowgate/; https://justinpickering.substack.com/p/video-game-review-shadowgate-old (judged unreliable: calls Lakmir evil)

>

## Shockwave (`53477d979c71429a`)

- **Classification:** substantive; error types: wrong rule, wrong item effect
- **Queue:** escalation (nes-native-untouched)
- **Manual:** Shockwave (USA) (Unl); page images inspected: yes (p01, p02, p03, p04, p06, p07)
- **Verification:** level D; remaining uncertainty: How two-player play works (alternating or otherwise) is not stated in the manual, so the text says only that one or two players can take part.

**Before:**

> The game tasks players with collecting the hidden crystals in each stage while racing against a clock. Deadly FireStars act as hazards throughout the areas. A password system allows players to resume their progress, with codes that depend on an entered name.
>
> To navigate stages, the character wields a weapon capable of breaking cracked blocks. This armament can also send a shockwave through solid blocks to push the final block in a connected row. Helpful bonus pickups include extra lives, hourglasses that add time, and items that freeze enemies. One or two players can take part.

**After:**

> The game tasks players with collecting the hidden crystals in each maze while racing against a clock. Deadly FireStars act as hazards throughout the areas. A password system allows players to resume their progress, with codes that depend on an entered name.
>
> To navigate the mazes, the spaceman wields a shock wave pistol capable of destroying broken blocks. The shock wave does not move the block it hits but pushes the blocks next to it, and when a block cannot move, the wave travels on until the last block in the line is affected. Helpful bonus pickups include extra lives, hourglasses that add time, and items that temporarily freeze the FireStars. One or two players can take part.

**What was wrong and why it changed:** Fixed the shock wave rule (it pushes adjacent blocks and passes along a line; 'solid blocks' are immovable in the manual); freeze item limited to the FireStars and marked temporary; 'stage' to 'maze'; weapon named as the shock wave pistol. M3.3 generalizations confirmed.

**Contradicted by NES evidence:**

- Shockwave travels through solid blocks to push the final block in a connected row — 'Solid Block' is the manual's indestructible, immovable block. The wave does not move the block it hits; it moves the adjacent blocks, and if the first cannot move it continues through neighboring blocks to the last block in line. Reworded (manual p03, p04 (images))

**Before:**

> Four narrative stages and a standalone halfpipe ramp make up the adventure. Guiding an unnamed skateboarder through side-scrolling environments, the player seeks to build a new halfpipe after the original is demolished. The hero skates through city streets, works a timed delivery route in a two-story mall, gathers scattered blueprint pages on a beach, and navigates a four-floor warehouse maze to rescue his girlfriend from the villain Icepick. > Four narrative stages and a standalone halfpipe ramp make up the adventure. Guiding an unnamed skateboarder through side-scrolling environments, the player seeks to build a new ramp after the original is demolished. The hero skates through city streets, works a timed delivery route in a mall, gathers scattered blueprint pages on a beach, and fights through a warehouse to recover a building permit and rescue his girlfriend, CJ, from the villain Icepick. The player can backtrack through areas, jump, and reprogram the action controls.
>
> Combat and bartering drive progress. Armed with a paint gun alongside throwable eggs and M-80s, the skater battles rival skaters, animals, and gang members. Trade goods such as CDs, cassette tapes, chili fries, and tacos turn up along the way, and skilled weapon use yields more of them.
