**Contradicted by NES evidence:**

- Seeks to build a new halfpipe after the original is demolished — The condemned and demolished structure is 'a rad ramp in your backyard' and the goal is to 'build a new ramp'; the Half-Pipe is the separate Double Trouble competition ramp. (manual story / p09)
- Trade goods: CDs, cassette tapes, French fries and tacos — The fries item is 'Chili Fries'. (manual p06 (image))

> Set across a city threatened by the ultimate source of evil, the game places the player in control of a Christian traversing a top-down overworld. The mission requires gathering six pieces of the Armor of God guarded by bosses to deliver the settlement from demonic influence. Earlier M3.2 correction (vials instead of a wind-and-dust bomb) confirmed.

- Fruits advance through role-playing style levels — manual: up to 4 of each fruit can be collected, letting the player throw that many at a time; no levels described (manual ocr Fruit of the Spirit)
- Angels provide power-ups and Bible trivia — manual: angel asks 5 Bible questions; rewards are Spirit Points and two hearts of Health, not power-ups (manual ocr Guardian Angel)

## Star Wars (`b9116f11828e39d3`)

- **Classification:** rewrite; error types: other-version detail, invented detail, wrong item effect
- **Queue:** main (nes-native-untouched)
- **Manual:** Star Wars (USA); page images inspected: yes (p04, p06, p09, p10)
- **Verification:** level D; remaining uncertainty: None material.

**Before:**

> Star Wars features side-scrolling platforming across multiple planets alongside cockpit and overhead flight segments.
>
> The player controls Luke Skywalker as he attempts to unite with the Rebellion against the Empire. Luke wields a lightsaber and spends Force points gathered from defeated foes to execute special maneuvers such as floating, speeding, and stopping time. Stages conclude with encounters against shape-shifting apprentices resembling Darth Vader, though the real Vader is confronted on the Death Star and Yavin IV. Rescued allies provide guidance and assist through an in-game menu. Space travel between planets requires piloting the Millennium Falcon from a cockpit view to eliminate opposing TIE fighters. **After:**

> Star Wars features side-scrolling platforming on Tatooine and aboard the Death Star alongside landspeeder, asteroid field and cockpit flight segments.
>
> The player begins as Luke Skywalker, crossing the Tatooine Desert by landspeeder and exploring its caves and Mos Eisley in search of the runaway droid R2-D2, Obi-Wan Kenobi and Han Solo, before rescuing Princess Leia from the Death Star cell block. Luke, Han and Leia can each be controlled, and only Luke can swing a lightsaber. Han and Leia have a single life each, though Obi-Wan can use the Force to revive them, while C-3PO and R2-D2 offer advice and R2-D2 can display Death Star maps. - Force points from defeated foes used for floating, speeding, stopping time — No Force-point system; Obi-Wan uses the Force only to revive Han or Leia (manual (all pages))
- Stages end with shape-shifting Darth Vader apprentices; real Vader on Death Star and Yavin IV — Not in NES game; enemies include Jawas, Sandpeople, Boba Fett, stormtroopers, trash compactor beast (manual enemies list and level descriptions)
- Millennium Falcon cockpit battle with TIE fighters between planets — Falcon gunner sequence occurs fleeing the Death Star toward Yavin, not between planets (manual p10 image)
- Final stage is an overhead X-wing maze toward a reactor duct before time expires — No overhead maze or timer described (manual OCR p.20 (X-wing guides down the trench to blow up the exhaust port))

**Contradicted by NES evidence:**

- Hiryu investigates a conspiracy involving mind-control weapons known as Zain units — manual: an evil project called 'ZAIN', 'the ZAIN mind-control weapon'; 'Zain units' is not the NES name (manual p05 (image))
- Plasma blade known as the Cypher — manual spells it 'Cipher'; 'plasma blade' not stated (Plasma Arrow is a separate ability) (manual p07, p11 (image))

**Other sources checked:** https://www.hardcoregaming101.net/strider-nes/; https://tasvideos.org/1410S

## Stunt Kids (`f3a140c16012c4e4`)

- **Classification:** rewrite; error types: invented detail, wrong name, wrong rule
- **Queue:** escalation (m32-recovered-manual)
- **Manual:** Stunt Kids (USA) (Unl); page images inspected: yes (p01, p02, p03, p04, p05, p06, p07, p08)
- **Verification:** level D; remaining uncertainty: None material. The cover and contents show riders Speedy Spike and Mad Brad, but the manual does not say whether the player chooses between them, so they are not named.

**Before:**

> The player operates a bike across obstacle courses, aiming to negotiate hazards and complete various tracks. Vehicles include options such as cars and rigs, and courses feature diverse level types like a log ride and a construction site. While navigating the tracks, the front wheel can be raised or lowered to handle drops, jumps, and landing stability.
>
> Driving demands careful speed management, as terrain like poles or hazards named Escargo drastically alter vehicle pace. A turbo function allows riders to break away from pursuers attempting to knock them off the bike. Play options provide single-player racing as well as two-player competitive modes.

**After:**

> Players ride a bike across set courses, racing against the clock alone or against each other in a two-player game. In one-player mode there are five worlds, each with six possible courses to choose from plus a bonus level at the end, and the player starts with three lives. In two-player mode, player 1 picks three courses from a selection of twelve, and the player with the lowest overall time wins.
>
> Courses fall into level types such as the countryside, a park and a construction site, and each obstacle calls for its own approach: some must be ridden slowly, others jumped or used as ramps. The rider can jump, pull a wheelie or lower the front wheel, and should land with the front wheel raised. A Turbo button helps escape hazards such as the eggs dropped by Free-Range, and coins collected along the way add bonus points.

**What was wrong and why it changed:** Rewrote from the NES manual: removed the invented 'cars and rigs' vehicle choice (garbled OCR), replaced the 'log ride' level type with the manual's level types (Countryside, Park, Construction site), corrected the claim that poles and Escargo alter pace (the list gives advised speeds; Escargo is a creature), and added the manual's world/course/lives structure and two-player rules.

**Contradicted by NES evidence:**

- Vehicles include options such as cars and rigs — No vehicle selection exists in the manual; 'Car'/'Rig' appear only as garbled OCR of the 'Select your level' screenshot. The rider uses a bike. (manual p03-p08 (images))
- Level types like a log ride and a construction site — Level types are Countryside, Park and Construction site; 'Tricky log ride' is only a screenshot caption, not a level type. (manual p06 (image))
- Terrain like poles or hazards named Escargo drastically alter vehicle pace — The obstacle list gives the advised riding speed for each obstacle (Poles: very slow); Escargo is listed as one of the 'Big Baddies' creatures, with no stated effect on pace. (manual p06, p07 (image))

> Set in the year 2525, an international terrorist known as X nears completion of an ultimate war weapon. After dispatched agents fail to halt the criminal scheme, intelligence operatives are deployed to eliminate the threat. The player pilots an armed vehicle across car, boat, and plane stages to battle enemy forces, encountering bosses such as the Amphibious Aerial Assault craft, the Turbo-Prop Space Cruiser, and a Weapons Factory.
>

In car stages, blue capsules supply special devices such as oil slicks, tire slashers, super bombs, and extra lives. Planes feature red power items along with super and homing missiles, while boat stages restrict the player to bullets. The game ends when all five starting lives are lost.

> Set in the year 2525, an international terrorist known as X nears completion of an ultimate war weapon. After the C.I.A.'s best agents fail to halt the criminal scheme and rookie agent Rachel does not return, an unofficial agent code-named Super Spy Hunter is called in. The player pilots an armed vehicle across car, boat, and plane stages over six missions, such as Aquapolis, Desert of Doom, and Collapsible Canyon, battling bosses such as the Armored Transport, Turret Terminator, and Turbo-Prop Space Cruiser.
>
> Destroying weapon vehicles yields capsules containing offensive tools and enhancements. In car stages, blue capsules supply special devices such as oil slicks, tire slashers, super bombs, and extra lives. - After dispatched agents fail, intelligence operatives (plural) are deployed — The C.I.A.'s best agents failed; rookie agent Rachel (Code HE03) has not returned; the C.I.A. then calls on a single unofficial agent code-named S.S.H. 'Super Spy Hunter'. (manual p03 (image))
- Bosses include the Amphibious Aerial Assault craft, the Turbo-Prop Space Cruiser and a Weapons Factory — Amphibious/Aerial Assault (Mission 5) and Weapons Factory (Mission 6) are mission names, not bosses. Bosses listed: Armored Transport, Turret Terminator, Laser Cannon, Magnetic Destroyer, Turbo-Prop Space Cruiser, and '?' for Mission 6. (manual p07-p08 (image), Levels of Game Play)
- Red items activate automatically and provide health refills, life gauge expansions, rapid fire, vehicle upgrades — Life Refill is a BLUE item. Red items are Power Up, Rapid Shooting, Cannon Control and Life Gauge; the red Life Gauge expands the gauge and also fills it. Rephrased. (manual p05 (image), booklet p.6-7; p07 booklet p.10)

A single participant can progress through successive title matches to earn increasingly larger trophies, rising from American to European, World, and finally Super Champion. Each of the four featured competitors possesses a distinct attack designed specifically for use against one designated rival. The game supports up to two players.

**What was wrong and why it changed:** Replaced the inaccurate grapple 'menu' with pin option with the manual's B-to-cycle, A-to-execute move selection and separate pin rule; added tagging; changed 'tournament matches' to title matches with the manual's championship ranks.

**Contradicted by NES evidence:**

- Grapple leads to a menu to select moves, execute attacks, or attempt pins — After a grab a move appears on screen; B cycles moves and A executes. Pinning happens after a move puts the opponent down; it is not a menu option. (manual p03-p04 (image))

- Levels from Florida beaches to Manhattan, the Technodrome, Shredder's lair, Krang's Spaceship — manual levels: Ft. Slaughterdale Beach, The Typhoon Tidal Pool, Brooklyn Bridge Is Falling Down, Welcome To The Jungle, The Sewer Pipe Nightmare, The Technodrome, Vertigo Point Tower, Krang's Spaceship. 'Florida' not stated; 'Shredder's lair' is a phrase inside the Technodrome entry; fixed (manual p06 right, p07 (images))

## Tetris (`9daa4bec3013ae7e`)

- **Classification:** rewrite; error types: other-version detail, wrong player mode, wrong rule

- **Verification:** level D; remaining uncertainty: The batch's attached manual is for the wrong release (Nintendo's Tetris); the Tengen manual was fetched from the same archive.org collection. The earlier M3.2 correction relied on the wrong manual.

**Before:**

> Falling blocks of various shapes are maneuvered and stacked by the player as they descend onto the play area. The core objective requires arranging these descending pieces to complete continuous horizontal lines. Whenever a complete row forms across the playing field, that line disappears, preventing the accumulated structures from reaching the top of the screen.
>
> Two different game types can be selected. A-Type serves as an endurance mode where the falling speed gradually increases while attempting to clear lines for high scores. B-Type challenges players to clear 25 lines while adjusting both the falling speed and the starting height of random blocks placed at the bottom.

**After:**

> Falling blocks of various shapes are maneuvered and stacked by the player as they descend onto the play area. The core objective requires arranging these descending pieces to complete continuous horizontal lines. Whenever a complete row forms across the playing field, that line disappears, preventing the accumulated structures from reaching the top of the screen.
>
> Five game-play variations can be selected: a one-player game, a two-player competition, a two-player cooperative game, a match against the computer, and a cooperative game with the computer. In every variation except the one-player game, both sides receive the same shapes in the same order. Each player chooses a starting difficulty level from 0 through 9 and a handicap of 0, 3, 6, 9 or 12 lines already stacked at the start. The pieces fall faster as more lines are cleared, and bonus points for singles, doubles, triples and four-line Tetrises are awarded each time a new difficulty level is reached.

**What was wrong and why it changed:** Second paragraph described Nintendo's NES Tetris (A-Type/B-Type, 25 lines). Rewrote it from Tengen's own manual: five game-play variations including simultaneous two-player and computer modes, shared piece order, level 0-9, line handicap, speed-up and level bonuses. First paragraph kept word for word.

**Contradicted by NES evidence:**

- A-Type endurance mode with gradually increasing speed — A-Type/B-Type are features of Nintendo's NES Tetris. Tengen's version offers 1 Player, 2 Player, Cooperative, Versus Computer and With Computer. (Tengen manual pages 4-5 (images); https://tetris.wiki/Tetris_(NES,_Tengen))
- B-Type: clear 25 lines with adjustable speed and starting height — No 25-line mode; Tengen has a handicap of 0, 3, 6, 9 or 12 pre-stacked lines and level select 0-9. (Tengen manual pages 4-5 (images))
- Earlier correction: game is single-player only (two-player claim contradicted) — The earlier audit used the Nintendo manual; Tengen's release has simultaneous two-player competitive and cooperative modes. (Tengen manual page 4 (image))

**Other sources checked:** https://tetris.wiki/Tetris_(NES,_Tengen)

**Before:**

> To the Earth operates as a light gun shooter where the player uses the NES Zapper to defend human civilization against an alien invasion. Set in the year 2050, the storyline tasks the player with transporting medicine from a base near Neptune across the Solar System to save humanity from extinction. > Target accuracy remains vital because missing a shot causes the spacecraft's shield energy to decrease. In the year 2050, the player pilots the spaceship The Tempest to deliver an antibacterial agent that will save humanity from extinction. To formulate the agent, the ship must obtain mineral components at four locations, Uranus, Saturn, Jupiter, and Earth, while the player shoots down enemy spacecraft, missiles, laser bombs, and asteroids and avoids hitting friendly ships.
>

Assisting the player are special items, including screen-clearing Smart Bombs earned by downing enough enemies in a row at full energy, comets that grant a Barrier Shield absorbing several missile shots, and energy refills offered when friendly ships cross the screen. Each location ends with a boss fight, the last against Nemesis, leader of the Raggosian forces.

>

**After:**

> Based on the 1990 film of the same name, the game casts the player as Douglas Quaid, a construction worker whose memories have been tampered with. Most of the adventure is played on foot through streets, subways, and interplanetary flight terminals, where Quaid punches or shoots thugs and special agents, jumps, crouches, and enters doors. Weapons such as a hand gun, machine gun, and lasers become available along the way, and energy canisters restore his five energy blocks. Quaid starts with three lives, and extra lives are hidden throughout.
>
> After accepting a free ride to Mars, Quaid takes the wheel in the Martian Transit Hub, a driving section where he drives forward and backward, turns, fires weapons, and drops land mines while avoiding Richter's car. Replaced with the manual's structure (mostly on-foot action through streets, subways and flight terminals; one driving section in the Martian Transit Hub), controls, weapons, energy blocks, lives, the ride to Mars, Richter and Cohaagen. Dropped 'single-player' and the driving perspective, which no source settles.

- Overhead racing segments — Driving section, not racing. Its perspective is uncertain: an NES review mentions an 'overhead taxi mission', but the manual's Transit Hub screenshot shows a vehicle on a Martian landscape; 'overhead' left out (manual p06-p07; justgamesretro.com)

Edogy, a menace from the underground world with designs on taking over California above and below ground, kidnaps Jake's friend Allison to lure her father, a professor, and soon holds them both. With help from his teacher, the old magician Zebediah, Jake sets out to rescue them and confront Edogy.
>
> Throughout the journey, the protagonist draws on twelve magic powers, including spells that damage every enemy on screen and transformations into a lion, an eagle, or a fish, all limited by a magic power gauge. Each of the five levels contains two or three stages and ends with a boss fight against one of Edogy's grotesque associates. Holding the fire button charges a stronger shot.

**What was wrong and why it changed:** Rewrote the plot from the US manual (Edogy kidnaps Allison to lure her professor father; no 'evil king', no 'discover their origin'); replaced 'summoning abilities' with the 12 magic powers and transformations; removed the unverified three-continue rule; added the manual's five-level structure and charge shot. Kept the opening sentence.

**Contradicted by NES evidence:**

- Strange attackers abduct his girlfriend Allison; Jake sets out to discover their origin and intentions — US manual: Edogy, an underground menace, kidnaps Allison to lure her father; Jake must rescue both. 'Discover origin and intentions' is not the US story; 'girlfriend' is not stated (Jake 'has this thing for' Allison). (manual p04 (image), ocr story)
- Halt an evil king seeking to unleash a subterranean army against the surface world — US manual: Edogy, the underground menace who dominates most of the underground world, plans to take over California above and below ground; he is not called a king. (manual p04 (image))
- Special summoning abilities — Jake has 12 magic powers (screen-clearing spells, healing, shields, stop time, transformations into lion, eagle, fish); no summoning (manual p05, p08 (image); ocr magic list)

**Other sources checked:** https://seafoamgaming.com/2025/05/11/jalecolle-famicom-ver-magic-john-totally-rad-switch-eshop-review/; https://tcrf.net/Totally_Rad (blocked: JavaScript/cookie wall)

> Town & Country Surf Designs - Thrilla's Surfari centers on obstacle navigation across various environments. The player controls Thrilla Gorilla on a mission to rescue his girlfriend, Barbi Bikini, after she is captured by the witch doctor Wazula. Progress leads through diverse environments including jungles, deserts, waterfalls, rivers, and submerged caverns. Thrilla navigates jungle and desert stages on a skateboard, rides a surfboard through river and waterfall areas, and maneuvers atop a shark within underwater caves.
>
> While advancing, the player steers around hazards, leaps over pits, and avoids hostile creatures such as giraffes, elephants, carnivorous plants, snakes, giant spiders, and electric eels. > Town & Country Surf Designs - Thrilla's Surfari centers on obstacle navigation across various environments. The player controls Thrilla Gorilla on a mission to rescue Barbi Bikini, who has been kidnapped by Wazula as a meal for Imu, the Volcano Master. Progress leads through jungles, rivers, deserts, lava rivers, waterfalls, and the ocean. Thrilla rides a skateboard on land, surfs the rivers and waterfalls, and rides a shark underwater, facing one of Wazula's bosses at the end of each level.
>
> While advancing, the player steers around hazards, leaps over pits, and avoids or lands on hostile creatures such as giraffes, angry warriors, voodoo skulls, giant cobras, scorpions, and electric eels. Collectible items include coconuts, which earn turns at a Shell Game for extra lives, bananas, which restore health, and diamonds, which grant temporary invincibility.

**What was wrong and why it changed:** Replaced the unsupported 'handstand maneuver' item with the manual's diamond pick-up; corrected the enemy list (removed elephants, carnivorous plants and giant spiders; added manual-listed foes); added Imu, the lava river and the ocean; dropped 'witch doctor'; added item effects and level bosses.

**Contradicted by NES evidence:**

- Enemies: giraffes, elephants, carnivorous plants, snakes, giant spiders, electric eels — Manual names electric eels, angry warriors, giraffes, voodoo skulls, soldier ants, giant cobras, scorpions, squids, clams, stone-throwing sea plants. Elephants, carnivorous plants and giant spiders are not mentioned. (manual p06, p07 (image))
- Handstand maneuver item gives temporary invulnerability except pits — The manual's invincibility pick-up is the Diamond; no handstand item or pit exception is described (manual p10 (image))

## Town & Country Surf Designs - Wood & Water Rage (`f3955370fe7ecc99`)

- **Classification:** substantive; error types: wrong rule, wrong control
- **Queue:** main (nes-native-untouched)
- **Manual:** T&C Surf Designs - Wood & Water Rage (USA); page images inspected: yes (p03, p04, p05, p06)
- **Verification:** level D; remaining uncertainty: None material.

**Before:**

> Mascots known as Da Boys compete across multiple skateboarding and surfing events. Street Skate Session places players in control of Joe Cool or Tiki Man as they navigate a timed obstacle course on a skateboard. Controlling speed and steering with the directional pad, players can jump, slow down by gripping the board, execute ollies over hazards, grind railings, and launch off ramps. Bailing costs a life, while completing a course awards bonus points based on remaining time and lives.
>
> Big Wave Encounter shifts the objective to survival as Kool Kat or Thrilla Gorilla surf a large wave. Surfers steer around hazards, leap off the wave crest, and collect bananas until passing a pier to complete the round. Colliding with obstacles costs a life. The third mode, Wood and Water Rage, alternates rounds between skateboarding and surfing with a chosen pair of characters.

**After:**

> Mascots known as Da Boys compete across multiple skateboarding and surfing events. Street Skate Session places players in control of Joe Cool or Tiki Man as they navigate a timed obstacle course on a skateboard. Controlling speed and steering with the directional pad, players can jump, kick to speed up, leap while holding the board, hop barriers as the board rolls underneath, grind railings, and launch off ramps. Crashes cost life symbols, while completing a course awards bonus points for the remaining time.
>
> Big Wave Encounter shifts the objective to survival as Kool Kat or Thrilla Gorilla surf a large wave. Surfers steer around hazards, leap off the wave crest, and collect bananas until reaching the beach to complete the round. Colliding with fish, seagulls, or pier supports costs life symbols. The third mode, Wood and Water Rage, alternates rounds between skateboarding and surfing with a chosen pair of characters.

**What was wrong and why it changed:** Fixed the skate controls (left slows down; holding the board is a jump variant; B kicks to speed up); replaced 'costs a life' with the manual's life-symbol system in both events; the completion bonus counts remaining time only; Big Wave rounds end on reaching the beach, and pier supports are hazards.

**Contradicted by NES evidence:**

- Slow down by gripping the board — LEFT slows down; LEFT plus A jumps while holding the skateboard; B kicks to speed up (manual p04 (image))
- Bailing costs a life — Players have life symbols; falling into the ocean or a crack or hitting an oil drum costs 3, other obstacles 2; game over when out of symbols or time (manual p04 (image))
- Completion bonus based on remaining time and lives — Only remaining time is added as bonus points (manual p05 (image))
- Round completes on passing a pier — Manual: complete the game when you reach the beach; pier supports are hazards costing a life symbol. TONL: reach the pier on the beach. Reworded to reaching the beach. (manual p06 (image); TONL)
- Colliding with obstacles costs a life — Costs life symbols: hazards like fish and seagulls 2, pier supports 1 (manual p06 (image))

**Other sources checked:** https://takeontheneslibrary.com/tag/tc/

## Toxic Crusaders (`c3fec0650f170991`)

> Toxic Crusaders is a side-scrolling action game designed for a single player. The player controls Toxie, a mutated hero who sets out to rescue his girlfriend Yvonne and his captured allies from Dr. Killemoff. Movement spans left, right, and into the foreground or background of each scene. Toxie jumps and strikes enemies or breakable objects using his fists and his mop. Each hit costs him one heart from his eight-heart energy meter and one level of power from his mop gauge. If all hearts run out, one life is lost from his starting pool of two.

At higher ranks, the mop fires projectiles or flies like a returning boomerang. Across six stages, Toxie traverses environments such as city streets, a high school, a factory, a highway on a skateboard, sewers, and Killemoff's headquarters. Every stage concludes with a boss battle.

**What was wrong and why it changed:** Reworded the damage sentence ('depletes both hearts from his eight-point life meter and weapon power') to state the manual's rule exactly: each hit costs one heart (of up to eight) and one mop level. All other sentences kept word for word.

## Track & Field (`a2812d80b3057aac`)

- **Classification:** substantive; error types: wrong control, wrong rule
- **Queue:** escalation (m32-audit-corrected)
- **Manual:** Track & Field (USA); page images inspected: yes (p03, p05)
- **Verification:** level D; remaining uncertainty: 'One missed hurdle, and you're history' is read as failing the event; the manual does not elaborate.

**Before:**

> Athletic competition forms the focus as players guide an athlete through eight events, including the 100-meter dash, long jump, hurdles, javelin throw, skeet shooting, triple jump, archery, and high jump. Running speed in athletic contests is built strictly by repeatedly pressing the A button, while the Control Pad directs jump angles, throws, and aiming across skill-based trials.
>
> Advancement requires matching or beating designated qualifying times, distances, or scores during every event. Incurring fouls or missing hurdles limits attempts, and failing to qualify in any contest immediately ends the game. Sessions can be played solo against the computer or between two players on alternating turns, with selectable novice and expert difficulty settings.

**After:**

> Athletic competition forms the focus as players guide an athlete through eight events, including the 100-meter dash, long jump, hurdles, javelin throw, skeet shooting, triple jump, archery, and high jump. Running speed in athletic contests is built strictly by repeatedly pressing the A button, while the Control Pad handles the timing and angle of jumps, the javelin release, and shot release in skill-based trials.
>
> Advancement requires matching or beating designated qualifying times, distances, or scores during every event. Fouls count as attempts in the long jump, the hurdles allow only a single heat in which one missed hurdle spells failure, and failing to qualify in any contest immediately ends the game. Sessions can be played solo against the computer or between two players on alternating turns, with selectable novice and expert difficulty settings.

**What was wrong and why it changed:** Fixed the Control Pad description (timing and angle of jumps, javelin release, shot release; aim in skill events belongs to the A Button) and the fouls/hurdles rule (in the long jump fouls count as attempts; the hurdles give one heat and a missed hurdle means failure). Earlier corrections (A button only; no life system) confirmed. Other sentences kept word for word.

**Contradicted by NES evidence:**

- Control Pad directs jump angles, throws, and aiming across skill-based trials — Page 5: Control Pad 'controls timing and angle of jump in athletic events, shot release in skill events'; A Button controls 'shooting aim and timing in skill events'; javelin is released with the Control Pad (page 8). Reworded (manual p03 (image), page 5)
- Fouls or missing hurdles limit attempts — Long jump: three attempts, 'fouls count as turns'; hurdles: one heat, 'one missed hurdle, and you're history!' (page 8). Missing a hurdle does not merely limit attempts. Reworded (manual p05 (image), page 8)

> Collecting all colored eggs scattered across each island grid is the primary objective while evading pursuers. ## Trojan (`a5ae39359aa5b169`)

- **Classification:** substantive; error types: other-version detail, unsupported specific, invented detail
- **Queue:** escalation (m32-audit-corrected)
- **Manual:** Trojan (USA); page images inspected: yes (p01, p02, p03, p04, p05, p06)

**Before:**

> Defeating the tyrannical warlord Achilles and his demonic army is the central mission in this side-scrolling action title. Set across an apocalyptic wasteland, the player guides the warrior Trojan through hostile territory to confront possessed gladiators and pirates. > Defeating Achilles, the head of the enemy forces, is the central mission in this side-scrolling action title. A two-player versus mode allows participants to fight in head-to-head matches.

Earlier correction (super-jump instead of springboards) confirmed. Hidden-room and bonus-item sentence kept word for word.

Before hitting the sand, an options screen permits adjusting the difficulty across three tiers, choosing a victory threshold of 5, 10, or 15 points, setting match length to a single game or best two out of three, and switching between normal serve-only scoring and rally point rules.

## Vindicators (`8104dc7acdaea42b`)

**Before:**

> Reaching the exit at the top of each multidirectional scrolling level serves as the primary goal while managing constantly draining tank fuel. One or two players maneuver tanks through hostile areas filled with obstacles and enemy forces. Progression requires finding a key to unlock the exit door, which either leads directly forward or sends the tank into a timed hub filled with power-ups. Failure to escape this bonus room before the timer expires penalizes the player by draining half of the vehicle's remaining fuel.
>

> One or two players drive Vindicators battle tanks against an attacking force of alien space stations, with 14 stations to wipe out. Inside each multi-level station, the goal is to locate and destroy its control center while fending off turrets, mines, enemy tanks such as the Aggressor and Darter, and flying saucers. Fuel must be constantly replenished by picking up fuel canisters, and keys let a tank leave one level and enter the next.
>
> The control center doubles as the Bonus Room: players grab as many objects as possible before the clock runs down and the room blows up, and failing to exit in time cuts the fuel level in half. Battle Stars collected along the way buy tank speed and fuel, improved shots, Force Shields, and two special weapons, homing Smart Shots and powerful Bomb Cannons. Bosses such as the Sentry Robot, GunGun, and Mega-Brain call for heavy use of these special weapons.

**What was wrong and why it changed:** Bounded rewrite from the NES manual: removed arcade exit-at-top, branching exit door and empty-fuel countdown; Bonus Room is the control center; shields and special weapons are bought with Battle Stars; added 14 stations, enemy and boss names.

- Collect stars as currency, fuel, shields and sub-weapons as pickups — Battle Stars and fuel canisters are picked up; shields, Smart Shots and Bomb Cannons are bought with Battle Stars (manual p04 (image))

**What was wrong and why it changed:** Replaced Japanese/encyclopedia story (Red Earth, Dr. Faryan's cave, Ken, Warwolf) with the US manual's Faryan, death slaves and Chief War Wolf; replaced 'enhanced reach' with manual werewolf powers; kept item mechanics; added five levels, Power Ray, alternating two-player and time limit.

**Contradicted by NES evidence:**

- Hero Ken, last of a changeling tribe, becomes Warwolf — US manual: player starts as Chief War Wolf; no Ken or changeling tribe; spelled War Wolf (manual p02, p06 (image))

**Other sources checked:** https://takeontheneslibrary.com/tag/were/

Landing on bankrupt forfeits that round's cash, landing on miss a turn skips the next turn, and free spins can be banked for later use. The highest earner advances to round four, selects a featured prize, and calls five consonants plus one vowel before trying to type the complete answer. > Operating as an Acme Detective Agency agent headquartered in San Francisco, the player investigates across historical eras to apprehend Carmen Sandiego and her henchmen. Equipped with a device called the Chronoskimmer, the agent journeys through fifteen centuries of human history spanning from 400 AD to the 1950s. The objective requires locating eighty villains across time and detaining them.
>

Choosing correctly among available travel routes triggers an animation of a gang member confirming the trail. Every action consumes portions of an authorized time limit. > Operating as an Acme Detective Agency agent headquartered in San Francisco, the player investigates across historical eras to apprehend Carmen Sandiego and her henchmen. Equipped with a device called the Chronoskimmer, the agent journeys through fifteen centuries of human history spanning from 400 AD to the 1950s. Each case involves tracking a thief, one of sixteen possible suspects, to a hideout somewhere in time.
>
> Investigations involve questioning witnesses and scanning areas to gather evidence: hints indicating the suspect's following destination and details regarding their physical traits or interests. Reaching the correct destination reveals a suspicious person or occurrence on the location panel. Searching and traveling consume portions of an authorized time limit. Successful cases require securing a proper arrest warrant and closing in on the criminal's hideout before time runs out. Advancing through cases earns promotions from Time Cadet through multiple ranks up to Super Time Sleuth.

Earlier M3.2 correction (warrant and hideout) confirmed.

**Contradicted by NES evidence:**

- Objective requires locating eighty villains across time and detaining them — There are sixteen possible suspects; each case tracks one thief to a hideout. 'About 80' refers to cases solved before the detective is retired from active duty, not villains. (manual p05 (image))
- Choosing correctly triggers an animation of a gang member confirming the trail — Manual: on the right track a suspicious person or occurrence appears on the location panel; V.I.L.E. members check the detective out when getting close. No 'confirming animation' of a gang member is described. (manual p08 (image))

In standard picture scenes, such as the train station, forest, fairground, city, and castle, the directional buttons move a search scope across the screen to pinpoint Waldo's position. Choosing an incorrect spot costs time on the countdown clock. On higher difficulty settings, the scope shrinks, environments grow larger and scroll, and Waldo shifts colors. A practice option restricts access to only the first three areas, while the other settings allow progressively less overall time.

- Magnifying glass moved with directional buttons — Manual calls it a search scope (manual p04 (image))

## Who Framed Roger Rabbit (`700ebc3c2dd27420`)

- **Classification:** rewrite; error types: wrong name, wrong rule, wrong item effect, invented detail, unsupported specific
- **Queue:** main (m32-audit-medium-risk)
- **Manual:** Who Framed Roger Rabbit (USA); page images inspected: yes (p01, p04, p10, p11)
- **Verification:** level D; remaining uncertainty: 'Eddie Valiant' surname rests on the screenshot sign on manual p04 and the film license; text uses 'Eddie'. Shops, meat/rattle distractors, wallet purchases and road blockades may exist in the game but could not be verified (archive.org and lostmediawiki were unreachable).

**Before:**

> Divided into an overhead overworld and side-scrolling interior areas, this action-adventure spans connected regions including Downtown Los Angeles, city outskirts, and Toontown. Players control private detective Eddie Valiant, accompanied by Roger Rabbit, to locate four scattered pieces of Marvin Acme's lost will and defeat Judge Doom. The top-down perspective is used to navigate streets, ride Benny the Cab, and reach structures while avoiding street traffic, bird hazards, and Weasel patrols that present escape riddles. 
>
> Side-scrolling sections allow exploration inside buildings, caves, and shops. Eddie searches furniture for clues and speaks to characters like Jessica Rabbit for assistance. Players defend against foes using chargeable punches, bricks, firearms, and exploding cigars, or use distractors like meat and rattles against unkillable enemies. Crowbars pry open doors, explosives clear road blockades, and collected wallets pay for retail inventory, with randomized item placements requiring comprehensive exploration.

**After:**

> Divided into an overhead map screen and side-view areas, this action-adventure spans four sections of 1940s Los Angeles: the city, the park, the warehouse district, and Toontown. Players control private detective Eddie Valiant, accompanied by Roger Rabbit, to locate four scattered pieces of Marvin's missing will and defeat Judge Doom. The overhead view is used to walk the streets, ride with Benny, and reach buildings while avoiding speeding cars and the Weasels. When the Weasels catch Roger, the player must choose the right punchline to a joke to free him.
>
> Side-view sections allow exploration of building exteriors, hallways, rooms, and caves. Eddie searches drawers and cabinets for clues and items, and asks passersby questions. Players defend against foes using wound-up punches, bricks, a six shooter, and exploding cigars. A thrown crowbar breaks door locks, a whistle calls Benny, and randomized item placements require thorough exploration. Passwords let a new game start with the objects collected earlier.

**What was wrong and why it changed:** Replaced the region list with the four sections named in the manual; replaced bird hazards and 'escape riddles' with speeding cars and the Weasel punchline-joke rule; dropped unconfirmed shops, Jessica Rabbit assistance, meat and rattles, road blockades and wallet purchases; corrected crowbar effect; used manual names (Benny, Marvin's will); added the manual's password feature.

**Contradicted by NES evidence:**

- Regions include Downtown Los Angeles, city outskirts, and Toontown — Four sections of 1940s Los Angeles: the City, the Park, Toontown and the Warehouse District; no 'outskirts' (manual p04 (image))
- Weasel patrols present escape riddles — When Weasels catch Roger, the player must pick the right punchline to a joke within nine 'toon' seconds; a wrong answer costs a clap board (manual p09 ocr, p10 (image))
- Crowbars pry open doors — Crowbar is thrown at a locked door to break the lock (manual p12 ocr)

**Other sources checked:** https://videofileblog.com/roger-rabbit-1989-nes-videogame-review/

> Three separate realms comprise the open structure of this adventure: the city of Piedup, the UnderWorld, and the Palace. Players direct the warrior Kuros, who arrives stripped of his memory, armor, and weapons after a lightning attack by the evil wizard Malkil. To defeat Malkil and restore the throne to King James, Kuros explores these interconnected areas, buying keys, food, drink, and gossip from shopkeepers with collected money. Players start with three lives, and the journey ends if all are lost.
>
> Progression requires finding the lost statues of the knight, thief, and wizard guilds. Returning a statue to its guild triggers a test that ends in a boss battle; passing it grants a disguise along with new weapons and powers, such as a crowbar, fireballs, or levitation. Malkil has stationed Guardians in front of important areas, and the secret passage to the King's Throne Room cannot be entered without the Four Gems.

**What was wrong and why it changed:** Used manual names (city of Piedup, UnderWorld, Palace, King James, King's Throne Room); 'ambush' made a lightning attack per the manual; replaced 'inns' and 'health items, clues' with the manual's shop purchases; removed unsupported bronze/silver/gold statue metals and the princess/dragon route to the gems; replaced 'building access' with manual-supported weapons and powers; kept the Four Gems requirement and added Malkil's Guardians.

**Contradicted by NES evidence:**

- Buys keys, health items and clues at inns with collected money — Money buys keys, food, drink and gossip; the screenshot shows a shopkeeper ('store' on p14); inns are not mentioned (manual p11 (image))

**Other sources checked:** https://www.hardcoregaming101.net/wizards-warriors-iii/

## Wolverine (`2d62114f3f139e8d`)

- **Classification:** substantive; error types: wrong item effect, wrong control, unsupported specific, invented detail
- **Queue:** main (nes-native-untouched)
- **Manual:** Wolverine (USA); page images inspected: yes (p01, p03, p04, p05, p06, p10)
- **Verification:** level D; remaining uncertainty: Jubilee and Psylocke are stated only generally ('join in on the action', LJN advertisement for this NES game); how they appear in play is unconfirmed, so the text stays general. Whether the two-player mode alternates turns is not stated.

**Before:**

> Captured and abandoned on a desolate island by adversaries Magneto and Sabretooth, Wolverine must navigate hostile hazards and opposing forces to reach a final showdown against his captors. The player guides the hero through multiple stages featuring traps and enemies, without end-of-level bosses until the last two areas.
>
> Controlling Wolverine involves jumping, ducking, punching, and kicking. Pressing the select button unsheathes his claws, which continuously drains energy during use, while touching hazards or foes also depletes health without granting momentary invulnerability. Food and beverage items like hamburgers and soft drinks restore lost health, and additional icons provide extra lives or summon fellow X-Men including Havok, Jubilee, and Psylocke for advice or short-term assistance. Defeating sufficient numbers of lesser enemies temporarily triggers a Berzerker mode.

**After:**

> Stranded on a deserted island, Wolverine enters a structure filled with traps that his arch enemy Sabretooth has built to do away with him. The player guides the hero through nine levels, including trials by air, water, and fire, a confrontation with Magneto, and a final battle. A two-player mode can be selected at the start.
>
> Controlling Wolverine involves moving, crawling, jumping, and punching, and he swims through underwater sections while watching an air gauge. Pressing the select button extends his claws, which make him invincible but quickly drain energy; when energy runs low, the same button calls Havok, once found, to take over while Wolverine regenerates. Burgers restore life energy, while Power Potions build strength and the Berzerker gauge, which also rises as he strikes enemies. One-Ups add to his three starting lives, and Free Game power-ups add continues. Fellow X-Men Jubilee and Psylocke also join the action.

**What was wrong and why it changed:** Replaced the unsupported capture premise with the manual's island and Sabretooth trap setup; replaced 'soft drinks' with Power Potions and their actual effect; removed unsupported kicks, the no-bosses claim and the no-invulnerability claim; reframed Havok's role per the manual; added the nine levels, swimming, lives and continues from the manual; kept Jubilee and Psylocke without the unconfirmed advice mechanism.

**Contradicted by NES evidence:**

- Hamburgers and soft drinks restore health — Burgers increase life energy; the drink is the Power Potion, which builds strength and the Berzerker level (manual p06 (image))

## Wonderland Dizzy (`8a604198ba3e2437`)

- **Classification:** substantive; error types: wrong player mode
- **Queue:** escalation (m32-recovered-research)
- **Manual:** none available; page images inspected: no
- **Verification:** level C; remaining uncertainty: No manual exists for this release. 'Evil wizard' for Zaks is supported by series sources (Magicland Dizzy) rather than a page about this exact NES release. Platforming is generic and not stated explicitly on the developer page.

**Before:**

> Rescuing the Yolkfolk from Wonderland serves as the player's primary goal after the evil wizard Zaks places a curse upon the forest of Keldor. The heroes journey down the Rabbit Hole into this themed setting to locate and save their trapped friends.
>
> Controlling Dizzy, Daisy, or both characters simultaneously shapes the adventure, which centers on platforming, solving puzzles, and aiding witches. **After:**

> Rescuing the Yolkfolk from Wonderland serves as the player's primary goal after the evil wizard Zaks places a curse upon the forest of Keldor. The heroes journey down the Rabbit Hole into this themed setting to locate and save their trapped friends.
>
> Controlling Dizzy, Daisy, or both characters as a pair shapes the adventure, which centers on platforming, solving puzzles, and aiding witches. When using both protagonists together, the player controls one at a time, and a Cheshire cat appears upon the death of the active character to pass all carried items over to the surviving partner. The game also provides an option featuring infinite lives.

**Other sources checked:** https://www.olivertwins.com/wonderlanddizzy; https://www.destructoid.com/?p=173794; https://www.gamegrin.com/news/lost-game-wonderland-dizzy-released-after-22-years-in-wilderness/

## World Class Track Meet (`ac766a8d99bfd8e9`)

- **Classification:** substantive; error types: wrong rule, unsupported specific
- **Queue:** escalation (nes-native-untouched)
- **Manual:** World Class Track Meet (USA); page images inspected: yes (p05, p06, p07, p08, p09, p10, p12, p13)
- **Verification:** level D; remaining uncertainty: The record year in the Olympics section is ambiguous in the scan (1962 or 1982), so it was removed. 'Olympic mode' corresponds to the manual's 'The Olympics'.

**Before:**

> Athletes compete in running and jumping contests driven by physical movement on a floor mat accessory. Runners gain maximum speed depending on which specific row of mat buttons is tapped, and lifting feet prior to the start signal results in a false start penalty. Four distinct competitions are available: the 100M dash, the 110M hurdles, the long jump, and the triple jump. Hurdles require timely leaps when white box indicators appear on screen borders, while jump events measure distance based on running approach and airtime.
>
> Two participants can race simultaneously side by side, or as many as six competitors can take turns. Tournament mode pits a single runner against a sequence of six computer opponents across both track events, where three false starts cause immediate disqualification. An additional Olympic mode allows participants to contest all four disciplines consecutively, benchmarking final scores against the 1982 world track records.

**After:**

> Athletes compete in running and jumping contests driven by physical movement on a floor mat accessory. Runners gain maximum speed depending on which specific row of mat buttons is tapped, and lifting feet prior to the start signal results in a false start penalty. Four distinct competitions are available: the 100M dash, the 110M hurdles, the long jump, and the triple jump. Hurdles require timely leaps when white box markers appear along the edge of the course, while jump events measure distance based on approach speed and take-off timing.
>
> Two participants can race simultaneously side by side, or as many as six competitors can take turns. Tournament mode pits a single runner against a sequence of six computer opponents across both track events, where three false starts cause immediate disqualification. An additional Olympic mode allows participants to contest all four disciplines consecutively, with each result converted to a 100-point scale referenced to world track records.

**What was wrong and why it changed:** Hurdle cue corrected to white box markers along the edge of the course; jump distance tied to approach speed and take-off timing instead of airtime; the unreadable record year removed and Olympics scoring described as a 100-point scale referenced to world track records.

**Contradicted by NES evidence:**

- Hurdlers jump when white box indicators appear on screen borders — 'Jump when you see the white box markers along the edge of the course' (edge of the course, not screen borders) (manual OCR 110M hurdles section (p.20))
- Jump distance based on running approach and airtime — The manual ties distance to approach speed and take-off timing; airtime is not mentioned (manual p10 (p.17), OCR long jump section)

## Wrath of the Black Manta (`3950d679fd6bbd5b`)

- **Classification:** substantive; error types: wrong name, wrong rule, unsupported specific
- **Queue:** main (nes-native-untouched)
- **Manual:** Wrath of the Black Manta (USA); page images inspected: yes (p03, p05, p06, p10, p11)
- **Verification:** level D; remaining uncertainty: The encyclopedia names the villain El Toro and a kidnapped student Taro and describes a first-person final stage; these may be in-game details but no NES-specific source could be reached, so they were left out.

**Before:**

> Controlling the Black Manta, the player attacks enemies with throwing stars and ninjutsu abilities called ninja arts across a side-scrolling adventure. The mission tasks the ninja with confronting a criminal gang and defeating El Toro, an evil mastermind responsible for widespread kidnappings that include a student named Taro.
>
> Five levels comprise the journey, during which the player may locate and rescue abducted children hidden in each area without affecting overall game progress. Successfully clearing a stage grants additional powers that the player selects from a pause screen to defeat adversaries and bosses more rapidly. In the fifth level, the perspective shifts partly to a first-person view, culminating in a rematch against an earlier boss before confronting El Toro directly.

**After:**

> Controlling the Black Manta, the player attacks enemies with thrown darts, a short sword, and special techniques called Ninpo Arts across a side-scrolling adventure. With crime and kidnapping gripping New York City, the mission tasks the ninja with confronting DRAT, a gang of drug runners and terrorists, defeating the drug lord, and rescuing his prisoner.
>
> Five levels comprise the journey, moving from New York City to Tokyo and Rio de Janeiro, back to New York, and finally to DRAT headquarters. Along the way, the player can rescue kidnapped children hidden in heavily guarded rooms, grab informants, and read letters for clues. Successfully clearing a stage grants new Ninpo Arts, such as a ring of fire, invisibility, or teleportation, which the player chooses on the Ninpo Arts screen and unleashes once the POW indicator is charged. Only four particular arts can defeat the final villain.

**What was wrong and why it changed:** Replaced 'throwing stars' and 'ninja arts' with the manual's darts, short sword and Ninpo Arts; replaced the unconfirmed names El Toro and Taro with the manual's DRAT and drug lord; removed the contradicted 'without affecting progress' claim, the unconfirmed first-person/rematch finale; added the manual's level locations, informants, letters and the four-art final boss rule.

**Contradicted by NES evidence:**

- Attacks with throwing stars — Regular weapons are Darts (thrown) and a Short Sword (close range); review calls them throwing stars (manual p05 (image))
- Ninjutsu abilities called ninja arts — The NES release calls them Ninpo Arts (four groups, ten arts) (manual p05, p06 (image))
- Rescuing hidden children does not affect overall progress — Manual: rescue every kidnapped kid, they might have important information; review: children point to hidden rooms with power-ups. Also the manual says the drug lord's prisoner must be rescued to win (manual p03, p10, p11 (image); classic-games.net)

**Other sources checked:** https://classic-games.net/nes/wrath-of-the-black-manta/

## Wrecking Crew (`f1eb29dd1c7b2b29`)

- **Classification:** substantive; error types: wrong name, wrong item effect, wrong rule
- **Queue:** recheck (m32-audit-low-risk)
- **Manual:** Wrecking Crew (World); page images inspected: yes (p03, p04, p05, p06, p07)
- **Verification:** level D; remaining uncertainty: 'Demolition engineers' paraphrase follows the official description; the manual does not use 'engineer'.

**Before:**

> Working as demolition engineers in hard hats, Mario and Luigi take on the task of clearing out enemy-infested building sites. One or two players navigate multi-tiered networks of ladders and scaffolding to smash every target object with a heavy mallet.
>
> The inability to jump requires players to carefully plan routes through each environment, as demolishing ladders or walls in the wrong order can leave remaining targets inaccessible. Along with indestructible barrels and obstacles, levels contain chain-reaction bombs, doors that send monsters safely into the background, and a disruptive foreman named Spike who attempts to knock the worker downward. Touching foes or stray fireballs costs a life, while trapping the character inside a barrel forces an immediate retreat.

**After:**

> Working as demolition engineers in hard hats, Mario and Luigi take on the task of clearing out enemy-infested building sites. One or two players navigate multi-tiered networks of ladders and scaffolding to smash every target object with a heavy mallet.
>
> The inability to jump requires players to carefully plan routes through each environment, as demolishing ladders or walls in the wrong order can leave remaining targets inaccessible. Along with indestructible drums and obstacles, levels contain dynamite that can blast several walls at once, doors into which monsters can be herded, and a disruptive foreman named Spike who attempts to knock the worker downward. Touching foes or stray fireballs costs a life, while getting covered by a drum forces the player to start over.

**What was wrong and why it changed:** Barrels -> drums (manual term); 'chain-reaction bombs' -> dynamite that blasts several walls at once; doors fixed to the manual's 'herd the monsters inside'; drum trap now 'start over' per the manual.

**Contradicted by NES evidence:**

- Indestructible barrels — manual calls them drums ('dead-end drum', among things that can't be demolished) (manual p04 right (image))
- Chain-reaction bombs — manual: dynamite knocks down walls on both sides / blasts several walls at once (manual p04 right, p05 right (images))
- Doors send monsters safely into the background — doors are not described as sending monsters into the background; fixed (manual p04 right (image): door opens when knocked, monsters go in and out; p06 right (image): 'Hammer open the door and herd the monsters inside')
- Trapped inside a barrel forces an immediate retreat — 'Covered by a drum: You have to start all over again from the beginning' (manual p07 right (image))

## Wurm - Journey to the Center of the Earth! (`a0354fb9c1c29e25`)

- **Classification:** substantive; error types: wrong rule, wrong name, unsupported specific
- **Queue:** main (nes-native-untouched)
- **Manual:** Wurm - Journey to the Center of the Earth! (USA); page images inspected: yes (p03, p04, p05, p06, p08, p10, p11, p12, p13)
- **Verification:** level D; remaining uncertainty: None material.

**Before:**

> Wurm - Journey to the Center of the Earth! features multiple genres across its gameplay modes. The story follows an underground expedition sent after earthquakes strike in 1999. Players direct the crew of an exploration vehicle commanded by Moby. While exploring subterranean depths, the group becomes involved in a war between peaceful humanoids and a hostile empire of monsters that targeted previous crews.
>
> Gameplay shifts between side-scrolling travel sections in the vehicle, overhead shooting levels, and first-person boss encounters. Boss creatures possess a probability meter that must reach one hundred percent before they can be destroyed. Moby also leaves the vehicle to explore ruins on foot in side-scrolling areas, using jumps, kicks, and a firearm against enemies. The game ends if the player runs out of fuel or depletes the life meter.

**After:**

> Wurm features multiple genres across its gameplay modes. The story follows an underground expedition sent after earthquakes strike in 1999. Players direct the crew of an exploration vehicle commanded by Moby, who searches for four earlier vehicles and their lost crews, including Ziggy. Deep below, the crew confronts the Nonmalta Empire, ruled by Sogalz, which holds the King of the Underworld Empire of Dinamur hostage.
>
> Gameplay shifts between horizontally and vertically scrolling shooting sections in the vehicle, which changes between tank, hover, and aerial forms, and first-person cockpit battles against bosses. In cockpit battles, talking to the crew in the right order raises a Possibility Factor that improves the odds of destroying the monster. Moby also leaves the vehicle to explore on foot in side-scrolling areas, using jumps, kicks, and the Starlight Gun against enemies. Energy capsules restore fuel, and the game ends when the life meter is depleted.

**What was wrong and why it changed:** Corrected the 'probability meter must reach 100%' rule to the manual's Possibility Factor (odds, raised by crew talk); replaced the unsupported 'war between peaceful humanoids and a hostile empire' with the manual's Nonmalta Empire, Sogalz and the hostage King of Dinamur; replaced 'overhead' with vertically scrolling; removed the unconfirmed fuel game-over and 'ruins'; added vehicle forms and lost-crew search from the manual. Shortened the title in the first sentence to avoid an exclamation mark.

**Contradicted by NES evidence:**

- Probability meter must reach one hundred percent before bosses can be destroyed — The Possibility Factor represents the chance of destroying the monster and is raised by talking to the crew in the right order; reaching 100% gives the best odds, it is not required (manual p11 (image))

## WWF WrestleMania (`a6f98e57ffb45441`)

- **Classification:** substantive; error types: unsupported specific, wrong rule
- **Queue:** recheck (m32-rejected-edited)
- **Manual:** WWF Wrestlemania (USA); page images inspected: yes (p04, p05, p07, p09, p11)
- **Verification:** level D; remaining uncertainty: 'Temporarily' for the red anger state is an inference (the manual ties it to taking hits, not to a duration).

**Before:**

> Controlling one of six professional wrestlers, the player competes in matches inside the ring using strikes, running attacks, and bodyslams. Combatants cannot exit the ring, and turnbuckle leaps are limited to the bottom corners. Move sets differ somewhat across the roster, and only Hulk Hogan can bodyslam André the Giant. Taking heavy punishment causes a wrestler to turn red with anger, which temporarily boosts attack strength.
>
> Play modes include single exhibitions and tournaments. Exhibitions pit one player against the computer or another participant. In single-player tournaments, the chosen fighter must overcome the other five opponents to earn the championship. Group tournaments allow up to six players across fifteen round-robin bouts, awarding the belt to the best record or breaking ties by the quickest victory.

**After:**

> Controlling one of six professional wrestlers, the player competes in matches inside the ring using strikes, running attacks, and bodyslams. Turnbuckle leaps start from the bottom of the ring, and move sets differ somewhat across the roster; two of the wrestlers cannot bodyslam at all. Taking heavy punishment causes a wrestler to turn red with anger, which temporarily boosts attack strength.
>
> Play modes include single exhibitions and tournaments. Exhibitions pit one player against the computer or another participant. In single-player tournaments, the chosen fighter must overcome the other five opponents to earn the championship. Group tournaments allow up to six players across fifteen round-robin bouts, with the most wins deciding the winner and ties broken by the shortest average time to pin opponents.

**What was wrong and why it changed:** Removed encyclopedia-only claims (cannot exit the ring; only Hogan can bodyslam Andre), reworded the turnbuckle rule to the manual, added the manual-supported note that two wrestlers have no bodyslam, and fixed the tie-break to shortest average pin time.

**Contradicted by NES evidence:**

- Belt awarded to best record, ties by quickest victory — most wins; tie goes to the wrestler who pinned his five opponents in the shortest average time (not quickest single victory); the manual's victory screen names the winner (belt not stated for multiplayer). Fixed (manual p05 left (image): whoever wins the most matches wins; tie goes to the wrestler who pinned his five opponents in the shortest average time)

**Other sources checked:** https://www.hardcoregaming101.net/wwf-wrestlemania/; https://tasvideos.org/7934S

## WWF WrestleMania - Challenge (`89df74e7b275929c`)

- **Queue:** main (nes-native-untouched)

- **Verification:** level D; remaining uncertainty: Whether the eight-man tournament awards a championship, and which wrestlers the two-player team uses, could not be confirmed. The quoted name "You" is the manual's label for the generic wrestler, not a second-person address.

**Before:**

> Professional wrestling bouts take place in an isometric ring viewed from a high angle. Players select from a roster of nine competitors, which includes eight real-world performers and a generic wrestler designated as Yourself. Each competitor possesses an individual moveset. During contests, meters displayed on the ring apron track each wrestler's stamina. Depleting this stamina bar leaves a wrestler susceptible to being pinned for a loss.
>

**After:**

> Professional wrestling bouts take place in an isometric ring viewed from a high angle. Players select from a roster of nine competitors, which includes eight real-world performers and a generic wrestler with no real-world identity. Each competitor possesses an individual moveset, including power moves and attacks from the top of the cornerpost. During contests, meters displayed on the ring apron track each wrestler's stamina. Depleting this stamina bar leaves a wrestler susceptible to being pinned for a loss.
>
> Contest formats include singles bouts, tag team matches, and three-on-three Survivor Series elimination events, with tagging done from the team's corner. Wrestlers can leave the ring to rest but risk a count-out. An eight-man tournament for one player pits the player against all eight stars in succession, starting with Brutus "The Barber" Beefcake. Two players can wrestle each other or join forces as a team against four computer-controlled duos.

**What was wrong and why it changed:** Corrected the generic wrestler's name to 'You'; removed the unsupported partner-command feature, the title/belt rewards and the 'distinct versions of the generic character' detail; restated the tournament and two-player team modes per the manual; added manual-supported cornerpost moves, tagging, ring exits and count-outs. Editorial adjustment: the manual's generic wrestler is named "You"; reworded so the overview does not address the reader.

**Contradicted by NES evidence:**

- Nine competitors: eight real performers and a generic wrestler designated as Yourself — Eight WWF superstars plus a wrestler named 'You' in the manual; 'Yourself' is not the manual's name (manual p17 (image), ocr p02 and performance charts)
- Participants can prompt computer-controlled partners to strike opposing computer-controlled wrestlers inside and outside the ring — From the top of the cornerpost, B attacks the opponent's out-of-ring teammate and A+B attacks one's own partner; no partner-command feature is described (manual ocr Cornerpost Moves)

## Xenophobe (`4b11689be770a7dd`)

- **Classification:** rewrite; error types: other-version detail, wrong rule
- **Queue:** main (m32-audit-medium-risk)
- **Manual:** Xenophobe (USA); page images inspected: yes (p02, p03, p04, p05, p06, p07, p08, p09)
- **Verification:** level D; remaining uncertainty: The manual spells the slime-spitting Xeno both 'Snotterpiller' and 'Snotterpillar', so the text describes it without naming it. Whether pods appear in the NES version could not be checked against an NES-specific source; the claim was removed.

**Before:**

> Players control a character navigating multi-floor environments to eliminate hostile alien invaders before a countdown timer expires. Movement between different floors requires riding elevators. Hostile aliens evolve through multiple life stages, beginning as stationary pods that can hatch into creatures capable of clinging to players and draining their health. If unaddressed, these organisms mature into rolling attackers and eventually jumping, spitting threats.
>
> Surviving these locations involves collecting stronger weaponry and restorative health items alongside point-granting collectibles. Missions conclude when the time runs out, through activating a station self-destruct mechanism after defeating enemies, or by fully eradicating the alien presence to safely secure the base. The game supports two players.

**After:**

> Hostile alien life forms called Xenos are infesting derelict space stations and moon bases, and the player, as an Exterminator, beams aboard each one to destroy as many Xenos as fast as possible before the station self-destructs. Clearing enough of them earns a bonus and restores some Health; otherwise the station is declared overrun. The eight stations have one to four floors connected by elevators, and wall buttons warp the Exterminator to other rooms.
>
> Xenos include the Critter, which latches on and must be thrown off, the Laser Ball, the Giant Slime Amoeba, the bomb-dropping Spiderion and a slime-spitting lizard-like creature. Destroying certain Xenos earns stronger weapons such as the Laser Pistol, Lightning Gun, Smoke Gun and bombs, and pick-up objects include medicine and other items that restore Health. One or two players can play at the same time on a split screen. When all Health is gone, the game ends with no continue.

**What was wrong and why it changed:** Removed the arcade-derived pod/Rollerbaby life cycle and the player-activated self-destruct ending; rewrote from the NES manual's objective, station structure, Xeno roster, weapons, pick-ups, simultaneous two-player split screen and Health rules.

**Contradicted by NES evidence:**

- Missions end when time runs out, by activating a station self-destruct after defeating enemies, or by eradicating the aliens — The station self-destructs on its own; clearing enough Xenos in time declares it cleared (bonus, 200 Health), otherwise it is overrun. No player-activated self-destruct. (manual p04-p05 (images))

**Other sources checked:** https://www.honestgamers.com/4063/nes/xenophobe/game.html (no gameplay detail)

Encounters include giant Floating Fortresses, whose weapons ports fire heavily and whose core can be bombed, and Solbak, an enemy information system whose destruction temporarily weakens enemy attacks. Extra fighters are awarded at 20,000 and 60,000 points and for every additional 60,000 points. One or two players can take part.

**What was wrong and why it changed:** Replaced unsupported terrain list (rivers, mechanical structures), 'ground radar stations', hidden structures and extra-life items with NES manual details: forest borders, bomb-sight behavior, Floating Fortress core and weapons ports, Solbak, score-based extra fighters and the one- or two-player option.

**Other sources checked:** https://www.hardcoregaming101.net/xevious/; https://www.nintendolife.com/games/nes/xevious/review

## Yo! Noid (`62a3551ce546fa7d`)

- **Classification:** substantive; error types: wrong item effect, wrong name, invented detail, unsupported specific
- **Queue:** main (m32-audit-medium-risk)
- **Manual:** Yo! Noid (USA); page images inspected: yes (p04, p05, p06, p07)
- **Verification:** level D; remaining uncertainty: The 20,000-point extra life may be accurate but no NES-specific source confirmed it, so it was removed.

**Before:**

> Stopping chaos throughout New York City to earn a massive pizza reward serves as the main goal. The player guides the Noid, who uses a super yo-yo to strike enemies and open large scrolls containing rare power-ups or screen-clearing special attacks. Magic points gathered from smaller scrolls fuel these special abilities. Because the protagonist lacks a life meter, touching an adversary or running out of time causes the loss of a life, though gaining 20,000 points grants an extra life.

The player guides the Noid, who uses a yo-yo to strike enemies and open large scrolls containing symbols for magic spells that attack the hooligans. Magic power gathered by jumping through smaller scrolls fuels these spells. Because the protagonist lacks a life meter, touching an adversary or running out of time causes the loss of a life, and each round starts with 140 units of time.
>
> Most stages require traversal on foot across areas such as the Wharf, Central Park and the rooftops, but certain sections place the character on the HyperBoard skateboard, inside the Ornithopter flying machine or atop the bouncing Pizza Crusher. After every odd-numbered round, the Noid competes in a pizza-eating duel that serves as the boss battle.

**Contradicted by NES evidence:**

- Large scrolls contain rare power-ups or screen-clearing special attacks — Large scrolls give the symbol for a magic spell that attacks the hooligans; no other power-ups, 'screen-clearing' not stated. (manual p05 (image))
- Minigames like a Pizza Crusher stage inspired by advertisements — Pizza Crusher is one of the Noid's inventions, a bouncing pizza masher used across the rooftops, not a minigame; advertising inspiration unsupported. (manual p06 (image); indiegamerchick)

**Other sources checked:** https://indiegamerchick.com/tag/yo-noid/; https://www.honestgamers.com/8577/nes/yo-noid/review.html

## Yoshi (`56a169bb3a610105`)

- **Classification:** substantive; error types: wrong rule
- **Queue:** main (m32-audit-medium-risk)
- **Manual:** Yoshi (USA); page images inspected: yes (p02, p03, p04, p05, p06, p07, p08, p09)
- **Verification:** level D; remaining uncertainty: Manual scan is low resolution; small text was read from the images. Luigi and the eight-item column limit rest on MarioWiki's NES-specific statements.

**Before:**

> Players control Mario as falling enemies drop into four vertical columns to piece together eggshells and free trapped Yoshis. Operating beneath the play field, Mario rotates adjacent columns to align incoming creatures with matching monsters atop existing stacks, clearing them from the board. Each column holds up to eight items before surpassing the boundary line, which causes a game over. Catching enemies between the lower and upper halves of an eggshell encases the creatures and hatches a Yoshi, yielding larger bonuses based on the amount enclosed.
>
> Two single-player options provide distinct goals: A-Type continues indefinitely until a loss occurs, while B-Type tasks players with clearing the entire screen across rounds featuring larger starting piles.
