Matches end when one contestant empties their field or the opponent tops out.

**After:**

> Players control Mario as falling enemies drop into four vertical columns to piece together eggshells and free trapped Yoshis. Operating beneath the play field, Mario swaps pairs of adjacent columns to align incoming creatures with matching monsters atop existing stacks, clearing them from the board. Each column holds up to eight items before surpassing the boundary line, which causes a game over. Catching enemies between the lower and upper halves of an eggshell encases the creatures and hatches a Yoshi, yielding larger bonuses based on the amount enclosed.
>
> Two single-player options provide distinct goals: A-Type continues indefinitely until a loss occurs, while B-Type tasks players with clearing the entire screen across rounds featuring larger starting piles. A competitive two-player mode features simultaneous play on separate fields, with a second participant controlling Luigi. Each round ends when one contestant empties their field or the opponent tops out, and the first player to win three rounds takes the match.

**What was wrong and why it changed:** Changed 'rotates adjacent columns' to swapping pairs of adjacent columns; clarified that emptying the field or topping out decides a round and that the first to three wins takes the match.

**Other sources checked:** https://www.mariowiki.com/M%26Y

## Yoshi's Cookie (`24b117a0830fcb91`)

- **Classification:** substantive; error types: wrong name, unsupported specific, wrong rule
- **Queue:** main (m32-audit-medium-risk)
- **Manual:** Yoshi's Cookie (USA); page images inspected: yes (p03, p06, p07, p08)
- **Verification:** level D; remaining uncertainty: None material.

**Before:**

> Divided into a progressive single-player Action Mode and a split-screen competitive multiplayer mode, the game places participants inside a cookie factory assisting Mario and Yoshi. Players confront a rectangular grid populated with multiple varieties of baked treats. Using an on-screen cursor, the player shifts entire rows or columns horizontally and vertically to align identical items.
>
> The primary objective across each level is to eliminate every cookie from the playing field. When an entire line consists of matching treats, those pieces vanish. Additional cookies enter steadily from the top and right edges, expanding the grid until an overflow triggers a game over. A special piece shaped like Yoshi's head periodically appears to serve as a wild card, standing in for any standard treat to help clear lines.

**After:**

> Divided into a single-player game and a split-screen competitive VS. game for two players, the game features Mario and Yoshi. Players confront a rectangular grid populated with multiple varieties of baked treats. Using an on-screen cursor, the player shifts entire rows or columns horizontally and vertically to align identical items.
>
> The primary objective across each single-player stage is to eliminate every cookie from the playing field. When an entire line consists of matching treats, those pieces vanish. Additional cookies enter steadily from the top and right edges, expanding the grid until an overflow triggers a game over. In the single-player game, a special piece shaped like Yoshi's head periodically appears to serve as a wild card, standing in for any standard treat to help clear lines. In the VS. game, clearing lines fills a point meter, and the first player to fill it wins the game.

**What was wrong and why it changed:** Removed the non-NES name 'Action Mode' and the unsupported cookie-factory setting; limited the Yoshi Cookie wild card to the single-player game (it is not a joker in VS.); added the VS. point-meter win condition from the manual.

**Contradicted by NES evidence:**

- Progressive single-player 'Action Mode' — The NES manual calls it the 1-player (1P) game; 'Action Mode' is not an NES name. (manual p03, p06, p07 (images))

**Other sources checked:** https://www.nintendolife.com/reviews/vc/yoshis_cookie_nes

## Young Indiana Jones Chronicles, The (`fd4884c98d9412eb`)

- **Classification:** substantive; error types: wrong count, wrong rule, wrong name
- **Queue:** escalation (nes-native-untouched)
- **Manual:** Young Indiana Jones Chronicles, The (USA); page images inspected: yes (p05, p06, p07, p08, p09, p10, p11, p12, p13, p14, p15)
- **Verification:** level D; remaining uncertainty: The Germany dogfight stage is a flying stage, so 'side-scrolling platform stages' is a slight generalization.

**Before:**

> Eight levels spread across three settings make up the journey, taking players through Mexico, France, and Germany. Guiding Indiana Jones through side-scrolling platform stages, the player confronts conflicts during the Mexican Civil War and World War I. Indiana starts with only his whip and must overcome hostile forces, ultimately defeating a boss enemy at the conclusion of each level.
>
> Breaking open boxes reveals gold, various items, and alternative armaments such as guns, daggers, grenades, and dynamite. Picking up a new weapon replaces the current one. Collected items and weapons double as Indiana's health pool, causing him to lose an acquired possession each time an enemy strikes him. Stripped of all possessions, Indiana defends himself using only bare fists, and receiving another hit results in death.

**After:**

> Eight stages spread across three levels make up the journey, taking players through Mexico, France, and Germany. Guiding Indiana Jones through side-scrolling platform stages, the player confronts conflicts during the Mexican Civil War and World War I. Indiana starts with only his whip and must overcome hostile forces, ultimately defeating a boss enemy at the conclusion of each stage.
>
> Breaking open wooden crates reveals gold, various items, and alternative armaments such as guns, knives, grenades, and dynamite. Picking up a new weapon replaces the current one. Shield items and weapons double as Indiana's health: each time an enemy strikes him, he loses his shield item first and then his weapon. Stripped of both, Indiana defends himself using only bare fists, and receiving another hit costs a life.

**What was wrong and why it changed:** Eight levels changed to eight stages across three levels; bosses guard each stage; boxes changed to wooden crates and daggers to knives; health rule corrected to shield item, then weapon; death changed to losing a life.

**Contradicted by NES evidence:**

- Eight levels across three settings (Mexico, France, Germany) — Manual: three main levels (Mexico, France, Germany), each split into stages; 2+2+4 = eight stages with eight bosses (manual p05 (p.8), p10 (p.19))
- Boss at the end of each level — 'the exit to every stage is guarded by a Boss' (manual p05 (p.8))
- Boxes yield gold, items, guns, daggers, grenades and dynamite — Wooden crates; the weapons are whip, rock, knife, pistol, rifle, machine gun, grenade, dynamite (and bomb in the dogfight); 'Knife', not dagger (manual p07 (pp.12-13), p09 (pp.16-17))
- Collected items and weapons act as health; one possession is lost per hit — Only the shield item (first) and then the weapon are lost; support items and gold are not (manual p05 (p.9))

## Zanac (`bdc9dfed1b03db47`)

- **Classification:** substantive; error types: wrong rule, unsupported specific, invented detail
- **Queue:** main (m32-audit-medium-risk)
- **Manual:** Zanac (USA); page images inspected: yes (p02, p03, p04, p05, p06, p07, p08)

**Before:**

> Piloting the AFX-6502 Zanac starfighter, the player shoots through an armada of alien defenses to destroy the mechanical entity known as the System. This single-player scrolling shooter tasks the pilot with eliminating enemy aircraft, meteors, reconnaissance planes, and stationary fortress bosses comprising ground turrets. Mini-boss starships also appear, resisting standard attacks and shifting color as they sustain damage.
>

**After:**

> Piloting the AFX-6502 Zanac starfighter, the player shoots through an armada of alien defenses to destroy the mechanical entity known as the System. This single-player scrolling shooter tasks the pilot with eliminating enemy aircraft, launched rocks, reconnaissance planes, and ground fortresses whose cores must all be destroyed within a time limit while the scrolling stops. Large airborne objects also appear, driving back most standard attacks.
>
> The ship uses a primary rapid-fire cannon alongside a secondary specialty weapon. Boxes that change color as they take hits release power chips that strengthen the cannon, while numbered items cycle through or enhance eight specialty weapons, including directional projectiles and shields. The System's aggressiveness adapts automatically to the player's firing frequency, offensive patterns, and success against fortresses. The game spans twelve areas.

**What was wrong and why it changed:** Replaced fortress 'turrets' with cores and the time-limit rule; replaced color-shifting mini-boss starships with resistant large air objects (the color change belongs to Boxes); removed 'blue' and the speed/count upgrade specifics; replaced power-up collection with fortress success as an ALC factor; added the twelve areas.

**Contradicted by NES evidence:**

- Stationary fortress bosses comprising ground turrets — Fortresses launch attacks from several cores; the scroll stops and they must be destroyed within a time limit. 'Turrets' not stated. (manual p04, p07 (images))
- Mini-boss starships resist standard attacks and shift color as they take damage — Large-scale air objects resist and drive back most weapons; the color change belongs to the Box (changes color at the 4th hit). (manual p06, p07 (images))
- System adapts to firing frequency, offensive patterns and power-up collection — ALC adjusts to rapid-fire rate, pattern of attack, skill level, air object appearances and fortress destruction or failure; power-up collection not stated. (manual p04 (image))

> Protecting Earth from environmental ruin caused by the toxic Lord Contaminous serves as the primary goal of the adventure. > Protecting Earth from environmental ruin caused by the toxic Lord Contaminous serves as the primary goal of the adventure. The player controls Zen, an alien ninja hired by the Gordons, the galaxy's environmental watchdogs, to stop Contaminous, protect the Earth boy Jeremy and secure the Geocrystal, a gem with the power to save the world. Zen fights with his Photon-Stick.
>
> Four disaster stages can be tackled in any order, mixing side-view and diagonal-view action. - Zen, an alien eco-warrior initially sent to recover a buried geocrystal — Zen is hired by the Gordons as their enforcer; the Earth boy Jeremy discovered the Geocrystal, and Zen must save Jeremy and pocket the Geocrystal. 'Buried' and 'initially sent to recover' not stated. (manual p04, p05 (images/ocr))
- Zen is accompanied by Jeremy Baker and the Recycled Heroes — Jeremy is captured and must be rescued; surname not given. The Recycled Heroes are created in the Bonus Stage with the Recyclotron and yield bonus items; they do not accompany Zen. (manual p13 (image); ocr bonus stage)
- Three-quarter perspective with multidirectional scrolling across four disaster areas — Four stages, but some are side-view and some diagonal-view. (manual p06, p08, ocr p07)

> Zombie Nation features side-scrolling shoot 'em up play where players direct a giant floating disembodied head. **Contradicted by NES evidence:**

- ...and prevent widespread zombification — The nation has already been turned into zombies; the goal is to liberate the zombie population. (manual p03 (image); ocr introduction)
